_doc: Pro scenarios. Field reference: the _doc in scenarios_hs.json.

scenarios.title: Rookie Dinner
scenarios.text: The veterans 'invite' the rookies to cover the team dinner at a fancy steakhouse: forty players, a private room, and a menu with no prices on it at all.

choices.label: Pay for the whole thing
choices.result: The whole bill, on your card, with a straight face. It's painfully expensive, and the veterans love you for it for the rest of the season.

choices.label: Split it with the other rookies
choices.result: Split evenly with the other rookies, after a quick huddle by the coat check. It's fair and friendly, and the rookie class gets closer for it.

choices.label: Politely pass
choices.result: A polite pass, with an excuse about your budget. A couple of veterans give you the cold shoulder for a month, and one of them respects you for it.

scenarios.title: Agent Meeting
scenarios.text: Three agencies want to represent you, and each one has a pitch: a famous name with forty clients, a careful agent with six, and your own reflection in the mirror.

choices.label: Sign with the big agency
choices.result: The big agency, with the famous name and the glossy folder. Big plans, big promises, and you're one of forty clients from the first meeting.

choices.label: Hire a small, careful agent
choices.result: The small, careful agent, who returns every call within an hour. Fewer promises, much more attention, and a plan written on one page.

choices.label: Represent yourself
choices.result: Yourself, at the kitchen table, reading contracts at midnight. It saves money, costs a lot of sleep, and teaches you more than any agent would.

scenarios.title: Contract Talks
scenarios.text: Your agent says the team wants to talk about an extension before the season. The general manager has a number in mind, and so do you, and they're far apart.

choices.label: Push for top dollar
choices.result: Top dollar, and nothing less. The talks get tense, the general manager stops smiling, and it takes a month to reach a number you can both live with.

choices.label: Take a team-friendly deal
choices.result: A team-friendly deal, signed in a week. Teammates notice, management notices, and the locker room thinks a little more of you.

choices.label: Wait until the season ends
choices.result: Wait until the season ends, and bet on yourself. Your agent sighs, the club shrugs, and every practice becomes a negotiation.

choices.label: Let the fans make your case
choices.result: Your public profile does the negotiating for you. Fans ask the club about you on every broadcast, and the offer gets better by Friday.

scenarios.title: Postgame Questions
scenarios.text: After a missed kick last week, the reporters are waiting at your locker, five of them, with their phones out and the same question ready to go.

choices.label: Own the miss
choices.result: Straight answers about the miss, no excuses, looking at each reporter in turn. It earns respect in the room, and the story dies by Wednesday.

choices.label: Blame the conditions
choices.result: The wind, the hold, the field: you blame the conditions. The quote doesn't land well at all, and {holder} hears about it before practice.

choices.label: Decline to talk
choices.result: No comment, today. You skip the circus, and the reporters write that you 'declined to talk', which follows you for a few days.

choices.label: Turn it into a rallying cry
choices.result: Your answer turns into a rallying cry, about the whole unit having each other's backs. The locker room plays your quote all week.

scenarios.title: Family and Finances
scenarios.text: Relatives keep asking for loans now that you're a pro: a cousin's car, an uncle's business, a great-aunt you've never met who has a very specific number in mind.

choices.label: Set a budget with an advisor
choices.result: A budget, built with an advisor, with one yearly amount for family help. Clear rules mean fewer awkward calls, and {parent} approves.

choices.label: Help everyone out
choices.result: Help for everyone who asks. It's generous and stressful, and by spring you realize you've stopped saying no to anything at all.

choices.label: Say no to everyone
choices.result: No, to everyone, every time. It's peace for your wallet and tension at every holiday, and {sibling} stops calling for a while.

scenarios.title: Team Hospital Visit
scenarios.text: The team is visiting the children's hospital this week: an afternoon of games, signed footballs and a ward full of kids who have been looking forward to it for a month.

choices.label: Stay all afternoon
choices.result: The whole afternoon, ward by ward, until the nurses chase you out. You'll remember one boy's face forever, and so will he remember yours.

choices.label: Join for the group photo
choices.result: A quick, kind visit and the group photo. You sign a few balls and leave on time, and a mother thanks you in the elevator.

choices.label: Skip it for treatment
choices.result: Skipped, for extra treatment on your hip. You get the recovery time, and you see the photos of everyone else the next day.

scenarios.title: Holder Chemistry
scenarios.text: {holder} wants extra time to work on timing this week: an hour after every practice, just the two of you and a bag of balls, in the cold.

choices.label: Extra reps every day
choices.result: Extra reps every day, snap, hold, kick, until the timing is perfect. By Friday you could do it with your eyes closed, and {holder} is grinning.

choices.label: Take a recovery day instead
choices.result: A recovery day instead, and an apology to {holder}. Your leg feels brand new by Sunday, and {holder} understands, mostly.

choices.label: Study the opponent's stadium
choices.result: The opponent's stadium, studied together on film for two nights. You both know every gust in that building before the bus leaves.

scenarios.title: Cold Snap
scenarios.text: The forecast says single digits and wind for Sunday. The equipment staff is already unpacking heated benches, and the veterans are wearing shorts to make a point.

choices.label: Practice outside all week
choices.result: Outside, every day, in the freezing wind. Your leg learns the cold, slowly, and so do your fingers, painfully, by Thursday.

choices.label: Practice indoors
choices.result: Indoors, warm and accurate all week. You feel great on Thursday, and not at all ready for the wind on Sunday.

choices.label: Ask the equipment staff for help
choices.result: The equipment staff, asked for help. Heated capes, the right cleats and a trick with hand warmers that you'll use for years.

scenarios.title: Trade Rumors
scenarios.text: Sports radio says the team might trade for another kicker before the deadline. The host has a 'source', and your phone has fourteen messages about it.

choices.label: Tune out the noise
choices.result: Kick, sleep, repeat, and no radio in the car. The noise fades by the deadline, and nobody gets traded for anybody.

choices.label: Ask the coach directly
choices.result: {coach}, asked directly in the hallway. You're the guy, the coach says, for now. 'For now' stays in your head all week.

choices.label: Read every rumor online
choices.result: Every rumor, read online, every single night until two. It's all you think about, and your practices show it clearly by Thursday.

scenarios.title: The Folder Follows You
scenarios.text: Your first month as a pro, the team's player-development director calls you in. Your college record followed you here, and the club wants to know what kind of player it signed.

authoring.premise: The team's player-development director calls the rookie in: the college record followed you here.
authoring.note: Reads the college wrong-path flags (planned_pro_reads in tools/college_graph/college_design.json).

choices.label: Ask for a weekly check-in
choices.result: You suggest a weekly check-in yourself and hand over your college coach's number. The director writes it in the file: rookie asked for structure.

choices.label: Say college is over
choices.result: You say the folder belongs to a different person and you'd rather be judged on what you do here. The director says that's fair. The file stays open.

choices.label: Bring your own copy
choices.result: You bring a copy of your college record with your own notes in the margins: what happened and what changed. The director keeps it and tells {coach} to stop worrying.
choices.lock_text: having already faced your record honestly

scenarios.title: The Old Crowd
scenarios.text: Three guys you used to run with in college show up in your new city on a Friday with a hotel suite booked and a plan for your first paycheck. Your phone has been buzzing since noon.

authoring.premise: Old college running buddies show up in your new city with a hotel suite and a plan for your first paycheck.
authoring.note: Reads the college wrong-path flags (planned_pro_reads in tools/college_graph/college_design.json).

choices.label: Dinner, then home
choices.result: You buy them dinner, laugh about the old days and are home by ten. They call you boring. You're at the facility at seven.

choices.label: Don't answer
choices.result: You let the phone buzz and stay in. It's lonely, and it's the first weekend in a while you don't regret anything.

choices.label: Go out with them
choices.result: You go out. Saturday's photos end up online, a team official calls on Monday, and {coach} hears about it before you're in the building.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Symposium
scenarios.text: The league's rookie symposium wants a player to speak about a mistake from college and what came after. The team's player-development director thinks your story is the one the rookies need to hear.

authoring.premise: The league's rookie symposium wants a player to talk about a college mistake and what came after.
authoring.note: Reads the college wrong-path flags (planned_pro_reads in tools/college_graph/college_design.json).

choices.label: Tell the whole story
choices.result: You stand in front of two hundred rookies and tell them about your worst college year without making yourself the hero. Afterward, a line of players waits to talk to you.

choices.label: Tell the safe version
choices.result: The version with the details smoothed over. It goes fine, the room claps politely, and nobody waits to talk to you afterward.

choices.label: Say no thanks
choices.result: No thanks, you'd rather not relive it in front of a room. The director understands and asks someone else, and you wonder about it later.

scenarios.title: The Reporter's Question
scenarios.text: At your first open locker room, a beat reporter skips the kicking questions and asks about your college record: 'Do you think the stories about you are fair?'

authoring.premise: At your first open locker room, a reporter skips the kicking questions and asks about your college record.
authoring.note: Reads the college wrong-path flags (planned_pro_reads in tools/college_graph/college_design.json).

choices.label: Answer it straight
choices.result: You say the stories are true, you're not proud of them and you'd rather be judged on what comes next. The quote runs in full, and it's the least dramatic thing in the paper.

choices.label: Say no comment
choices.result: You say you're only taking football questions. The reporter writes that you 'declined to address' your past, which reads worse than anything you could have said.

choices.label: Push back
choices.result: You say the stories were overblown and the reporter should do some homework. It's the most-shared clip of the week, and {coach} asks you to stop by the office.

scenarios.title: Rookie Camp
scenarios.text: Camp opens with four kickers on the roster and one job. The special teams coordinator has called you by the wrong name twice, and {coach} hasn't called you anything at all.

authoring.premise: Camp opens with four kickers on the roster and one job. The veteran special teams coordinator calls you by the wrong name twice.

choices.label: Be the first one on the field
choices.result: You're stretching on the field at six every morning before the trainers unlock the door. By the second week, {coach} knows your name and uses it.

choices.label: Learn the room before the field
choices.result: You spend the first week listening: who the veterans trust, which snapper the coaches like, where the rookies sit at lunch. It's slow, and nothing in that locker room surprises you after it.

choices.label: Kick like it's already yours
choices.result: You walk in like the job is yours and kick like it too. Two veterans love it. One of the other kickers stops talking to you entirely.

choices.label: Do what got you here
choices.result: You've been in rooms where nobody expected anything from you. You kick, you say little, and you keep a notebook of every correction. {coach} borrows the notebook in week two.
choices.lock_text: having trained with a pro or rebuilt a reputation before

scenarios.title: The Kicker You're Replacing
scenarios.text: The kicker whose job you're taking has been here eleven years. His locker is next to yours, and he can make your first month easy or impossible.

authoring.premise: The kicker whose job you're taking has been here eleven years. He can make your first month easy or impossible.

choices.label: Ask him to teach you
choices.result: You ask him straight out how he lasted eleven years. He stares at you for a while, then starts talking and doesn't stop for an hour.

choices.label: Compete and keep your distance
choices.result: You stay polite and give him nothing. Every kick in camp becomes a quiet contest, and both of you get better.

choices.label: Freeze him out
choices.result: You sit with the younger players, laugh at the right jokes about his age and let the room decide who's in charge. You win the room. You also notice who stopped laughing.

scenarios.title: Your First Real Payday
scenarios.text: Your first real paycheck lands, and it has more zeros than {parent} made in a year. Your phone starts buzzing before you've finished reading the number.

authoring.premise: Your first real paycheck lands, and it has more zeros than {parent} made in a year.

choices.label: Save most of it
choices.result: You put most of it into an account you promise not to touch and buy one thing: a mattress that isn't from a dorm. It's dull, and you sleep very well.

choices.label: Spend it like you earned it
choices.result: You buy the car, the watch and dinner for the whole rookie class. It feels incredible for about a month.

choices.label: Pay off {parent}'s debts
choices.result: {parent} refuses twice when you ask for the number on every bill, then gives in the third time. The calls home sound different after that: lighter, and a lot longer.

choices.label: Split it the way you always have
choices.result: You do what you did with your first paycheck at sixteen, just with more zeros: a third saved, a third home, a third yours. It's an old habit, and it holds.
choices.lock_text: having handled your first paychecks wisely

scenarios.title: Rookie Duties
scenarios.text: The veterans hand the rookies a list: breakfast for the unit every Friday, carrying the pads, a song on the team plane. Most of it is fun. One item, a stunt in a hotel hallway, isn't.

authoring.premise: The veterans hand the rookies a list: breakfast for the unit every Friday, the luggage, the karaoke on the team plane. Some of it is fun. One item isn't.

choices.label: Do the list, skip the stunt
choices.result: You do every chore with a grin and tell the captain, privately, you're not doing the hallway stunt. He shrugs and crosses it off.

choices.label: Do all of it
choices.result: You do everything on the list, the stunt included. The veterans cheer, a rookie gets hurt doing the same one, and the coaches hold a meeting about it.

choices.label: Turn the song into a show
choices.result: You go all in on the plane song, with costumes. It's the best one in years, and the veterans stop giving you the worst chores.

choices.label: Fix the list with the captain
choices.result: You ran this kind of tradition in college, so you sit down with the captain and rewrite the stunt into something nobody gets hurt doing. It's a quiet win.
choices.lock_text: having run freshman traditions in college

scenarios.title: The Long Snapper
scenarios.text: The long snapper has been in the league fourteen years and has opinions about everything, including your warmup, your shoes and the way you say 'hold'.

authoring.premise: The long snapper has been in the league fourteen years and has opinions about everything, including your warmup.

choices.label: Listen to every opinion
choices.result: You let him talk. Half of it is nonsense. The other half fixes a timing problem you didn't know you had.

choices.label: Push back on the warmup
choices.result: Your warmup isn't changing, you tell him, and you don't blink. He respects it more than you expected and starts timing his snaps to your count by the end of the week.

choices.label: Keep it professional
choices.result: You say thanks, keep it short and do your own thing. The snaps are fine. The friendship never quite starts.

scenarios.title: Curfew on the Road
scenarios.text: First road trip. Curfew is eleven, and the veterans say curfew is for rookies who want to stay rookies. Three of them are already in the lobby.

authoring.premise: First road trip. Curfew is eleven, and the veterans say curfew is for rookies who want to stay rookies.
authoring.note: Pressure scene: clean no. The wrong choice sets pro strike stayed_out_pro.

choices.label: Stay in
choices.result: You order room service, watch film and are asleep by ten-thirty. At breakfast you're the only rookie who isn't wearing sunglasses.

choices.label: Go to dinner, back by eleven
choices.result: Dinner with the veterans is loud and fun, and you laugh at every story. You leave before dessert. A couple of them call you a rookie; a couple of them nod.

choices.label: Go out with them
choices.result: You go out and come back at three. Bed check was at eleven, and your name is on the list {coach} reads out at breakfast.

scenarios.title: Where You Live
scenarios.text: Half the roster lives in the same glass tower downtown, with a rooftop pool and a doorman who knows everyone's name. The rent is a quarter of your salary.

authoring.premise: Half the roster lives in the same glass tower downtown. The rent is a quarter of your salary.

choices.label: Rent something modest
choices.result: You rent a two-bedroom twenty minutes from the facility, above a bakery. The teammates call it 'the bakery'. You save more in a month than some of them save in a year, and the commute is short.

choices.label: Move into the tower
choices.result: The lease in the tower gets signed on a Tuesday. The pool parties are legendary and the elevators are full of teammates, and the rent comes out of every check like a tax.

choices.label: Room with a teammate
choices.result: Splitting a place with another rookie is cheaper and louder than you planned. You never eat dinner alone, and you learn more about him than you ever wanted to.

scenarios.title: Homesick in {town}
scenarios.text: Nobody in {town} knows your name yet. Practice ends at four, the apartment is very quiet on Tuesday nights, and the only voice you hear after dinner is the television.

authoring.premise: Nobody in {town} knows your name yet, and the apartment is very quiet on Tuesday nights.

choices.label: Call home every night
choices.result: You call home every night for a week. {parent} starts saving up stories for you like he used to before school, and {sibling} grabs the phone at the end to complain about homework.

choices.label: Make the city yours
choices.result: You pick one new neighborhood every Tuesday and walk it until dinner. By October, {town} has a coffee shop that knows your order.

choices.label: Bury it in work
choices.result: Every quiet night ends in the film room. You become the best-prepared rookie on the roster and the loneliest one, and the cleaning crew starts saying goodnight to you.

choices.label: Keep the Sunday call
choices.result: You kept the Sunday call through four years of college, and you keep it now. The first Sunday in {town}, {sibling} answers and talks for an hour.
choices.lock_text: having promised to call home every week

scenarios.title: The Practice Squad Friend
scenarios.text: The receiver you've eaten lunch with since camp gets cut on a Tuesday morning. At noon he's still sitting in his car in the players' lot.

authoring.premise: The receiver you've been eating lunch with since camp gets cut on a Tuesday morning. He's still in the parking lot at noon.

choices.label: Sit in the car with him
choices.result: You knock on the window and sit in the passenger seat for an hour. You don't say much. He drives away a little steadier.

choices.label: Make a call for him
choices.result: You call a coach you know at another club and say the receiver's name twice. He gets a workout the next week.

choices.label: Leave him alone
choices.result: You walk past to your own car. It's not your business, and it could be you next year. You think about it the whole drive home.

scenarios.title: Meeting the Owner
scenarios.text: The owner throws a party for the rookies at his house and spends twenty minutes telling you exactly what kickers are worth, which is not much.

authoring.premise: The owner throws a party for the rookies at his house and spends twenty minutes telling you what kickers are worth.

choices.label: Smile and agree
choices.result: You smile, agree and get a second drink of lemonade. He likes you. You feel slightly worse about yourself on the drive home.

choices.label: Make him laugh
choices.result: Kickers are the only players who show up every week without hurting anyone, you tell him. He laughs harder than you expected and remembers your name all season.

choices.label: Tell him he's wrong
choices.result: Politely, and with numbers, you explain why he's wrong. The room goes quiet, his wife changes the subject, and {coach} has heard all about it by Monday morning.

scenarios.title: The Quote
scenarios.text: You said something careless to a beat reporter about the kicker you replaced, half a joke, and by morning it's the headline on the team's biggest fan site, with his photo beside yours.

authoring.premise: You said something careless to a beat reporter about the veteran you replaced, and it's the headline.

choices.label: Apologize to his face
choices.result: You find him in the weight room and apologize, no excuses. He accepts it more gracefully than you would have, and the room watches you both walk out together.

choices.label: Say it was taken out of context
choices.result: Out of context, you tell another reporter. The original reporter posts the full recording an hour later, and now the story is that you said it twice.

choices.label: Wait for it to pass
choices.result: A week of silence lets it blow over online. The veterans remember it longer, and for a month nobody saves you a seat at lunch.

choices.label: Handle it the way you learned to
choices.result: You've done this before. You call the reporter back, own the quote, and apologize to the veteran before lunch. It's over by dinner.
choices.lock_text: having been through a public mistake before

scenarios.title: Your First Autograph Line
scenarios.text: A kid in a jersey with your number on it is first in line at the autograph table. You didn't know they made your number.

authoring.premise: A kid in a jersey with your number on it is first in line. You didn't know they made your number.

choices.label: Take your time with him
choices.result: The jersey, the ball and his little brother's hat all get signed, and you ask about his own team. The line behind him grows, and nobody seems to mind.

choices.label: Ask his parents for a photo
choices.result: His parents say yes to a photo, and you post it with his first name only. It's the best-liked thing you've ever posted, and his coach prints it for the team.

choices.label: Keep the line moving
choices.result: You sign, smile and keep the line moving like the team's staff asked. Two hundred people get an autograph, and none of them get a moment.

scenarios.title: Rookie Year Ends
scenarios.text: The season's over, and the locker room empties in one afternoon: duffel bags, handshakes, a line at the equipment window. By dinner you're alone in {town} with no idea what pros do in the offseason.

authoring.premise: The season's over. The locker room empties in an afternoon, and you realize you have no idea what pros do in the offseason.

choices.label: Copy three veterans' summers
choices.result: Three veterans give you three different summers, and you steal the best piece of each. It's the most organized offseason you've ever had, and {holder} texts you a lifting plan every Monday.

choices.label: Go home for a month
choices.result: A month at home doing nothing: {parent}'s cooking, your old bedroom, {best_friend} on the porch every night. You come back rested, a little out of shape and happier than you've been since the draft.

choices.label: Train like you're still in camp
choices.result: You never stop. Six days a week, all summer. By August your leg is the strongest it's been, and you're tired before camp starts.

scenarios.title: The Second-Year Wall
scenarios.text: Year two. The novelty is gone, the scouting reports on you are thicker, the rookie snapper calls you 'sir', and your legs remember every kick of last season when you get out of bed.

authoring.premise: Year two. The novelty is gone, the scouting reports on you are thicker, and your legs feel every one of last season's kicks.

choices.label: Change something small
choices.result: You change one thing, a half-step in your approach, and chart it for a month. It takes, and it surprises the coaches watching you.

choices.label: Change nothing
choices.result: You decide last year's routine earned you this year, and you keep every piece of it. Some weeks it works perfectly. Some weeks it's just a routine.

choices.label: Take on a rookie
choices.result: {backup}, the new rookie specialist, gets your lunch table, your notes and your Tuesday nights, the way someone once gave you theirs. It costs you time, and it makes the room yours.

scenarios.title: Your Story, Secondhand
scenarios.text: A college teammate calls from his rookie symposium: they told a story about a player who owned his mistakes and came back, and it sounded a lot like you.

authoring.premise: A former teammate from college calls from his rookie symposium: they told a story about someone who sounds a lot like you.
authoring.note: College callback scene: opens only for players with a college comeback; pairs with pro_rookie_symposium.

choices.label: Tell him the real version
choices.result: The parts that didn't make the speech come out: the bad nights, the early workouts, the people who wouldn't look at you. He goes quiet, then thanks you.

choices.label: Say they meant someone else
choices.result: They must have meant someone else, you say, and change the subject. It's easier than talking about it, and the story sits with you all week.

choices.label: Call the people who helped
choices.result: You hang up and call the coach who gave you the chance. The coach doesn't say much, and doesn't need to.

authoring.premise: Three weeks of misses in practice and the coaches have stopped talking to you about it, which is worse.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15 weeks). Locks open with experience (kick_slumps, age).

authoring.premise: {coach} watches your warmup with folded arms and doesn't say a word.
You're inactive this week. Your name is on the board, and your helmet is in your locker.
authoring.note: Every engine flag is sticky from high school, so the present-state check is needed.

authoring.premise: You're active again. The kicker who replaced you is clearing out his stall.
You haven't missed in a month, and everyone wants to talk about it except you.

scenarios.title: Don't Talk About It
scenarios.text: The specialists have a superstition: nobody says the streak out loud. A rookie just said it at lunch, loudly, with the whole table listening, and the snapper has put down his fork.

authoring.premise: The specialists have a superstition: nobody says the streak out loud. A rookie just said it.

choices.label: Laugh and reassure him
choices.result: Laughing, you tell the rookie it's fine. The room relaxes, the snapper picks up his fork, and the streak goes on.

choices.label: Change absolutely nothing
choices.result: Your routine stays exactly the same, down to the socks, the parking spot and the brand of gum. The specialists approve in total silence.

choices.label: Make the rookie buy lunch
choices.result: Lunch for the specialists, every day for a week, on the rookie. It becomes a tradition, and he takes it well.

scenarios.title: The National List
scenarios.text: Your name is on the national list for the league's best kicker, and the team's PR staff has eleven interview requests on a whiteboard, color-coded by urgency.

authoring.premise: Your name is on the national list for the league's best kicker, and the team's PR staff has eleven requests for you.

choices.label: Do all eleven
choices.result: All eleven, in a week. Your face is everywhere, you say the same three things forty times, and you sleep badly.

choices.label: Pick three and do them well
choices.result: Three interviews, chosen carefully and done well. One of them becomes the definitive piece about you, the one people still quote.

choices.label: Do none and keep kicking
choices.result: None at all. You keep kicking, the PR staff sighs and erases the whiteboard, and the list says what it says without your help.

scenarios.title: The Skills Contest
scenarios.text: The league invites you to the long-distance contest at the all-star week: a stadium, a television audience, and nine of the strongest legs in the league.

authoring.premise: The league invites you to the long-distance contest at the all-star week.
authoring.note: kick_challenge (competition) per the gameplay handoff.

choices.label: Train for it like a playoff
choices.result: Two weeks of training for one contest. You go, compete hard, and come home with a trophy shaped like a goalpost.

choices.label: Go for the fun
choices.result: The week, spent with kickers from every club: dinners, card games, stories. You finish fourth and have the best time of anyone.

choices.label: Decline and rest your leg
choices.result: A polite decline, and your leg gets a week of rest. The contest happens without you, and you watch it from your couch, cheering.

authoring.premise: The afternoon talk show has a segment called 'Cut the Kicker', and your {parent} listens to it every day.
Your foot won't swing through the ball in practice. Not tired, not hurt, just stuck.

scenarios.title: The Coach for Hire
scenarios.text: A private kicking coach who rebuilt three pro careers offers you his whole offseason: his field, his methods, his famous temper. The price is a number your agent repeats twice.

authoring.premise: A private coach who rebuilt three pro kickers offers you his offseason, for a price.

choices.label: Hire him for the summer
choices.result: The summer belongs to him: brutal drills at dawn, video at night, a temper that softens by July. Your leg feels new by August, and you've never been so tired.

choices.label: Stay with the club's staff
choices.result: The club's staff knows your body, so you stay. It's less glamorous and steady, and the trainers quietly appreciate the vote of confidence.

choices.label: Take most of the summer off
choices.result: Most of the summer, off: lake, family, sleep. You come back rested, a little rusty, and happier than you've been in a long time.

choices.label: Check his record first
choices.result: Two of his former clients, called before you decide. Both rave about the results and warn you about the temper. You hire him with your eyes open, and it shows.
choices.lock_text: having checked out trainers before

authoring.premise: {coach} plays every miss of your season back to back in an empty meeting room.
Your plant leg is sore in a way the trainers can't find on a scan.

scenarios.title: The Backup Wants Your Job
scenarios.text: {backup} is on the practice squad and has been kicking very well where the coaches can see: long ones after practice, clean ones in team drills, and a few reporters have noticed.

authoring.premise: {backup} is on the practice squad and has been kicking very well where the coaches can see.

choices.label: Kick with {backup}
choices.result: You ask {backup} to share your warmups. It makes you both better, and it makes the coaches' decision harder, which is fine.

choices.label: Out-work {backup}
choices.result: Every day for a month, you stay later than {backup}. The coaches notice the hours more than the kicks, and {backup} starts leaving earlier, which tells you something.

choices.label: Let the coaches decide
choices.result: The practice squad isn't your problem, you decide. Your kicking stays the same, and so does the whispering, and {backup} stops saying good morning.

scenarios.title: The New Holder Midseason
scenarios.text: {holder} is hurt, and the replacement holder is a backup quarterback who has never held for a kick. The quarterback has soft hands, a nervous laugh and four days before Sunday.

authoring.premise: {holder} is hurt, and the replacement holder is a backup quarterback who has never held for a kick.

choices.label: Teach the new holder
choices.result: You stay after practice every day with the backup quarterback until the laces spin right. By Friday the holds are clean.

choices.label: Ask for the punter instead
choices.result: The punter has held before, you point out to {coach}. The coach agrees, the punter shrugs, and the relieved quarterback buys you lunch the next day.

choices.label: Visit {holder}
choices.result: You visit {holder} in the training room and bring the new holder along for a lesson. Two holders and a kicker in one cramped room, laughing.

scenarios.title: The Incentive Clause
scenarios.text: Your contract pays a bonus if you hit ninety percent this season, and your agent keeps texting you the math: where you are, what's left, what one miss would mean.

authoring.premise: Your contract pays a bonus if you hit 90 percent this season, and your agent keeps texting you the math.

choices.label: Ask your agent to stop
choices.result: No more math, please, you text back. You'll find out at the end of the season, and the next three months are quieter.

choices.label: Chase the number
choices.result: The number goes on your locker, and you chase it every practice. It's motivating, and some nights it's all you can think about.

choices.label: Forget the bonus
choices.result: Forgotten, on purpose, and the agent's texts go unread. If it comes, it comes, and you kick more freely than you have in years.

scenarios.title: The Kicker Brought In
scenarios.text: The club signs a kicker with a bigger leg and a lower salary and puts him at the locker next to yours. He's polite, twenty-three, and kicks sixty-yarders in warmups for fun.

authoring.premise: The club signs a kicker with a bigger leg and a lower salary, and puts him at the locker next to yours.
authoring.note: Prime-age version; PRO_133 is the veteran version.

choices.label: Out-prepare him
choices.result: Every day, better prepared than him. He has the leg; you have the habits. By October the coaches have noticed which one matters.

choices.label: Get to know him
choices.result: Lunch, then dinner, then a friendship. He's nervous and decent, and you both kick better without the tension in the room.

choices.label: Ask {coach} the plan
choices.result: The plan, asked for straight out in the hallway. {coach}'s answer is honest: it's an open competition. It stings, and it helps to know.

authoring.premise: Every kick in practice now feels like a negotiation.

scenarios.title: The Kick Everyone Saw
scenarios.text: A clip of your practice-field trick shot, the ball off the crossbar and into a trash can forty yards away, goes around the league overnight. Your phone has two hundred new messages.

authoring.premise: A clip of you in a practice-field trick shot goes around the league.
authoring.note: Practice clip only; no game result.

choices.label: Make a few more
choices.result: You film a series with the specialists. It's fun, the club's social media team loves it, and the coaches don't.

choices.label: Let it be one clip
choices.result: A thank-you post, and that's all. The clip fades in a week, the coaches never mention it, and you're a little sorry you didn't enjoy it more.

choices.label: Use it for charity
choices.result: You turn the clip into a charity challenge: a donation for every kid who sends in their own trick shot.

scenarios.title: The Bad Week
scenarios.text: You snapped at {holder} in practice, walked past {coach} without a word and skipped the team meal. It's Wednesday, and it's been that kind of week.

authoring.premise: You snapped at {holder}, ignored {coach} and skipped the team meal. It's been that kind of week.

choices.label: Apologize to {holder}
choices.result: A real apology to {holder} before practice, no excuses. The holds are better that afternoon, and {holder} buys you a coffee.

choices.label: Tell {coach} what's going on
choices.result: What's actually going on comes out in {coach}'s office: sleep, family, the pressure. The coach listens and gives you a lighter week.

choices.label: Take one night completely off
choices.result: One night, completely off: no film, no phone, no football, just a long walk and a bad movie. It resets you, and Thursday is a better day.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: Prove It
scenarios.text: It's the last year of your rookie deal, and the front office wants to see one more season before it talks numbers. Your agent says the word 'prove' three times in one phone call.

authoring.premise: It's the last year of your rookie deal, and the front office wants to see one more season before they talk.

choices.label: Put your head down
choices.result: No contract talk, no reading, just kicking. Your agent handles the rest, and the season feels lighter for it, until the last month.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what they need
choices.result: {coach} gives you an honest answer in the hallway: two things, both fixable, neither about your leg. You fix them both by midseason, quietly.

choices.label: Push for a deal now
choices.result: An extension before the season, your agent asks. The club says no, politely, and you spend the season wondering if asking was a mistake.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: The Payday
scenarios.text: This is the contract that could set up your family for life, if you earn it this season. Your agent has a number in mind, and so does the club, and they're far apart.

authoring.premise: This is the contract that sets up your family for life, if you earn it this season.

choices.label: Make the season undeniable
choices.result: Every practice counts, every rep, every film session. Nothing about this season will be an accident, and you're exhausted and proud by December.

choices.label: Let your agent do the talking
choices.result: Every contract conversation goes to your agent, and you keep your head on kicking. It works, mostly, though you check your phone after every practice.

choices.label: Talk it through at home
choices.result: A long evening at home, talking it through. Their calm becomes your calm, and you sleep better for the rest of the season.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: One More
scenarios.text: At thirty-six, the next contract is one year at a time, and everyone in the building knows it, including the twenty-two-year-old kicker on the practice squad.

authoring.premise: At your age, the next contract is one year at a time, and everyone in the building knows it.

choices.label: Earn the next year every day
choices.result: Every practice treated as the interview it is. The coaches notice the veteran who never takes a rep off, and so does the rookie.

choices.label: Talk numbers honestly
choices.result: Your agent and you, talking numbers honestly: one year, fair money, and an out if your body says so. It's a calm conversation.

choices.label: Talk it over at home
choices.result: One more, you both say at the kitchen table, and you both mean it completely. {love_interest} squeezes your hand and doesn't let go.

authoring.premise: The club wants you back. Your agent wants to wait for the market.

scenarios.title: The Hometown Discount
scenarios.text: The club offers less than the market and asks you to take it because 'you're family here'. The general manager says it twice, and puts his hand on your shoulder the second time.

authoring.premise: The club offers less than the market, and asks you to take it because you're family here.

choices.label: Take the discount
choices.result: The discount, accepted. The club remembers it, and so does the locker room, and you never quite know if it was generous or foolish.

choices.label: Meet in the middle
choices.result: The middle ground, found by your agent over two weeks of calls. Everyone is a little unhappy and fine, which your agent says is how you know it's fair.

choices.label: Test the market next spring
choices.result: Next spring's open market, it is. You kick like it all year, and every practice feels like an audition for twenty-nine other clubs.

scenarios.title: The Holdout Talk
scenarios.text: Your agent slides the club's offer across a restaurant table: less than a kicker in your division got last spring, with a pay cut in year two. 'We hold out,' your agent says. 'You stay home from camp until they pay you what you're worth.'

authoring.premise: Your agent says the only way to get paid is to stay home from camp.
authoring.note: A temptation, not a mechanic: the game has no holdouts. Holding firm costs retention and the coach.

choices.label: Sign it and say why
choices.result: You sign, then tell your agent you'd rather kick for a fair number than sit at home waiting for a better one. Your agent calls it leaving money on the table. {coach} calls it the best news of the week.

choices.label: Hold out
choices.result: You stay home when camp opens. The club fines you every day, talk radio calls you greedy, and two weeks later you sign for a little more and walk into a locker room that moved on without you.

choices.label: Call the general manager yourself
choices.result: You call the general manager directly, which agents hate. You get a better guarantee in year two and an agent who sulks for a month.

choices.label: Ask for the honest read
choices.result: The agent you hired for honesty admits the offer is fair for a kicker and a holdout would cost more than it gains. You sign, and you don't regret it.

scenarios.title: Starting Over
scenarios.text: The last club let you go at the end of camp: a ten-minute meeting, a plastic bag for your cleats and a security guard who walked you to the parking lot. Ten days later you're in a stranger's locker room, and the kicker you're replacing still has his name above the stall.

choices.label: Learn every name by Friday

choices.result: You keep your head down, kick until the trainers send you in and let the work introduce you. It's lonely. It's also the cleanest practice week you've had in a year.

choices.label: Call {parent} before the first practice
choices.result: You call {parent} from the hotel parking lot. He doesn't ask what went wrong; he asks what the new place smells like. You laugh for the first time in ten days.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what they heard
choices.result: You've rebuilt a reputation before. On day one you walk into {coach}'s office and ask what they heard about you at the last club, and you answer every part of it.
choices.lock_text: having taken the long way back

authoring.premise: First day at {club}. Your name is on tape above a locker that still has someone else's sticker on it.

scenarios.title: A Holder at the New Club

authoring.premise: {holder} spins the laces differently than anyone you've worked with.
The new contract is in {town}. Your partner has a job and friends where you live now.
You'll be in {town} during the season, and your family will be a flight away.

scenarios.title: Your Old Team Comes to Town

authoring.premise: Your old club is on the schedule. Half the locker room over there still texts you.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Bigger Client
scenarios.text: Your agent just signed a star quarterback. Your last three calls went to voicemail, and the fourth went to an assistant who asked how to spell your last name.

authoring.premise: Your agent just signed a star quarterback, and your calls go to voicemail.

choices.label: Say something now
choices.result: A short email to your agent: what you need this year, and by when. The reply comes from the agent personally, a day late and genuinely apologetic, with a meeting date.

choices.label: Let it slide
choices.result: The agent's busy, you tell yourself, and it'll even out. It doesn't. You stop expecting calls back, and you start finding out things from reporters.

choices.label: Vent to the locker room
choices.result: Complaints about your agent, to anyone who'll listen. Two teammates say theirs is worse, and a reporter hears about all of it by Friday.

scenarios.title: Firing Your Agent

authoring.premise: Your agent has missed two deadlines this year. Firing him means starting over with someone new.

choices.label: Fire your agent
choices.result: You send a short letter and make three calls to find someone new. It's awkward for a month and a relief after that.

choices.label: Give one last chance
choices.result: You sit down with your agent and lay out exactly what has to change. Things get better for a season, mostly.

choices.label: Stay and say nothing
choices.result: A bad agent you know beats a new one you don't, you decide. The next deadline gets missed too, and you find out from a teammate.

scenarios.title: The Good Agent
scenarios.text: An agent with six clients asks for an hour. The pitch has no private jets and no promises, just a plan so plain it's almost funny.

choices.label: Sign with the plain plan
choices.result: Signing with them is quiet. The calls get answered, the deadlines get met, and nothing about it will ever make a highlight reel, which is exactly what you hired.

choices.label: Stay with the big agency
choices.result: The big agency's name opens doors, so you stay. Some doors do open. Some just have a receptionist behind them who never remembers how to spell your name.

choices.label: Ask what they'd fix first
choices.result: What would they fix first? The answer is specific and a little uncomfortable: your social media, your trainer, your spending. You hire them on the spot.

authoring.premise: You got the job at a Tuesday tryout. Now you live in a hotel by the airport until somebody says otherwise.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Traded Away
scenarios.text: The club traded your holder's best friend at midnight. {holder} found out from a phone notification, sitting in the parking lot after practice, and hasn't said much since.

authoring.premise: The club traded your holder's best friend at midnight. He found out from his phone.

choices.label: Check on {holder}
choices.result: First thing in the morning, you find {holder}, and you stay through lunch. Nothing much is said, and it helps.

choices.label: Talk to the specialists
choices.result: A few words to the specialists about how the business works, and how to look after each other in it. The young ones need it.

choices.label: Keep your head low
choices.result: It's the business, and you know it could be you. You keep your head low and your phone face down.

scenarios.title: A Coach Out of a Job
scenarios.text: The head coach is fired after a Monday team meeting, in front of everyone, with a two-sentence statement from the owner. That night, {coach}'s office lights are still on at eleven.

authoring.premise: The head coach is fired after a team meeting. {coach}'s office lights are on late.

choices.label: Check on {coach}
choices.result: A knock on the lit office door at eleven. You talk for an hour about the head coach, the business and the next three weeks, and {coach} thanks you at the door.

choices.label: Steady the specialists
choices.result: The specialists, gathered the next morning: same routine, same standards, whoever the coach is. The week goes on, and the young players watch how you do it.

choices.label: Wait and see
choices.result: Head down, waiting to see who comes next. It's the business, and you've seen enough of it to know that worrying changes nothing, mostly.

scenarios.title: The General Manager's Nephew

authoring.premise: The new general manager is the owner's nephew, and he has opinions about kickers.

choices.label: Teach him about kicking
choices.result: A polite meeting, and a gentle education: what the spreadsheet misses, what the film shows, what a kicker actually does. He takes notes, which surprises you.

choices.result: No meeting needed. You let your practices speak for you, and by midseason he quietly stops sending you spreadsheets about kickers.

choices.label: Invite him to practice
choices.result: An invitation to watch a special teams practice from the field. He holds a ball for you, badly, and leaves with a new respect for the job.

scenarios.title: Loyalty or the Paycheck
scenarios.text: Another club would pay you double, your agent says, with the offer in writing. This one gave you your first chance when nobody else would. The general manager is waiting for your call.

authoring.premise: Another club would pay you double. This one gave you your first chance.

choices.label: Stay
choices.result: You stay. The club remembers it, the locker room remembers it, and so do you, every time you drive past the old stadium.

choices.label: Explore it
choices.result: Your agent explores the offer, fully and openly. You kick the season like a free agent, and the club starts calling more often.

choices.label: Ask your club to match
choices.result: Your club, asked to come closer to the other offer. They meet you partway, and you sign, a little richer and still at home.

scenarios.title: The Big Check
scenarios.text: Your signing bonus clears on a Tuesday. Within an hour your phone lights up with cousins, a car dealer, two realtors and someone from high school who wants to 'catch up'.

authoring.premise: The signing bonus clears. Your phone lights up with cousins.

choices.label: Put it somewhere boring
choices.result: You put almost all of it somewhere boring and tell everyone it's tied up. Nobody believes you, and nobody can get to it.

choices.label: Celebrate properly
choices.result: The whole family, on a trip, and then the house with the pool. It's the best summer anyone in your family has had, and the pool bill arrives in September.

choices.label: Set aside a family share
choices.result: You set aside one share for family and tell them it's the only one. The cousins grumble. {parent} quietly approves.

scenarios.title: The Honest Advisor
scenarios.text: A financial advisor recommended by your long snapper walks you through a plan so boring it's almost funny: index funds, a budget, a rule about cars.

authoring.premise: A financial advisor recommended by your snapper walks you through a plan so boring it's almost funny.

choices.label: Hire the boring advisor
choices.result: You hire the advisor and follow the rule about cars, mostly. Nothing exciting happens to your money, which is the point.

choices.label: Ask for more upside
choices.result: More upside, you say. The advisor says no, explains why in plain words and doesn't budge. You hire them anyway, partly because they wouldn't budge.

choices.label: Pass for now
choices.result: You say you'll think about it and never call back. The money sits in a checking account doing nothing at all.

scenarios.title: The Advisor With the Yacht
scenarios.text: A financial advisor who manages three of your teammates invites you onto his boat and talks about 'real returns', the kind 'the boring guys' can't get you.

authoring.premise: A financial advisor who manages three teammates invites you onto his boat and talks about 'real returns'.

choices.label: Hand over your money
choices.result: Papers get signed on the boat, between lunch and the sunset. The first statements look incredible, and he always answers when you call, even on weekends.

choices.label: Ask for audited statements
choices.result: Audited statements and one reference outside football, please. He laughs, changes the subject and refills your lemonade, and you never sign anything.

choices.label: Enjoy the boat, sign nothing
choices.result: You enjoy the afternoon, eat his food and sign nothing. Your teammates call you paranoid on the drive home, and two of them sign with him the next week.

choices.label: Send it to the people you trust
choices.result: You send his paperwork to the people who already handle your money. Their reply is one word: 'No.' Then a second message: 'Warn your teammates.'

scenarios.title: The Missing Money
scenarios.text: Your bank calls on a Tuesday morning: a transfer you didn't authorize, the third one this year. The advisor with the boat isn't answering, and his office number goes to a recording.

authoring.premise: Your accounts are lighter than they should be, and the advisor isn't answering.
authoring.note: Works now with flags and stress; the stolen 40% lands with R3.

choices.label: Call a lawyer before practice
choices.result: You make the calls in the parking lot. By Friday the accounts are frozen, a forensic accountant is on it, and you know the number: four of every ten dollars you've earned.

choices.label: Call {parent}
choices.result: You call {parent} and say the number out loud. He's quiet for a long time, then tells you about the year he lost his job and what he did the next morning. You write it all down.

choices.result: You tell nobody, including the three teammates he also manages. You tell them everything's fine, which is a lie, and spend the season doing math in the training room.

choices.label: Call your agent first
choices.result: Your agent has seen this before. Within an hour you have a lawyer, an accountant and a plan, and a warning to call the other three players he manages before the news does.

scenarios.title: The Lawsuit
scenarios.text: Your lawyer says you can sue the advisor who took your money. It'll take three years, cost a fortune in fees, and your name will be in every story about it.

authoring.premise: Your lawyer says you can sue the advisor. It'll take three years and your name will be in every story.

choices.label: Sue him
choices.result: You file. The case drags on for years, you testify twice, and some of the money comes back long after you've stopped counting on it.

choices.label: Report him and move on
choices.result: You file the report with the regulators and let them handle it. He's barred from the business a year later. You never see a dime.

choices.label: Join with the other players

scenarios.title: The Restaurant
scenarios.text: An old college teammate wants your name and your money on a steakhouse downtown. He has a chef, a location and a business plan he wrote last night, and he keeps saying 'can't miss.'

authoring.premise: An old college teammate wants your name and your money on a steakhouse downtown. He has a chef, a location and a business plan he wrote last night.

choices.label: Put your money in
choices.result: You sign the papers at his kitchen table. Your name goes up in lights in March, and you eat there twice a week because it's yours.

choices.label: Ask to see real numbers
choices.result: A real plan, the lease and an accountant's review, please. He's offended, sends half of it, then stops answering. You keep your money and lose some of a friendship.

choices.label: Lend your name, not your money
choices.result: The opening night, a photo line and nothing more: your name, not your money. He's disappointed and says so, then takes the deal.

choices.label: Send it to your advisor
choices.result: Your advisor reads the plan in an afternoon and circles four things that would sink it. You send the list to your old teammate as a favor. He fixes two of them and opens without you.
choices.lock_text: having an advisor you trust

scenarios.title: The Restaurant Is Failing

authoring.premise: The steakhouse is losing money every week, and your name is on the sign.

choices.label: Close it now
choices.result: You close it, pay the staff two weeks' wages from your own pocket and take your name down yourself. It hurts, and it's over.

choices.label: Put more money in
choices.result: Another check, to keep it open one more season. The food gets better, the reviews get kinder, and the losses don't change at all.

choices.label: Sell your share to your partner
choices.result: You sell your share to your old teammate for whatever he can pay. You lose most of it and keep the friendship, barely.

choices.label: Let your advisor run the exit
choices.result: Your advisor finds a buyer for the lease and the equipment within a month. You lose money, but a lot less than you would have.
choices.lock_text: having an advisor you trust

scenarios.title: The Car Dealership
scenarios.text: A car dealership wants you as a partner: your face on the billboards, your money in the lot, and a guaranteed parking space with your name on it.

authoring.premise: A dealership wants you as a partner: your face on the billboards, your money in the lot.

choices.label: Become a partner
choices.result: You sign. Your face goes up on the highway, and every teammate calls you about a deal. The dealership's books are the dealer's business, until they aren't.

choices.label: Do the ads, skip the ownership

choices.label: Keep your name off the lot
choices.result: No dealership, no billboard, no parking space. Your money stays where it is, and the dealership signs a weatherman, whose face you see every day.

scenarios.title: The Friend's Start-Up
scenarios.text: {best_friend} is starting a company, a real one with a plan, a lawyer and two hires, and asks you over dinner to be the very first investor. They've practiced the pitch.

authoring.premise: {best_friend} is starting a company and asks you to be the first investor.

choices.result: You write the check because it's {best_friend}, and because the plan is actually good. You get a seat at their first board meeting and don't understand half of it.

choices.label: Invest a little, and say why

choices.label: Say no as a friend
choices.result: You say you don't mix friendship and money, and you mean it kindly. {best_friend} says they understand, and calls a little less often.

scenarios.title: The Start-Up Calls

authoring.premise: {best_friend}'s company is either about to make it or about to fold, and they need one more check.

choices.label: Write the last check

choices.label: Help them find another investor
choices.result: Two people from the owner's gala, introduced to {best_friend} by you over coffee. One of them writes the check within a week.

choices.label: Ask your advisor to look first
