choices.lock_text: having an advisor you trust

scenarios.title: The Tax Letter, Pro
scenarios.text: You owe taxes in every state where you played a road game, and your old accountant didn't file most of them. The letters have started to arrive.

authoring.premise: You owe taxes in every state you played a road game in, and your old accountant didn't file most of them.

choices.label: Hire a sports accountant
choices.result: You hire an accountant who does nothing but athletes. It takes a month of paperwork and a painful check, and it's done.

choices.label: Ignore the letters
choices.result: The letters go in a drawer. They come back with penalties, then with a lawyer's name on the envelope, and every one of them makes your stomach drop.

choices.label: Ask the veterans at lunch
choices.result: Every veteran at the lunch table has a horror story and a phone number. You call the one who sounds least scary, and she fixes it in a month.

choices.label: Pay it from the account you never touch
choices.result: You pay it from the account you've never touched since your first paycheck. It's a big number, and it doesn't keep you up at night.
choices.lock_text: having handled money carefully since your first paycheck

authoring.premise: {sibling} needs money and doesn't want {parent} to know.

scenarios.title: The Cousin Nobody Remembers
scenarios.text: Someone from your hometown with your last name, a folder of drawings and a business idea is waiting by your car after practice. He says you met at a wedding when you were nine.

authoring.premise: Someone from your hometown with your last name and a business idea is waiting by your car.

choices.label: Hear the pitch, then check it
choices.result: You listen, take the paperwork and have your agent look at it. The idea is real; the numbers aren't. You say no with reasons.

choices.label: Buy him lunch, not the idea
choices.result: You buy him lunch and talk about family for an hour. You don't invest, and he leaves happier than he came.

choices.label: Say no before he finishes
choices.result: No, before he's finished his first sentence, and you get in your car. It's quick and a little cold, and {parent} hears about it from three relatives by Sunday.

scenarios.title: {parent}'s House
scenarios.text: You could pay off {parent}'s mortgage this week with one transfer. He's told you not to, twice, in the voice he used when you were twelve.

authoring.premise: You could pay off {parent}'s mortgage this week. He's told you not to, twice.

choices.label: Do it anyway
choices.result: You pay it off and tell him after. He's furious for an hour and doesn't speak at dinner. A month later, he still has the letter from the bank on his fridge.

choices.label: Ask what he'd accept
choices.result: You ask {parent} what he would actually accept. He agrees to a loan with no interest, insists on paying it back, and pays it back early.

choices.label: Respect his wish
choices.result: You respect his wish and let it go. He's proud of that, in his quiet way, and you send money to his church instead.

choices.label: Do it the way that worked before
choices.result: You set it up the way you did last time: quietly, through the bank, with his name on everything. He grumbles and signs.
choices.lock_text: having helped your family with money before

scenarios.title: The Foundation
scenarios.text: Your charity foundation's director is spending more on galas than on kids: the books show a ballroom, a band and a photographer, and only two new programs all year.

authoring.premise: Your charity foundation's director is spending more on galas than on kids.

choices.label: Replace the director
choices.result: A new director, hired by you after a hard conversation with the old one. You run the next year closely, and the programs double.

choices.label: Audit the books
choices.result: An outside audit, every line, with new rules on spending afterward. The director stays, chastened, and the money starts reaching kids.

choices.label: Trust the director
choices.result: The galas raise money too, you tell yourself, and you let it run. The next annual report is glossy and thin.

scenarios.title: The Watch, the Car, the Chain
scenarios.text: The locker room has a dress code nobody wrote down: the watch, the car, the chain. It costs about what you made as a rookie.

authoring.premise: The locker room has a dress code nobody wrote down, and it costs about your rookie salary.

choices.label: Keep up
choices.result: You buy the watch and the car. You look the part, and every month the statement looks a little worse.

choices.label: Opt out with a joke
choices.result: The same old truck shows up every day, and you call it 'retro'. It becomes a running joke in the locker room, and nobody actually minds; one rookie copies you.

choices.label: Ask a veteran who went broke
choices.result: The oldest player on the roster takes his watch off when you ask about it, sets it on the table and tells you what it cost him in the end.

scenarios.title: Broke at Thirty-Three
scenarios.text: The money's gone faster than the career. There's a mortgage, a family, a car payment, and maybe three seasons left in your leg, if you're very lucky.

authoring.premise: The money's gone faster than the career, and you have a mortgage, a family and maybe three seasons.

choices.label: Make a hard plan
choices.result: An honest advisor and a hard plan: a smaller house, no new cars, a budget taped to the fridge. It hurts, and it works.

choices.label: Tell your family everything
choices.result: You tell your family everything at the kitchen table. It's the worst conversation of your life and the best one; nobody leaves.

choices.label: Kick for one more contract
choices.result: You decide to kick for one more contract like your family depends on it. It does, and every practice feels heavier.

scenarios.title: The Pension Meeting
scenarios.text: The players' union holds a meeting about pensions and retirement plans in a hotel conference room. Six players show up, and you're the youngest by four years.

authoring.premise: The players' union holds a meeting about pensions and retirement plans. Six players show up.

choices.label: Go and take notes
choices.result: Notes on everything, for two hours. It's boring and important, and you understand your pension for the first time in your career.

choices.label: Bring twelve teammates next time
choices.result: Twelve teammates at the next meeting, recruited by you one at a time. The union rep looks at you like you've performed a miracle.

choices.label: Skip it
choices.result: Retirement feels far away, so you skip it. The six who went start a group chat, and you're not in it.

scenarios.title: The Proposal
scenarios.text: You've carried a ring around in your gym bag for three weeks, waiting for a right moment that never seems to come during a season.

authoring.premise: You've been carrying a ring around for three weeks, waiting for the right moment that won't come during a season.

choices.label: Ask tonight
choices.result: You stop waiting for the perfect moment and ask in the kitchen, still in your practice clothes. {love_interest} laughs, cries and says yes, in that order.

choices.label: Ask {parent} first
choices.result: You call {parent} first, which nobody does anymore. He's quiet, then tells you how he asked your mother. You propose that weekend with his story in your head.

choices.label: Wait until you're sure
choices.result: The ring goes back in the bag for another month. You're not ready, and you think {love_interest} can tell that something's different.

scenarios.title: The Wedding
scenarios.text: The wedding is this offseason. The guest list is a fight: {parent} wants half your hometown, {love_interest} wants forty people, and your agent wants a magazine there.

authoring.premise: The wedding is in the offseason. The guest list is a fight.

choices.label: Forty people, no cameras
choices.result: Forty people and no cameras, in a garden. {parent} grumbles for a week beforehand and then dances until midnight with everyone.

choices.label: Invite the whole town
choices.result: You invite everyone. It's loud, enormous and a little out of control, and your hometown talks about it for years.

choices.label: Let the magazine in
choices.result: You let the magazine shoot it. The photos are beautiful and everywhere, and some of the day belongs to strangers.

scenarios.title: The Due Date
scenarios.text: The baby is due the same week as a road game across the country, and {coach} has already asked, gently, what your plan is. {love_interest} hasn't asked at all.

authoring.premise: The baby is due the same week as a road game across the country.

choices.label: Stay home for the birth
choices.result: You tell {coach} you're staying home, whatever it costs. You're there when the baby arrives, and you'd make the same call a hundred times.

choices.label: Fly out and fly back
choices.result: You fly out for the game and take the first flight home. You miss the birth by four hours and meet your kid in a hospital hallway at dawn.

choices.label: Ask {coach} for a plan
choices.result: You sit down with {coach} and work out a plan: a phone in the trainer's pocket and a jet on standby. It's complicated, and it works.

scenarios.title: First Day of School
scenarios.text: Your kid's first day of school falls on a Thursday practice day. The backpack has been packed since Sunday, and there's a photo planned by the front door at seven-thirty.

authoring.premise: Your kid's first day of school is a Thursday practice.

choices.label: Ask to come in late
choices.result: An hour's grace from {coach}, granted without a pause. You're there for the photo, the backpack, and the wave at the classroom door.

choices.label: Go to practice and watch the video
choices.result: Practice, and a video from home at lunch. You watch it four times in the locker room, and {holder} watches it with you.

choices.label: Plan the whole morning
choices.result: The morning, planned to the minute with {coach} and the family: drop-off at seven-forty, meeting at eight-fifteen. You make both, barely.

authoring.premise: A school recital, a road trip, and a kid who has asked three times if you'll be there.
Your partner has been offered the job of a lifetime, in a city with no team.

scenarios.title: {parent} Is Getting Older
scenarios.text: {parent} forgets the name of a neighbor he's known for twenty years, in the middle of a story on the phone. He laughs it off. You don't.

authoring.premise: {parent} forgets the name of a neighbor he's known for twenty years.

choices.label: Go home for the bye
choices.result: Home for the bye weekend, every minute with him: the hardware store, the porch, the old stories. He tells the neighbor story right this time.

choices.label: Find him a specialist
choices.result: A specialist, found and booked, and you join the first appointment by video. It's probably nothing, the doctor says, and you hold on to 'probably'.

choices.label: Call every other day
choices.result: Every other day, a phone call, ten minutes or an hour. It's not much, it's something, and he starts saving stories for you.

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Last Season in the Stands
scenarios.text: {parent} tells you on the phone that this is the last season he'll make the six-hour drive to watch you. His eyes aren't good at night anymore, he says, and the back seat hurts.

authoring.premise: {parent} says this is the last season he'll make the drive to watch you.

choices.label: Meet him at the fence every game
choices.result: At the fence after every home game, all season. He tells you what he saw from the stands, the same way he did when you were twelve, and you listen to every word.

choices.label: Arrange rides so he keeps coming
choices.result: Rides, arranged with a neighbor and a car service, so the drive stops being the problem. He makes every home game and complains about the driver's music every time.

choices.label: Thank him for every drive
choices.result: A long call, thanking him for every drive, from the first peewee game to this one. He waves it off, and his voice goes quiet in the middle.

scenarios.title: {sibling}'s Own Shot
scenarios.text: {sibling} has a tryout of his own, with a semi-pro team three hours from home, and he wants you there. He's never asked you for anything before.

authoring.premise: {sibling} has a tryout of his own, and he wants you there.

choices.label: Be at the fence
choices.result: A flight in, and you stand behind the fence all morning. He looks for you before every kick, and finds you every time.

choices.label: Coach him by phone
choices.result: The night before, by phone: one thought, one routine, nothing else. He calls after the tryout to tell you it worked, and he sounds like a different person.

choices.label: Send a message and watch later
choices.result: A message in the morning, the video at night. He understands, mostly, and doesn't mention it again, which tells you something.

choices.label: Tell him what you learned
choices.result: You tell {sibling} the hardest thing you ever learned: show up, tell the truth, let the rest go. Then you're there at the fence.
choices.lock_text: having learned what showing up means

authoring.premise: {best_friend} asks for tickets every week and brings a different stranger every time.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

scenarios.title: The Coach Who Taught You
scenarios.text: Your high school coach is retiring after thirty-one years, and the school wants you to speak at the dinner. The gym will be full of people who knew you at fifteen.

authoring.premise: Your high school coach is retiring, and the school wants you to speak at the dinner.

choices.label: Speak from the heart
choices.result: What that coach did for you, said plainly to a full gym. They stand at the end, and your old coach can't look up from the table.

choices.label: Bring the current team
choices.result: The current high school team, invited to the dinner by you, in their jerseys. Your old coach sees the whole program in one room and laughs through tears.

choices.label: Send a letter to be read
choices.result: A letter, read aloud by the principal. It's lovely, and you wish, reading the reports, that you'd been there in person.

choices.label: Tell the story of the trust
choices.result: How that trust was earned, and how you had to earn it again later: you tell the whole story. Your old coach nods along to every part of it.
choices.lock_text: having earned a coach's trust before

scenarios.title: {tyler} in the Same Division
scenarios.text: {tyler} signs with a team in your division, and the sports channel has already made the graphic: the two of you, face to face, twice a year.

authoring.premise: {tyler} signs with a division rival, and the media has already made the graphic.

choices.label: Call {tyler} and laugh about it
choices.result: You call {tyler} and laugh about the graphic. You agree to give the reporters nothing, and you both mostly keep that promise.

choices.label: Put the graphic on your locker
choices.result: The graphic goes on your locker. Every practice before those two games has a little more in it, and {tyler} hears about the locker from a reporter.

choices.label: Plan a dinner after the first game
choices.result: You text {tyler} a restaurant name and a time: after the first game, win or lose. He sends back a thumbs-up and a picture of the two of you at sixteen.
choices.lock_text: having earned {tyler}'s respect before

choices.label: Make peace first
choices.result: You remember what you said about {tyler} in college, and you call to say it was out of line. It's an awkward call, and the rivalry gets cleaner after it.
choices.lock_text: having trash-talked {tyler} in college

scenarios.title: {tyler} Gets Cut
scenarios.text: {tyler} is released on a Monday morning. He calls you before he calls his agent, and for a long time neither of you says anything.

authoring.premise: {tyler} is released on a Monday. He calls you before his agent.

choices.label: Listen for an hour
choices.result: An hour on the phone, mostly listening. He doesn't want advice, and you don't give any, and he thanks you twice.

choices.label: Make a call for him
choices.result: A special teams coach you know gets a call from you, and you say {tyler}'s name twice. He has a workout by Friday.

choices.label: Promise to talk soon
choices.result: A message, warm and short, and a promise to talk soon. You mean it, and it still takes three weeks before you actually call.

scenarios.title: {tyler}'s Second Act
scenarios.text: {tyler} is in the broadcast booth now, wearing a headset and a tie, and he's calling your games. The first time he says your name on air, he pauses a little too long.

authoring.premise: {tyler} is in the broadcast booth now, and he's calling your games.

choices.label: Have dinner the night before
choices.result: Dinner the night before, at the old diner. He tells you exactly what he'll say on air, and none of it is mean, and some of it is kind.

choices.label: Give him a good story
choices.result: A story for the broadcast, told to him on the field during warmups. He tells it better than you ever could, and it becomes the clip of the week.

choices.label: Laugh about it
choices.result: Every time the camera finds you, you know he's grinning in the booth. You laugh about it with {holder}, and it makes the games lighter.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Kicker You Mentor
scenarios.text: The club drafts a kicker in the fourth round and asks you to show the rookie how things work. Everybody in the building knows what that means, including the rookie.

authoring.premise: The club drafts a kicker and asks you to show the rookie how things work, knowing what that means.

choices.label: Teach him everything
choices.result: Everything, generously: the routines, the wind, the coaches' moods. He'll take your job someday, and he'll do it right, and he'll know who taught him.

choices.label: Teach him the basics
choices.result: The basics, taught well, and the rest kept for yourself. He learns fast anyway, and you notice him watching your routine from across the field.

choices.label: Leave it to the coaches
choices.result: The coaches can teach him, you decide, and you keep your distance all camp. The room notices, and so, unfortunately, does {coach}.

choices.label: Do it the way you've done it
choices.result: You've done this before, so you know what to teach and when: the routine in week one, the wind in week three, the nerves before his first game.
choices.lock_text: having mentored before

scenarios.title: The Mentee Takes Your Job
scenarios.text: The kicker you taught is better than you now, everyone can see it, and {coach} wants to tell you before the depth chart comes out on Monday.

authoring.premise: The kicker you taught is better than you now, and {coach} wants to tell you before the depth chart comes out.

choices.label: Congratulate your old student
choices.result: You congratulate your old student before {coach} can finish. The kid is embarrassed and proud, and so are you, and you buy lunch.

choices.label: Fight for it
choices.result: Every day of camp, you fight for it. You lose, barely, and your old student says the competition made the difference for both of you.

choices.label: Ask about your role
choices.result: What's your role now? {coach}'s answer is honest: insurance, and the room's best teacher. It hurts, it's true, and you accept it.

scenarios.title: The Holder's Last Season
scenarios.text: {holder} is retiring after this season and wants every hold to count. They've started bringing a notebook to practice, writing down each one, with the date and the weather.

authoring.premise: {holder} is retiring after this season and wants every hold to count.

choices.label: Celebrate every practice
choices.result: Every practice becomes a small celebration: a joke, a photo, a cake on the fortieth birthday. {holder} cries twice, happily.

choices.label: Make every kick count
choices.result: Every kick in practice, for {holder}, like it's the playoffs. The notebook fills up with good ones, and {holder} reads them to you on Fridays.

choices.label: Train the next holder
choices.result: The next holder gets trained by both of you, all season, so the job is in good hands. {holder} calls it the best thing you ever did for them.

scenarios.title: The Snapper Retires
scenarios.text: The long snapper you've trusted for years is done: his back, his age, his wife's patience. He asks you, of all people, to speak at his farewell dinner.

authoring.premise: The long snapper you've trusted for years is done, and he asks you to speak at his farewell.

choices.label: Speak from the heart
choices.result: What it's like to trust someone without ever looking back: you tell the room. He cries first, and then everyone else does.

choices.label: Keep it light and true
choices.result: Three funny stories and one true one. The room loves it, and he asks for a copy of the speech to show his kids.

choices.label: Say a few words
choices.result: A few short words and a raised glass of water. He hugs you anyway, hard, and says it was perfect, and his wife writes you a note.

authoring.premise: A teammate's arrest is on every channel. He asks you to vouch for him at the hearing.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

scenarios.title: The Concussion
scenarios.text: A teammate who has had too many concussions takes another hit in practice and hides it. You saw it happen, and he saw you see it.

authoring.premise: A teammate who has had too many concussions is hiding another one, and you saw it happen.

choices.label: Tell the trainers
choices.result: The trainers hear it from you before the next drill. He's angry for a week and won't look at you, then thanks you in the parking lot.

choices.label: Talk to him first
choices.result: Away from everyone, by the water cooler, you convince him to tell the trainers himself. It costs you an hour and some of his pride.

choices.label: Look the other way
choices.result: Looking the other way, you let it go. He plays the next game, and you watch him every single snap, wondering if you were wrong.

scenarios.title: The Letter From a Kid
scenarios.text: A letter arrives at the facility from a kid you met in a hospital years ago. He's twelve now, and walking, and he's enclosed a photo of himself standing next to a football.

authoring.premise: A letter from a kid in a hospital you visited years ago: he's walking now.

choices.label: Write back
choices.result: A handwritten reply, two pages, with a signed photo of your own. He frames it, and his mother sends you a picture of it on his wall.

choices.label: Invite him to a practice
choices.result: An invitation to practice, for him and his family. He walks onto the field himself, slowly, and the whole team stops to clap.

choices.label: Keep the letter
choices.result: The letter goes in your locker, next to your cleats. On bad days you read it again, and it fixes something every time.

choices.label: Go back to the hospital
choices.result: You go back to the hospital where you met him, and you bring his letter to show the kids there.
choices.lock_text: having volunteered for years

authoring.premise: A gossip site prints a story about your marriage that's mostly made up.
You've been home eleven nights since August, and your partner has stopped asking when you'll be back.

scenarios.title: The Reunion
scenarios.text: Your high school reunion is the weekend after the season ends. Twenty years, a gym with streamers, and everyone wants to know what the league is really like.

authoring.premise: Your high school reunion is the weekend after the season, and everyone wants to know what the league is like.

choices.label: Tell stories all night
choices.result: Stories, all night, to a growing circle by the bleachers. Your old friends laugh in the same places they always did, and {best_friend} finishes your sentences.

choices.label: Ask about their lives instead
choices.result: Their lives, asked about, one by one. They're more interesting than the league: a nurse, a farmer, a pilot, a teacher who still remembers your essay.

choices.label: Skip the reunion
choices.result: Skipped, and you see the pictures later online. Everyone looks older, and so do you, and you feel the miss more than you expected.

scenarios.title: A College Teammate's Wedding
scenarios.text: Your old college roommate is getting married in June and wants you to give the toast. He's sent a list of stories you're not allowed to tell, and it's longer than the speech.

authoring.premise: Your old college roommate is getting married, and he wants you to give a toast.

choices.label: Write a great toast
choices.result: A great toast, written over three weeks and delivered from memory. The bride's grandmother hugs you twice, and the groom mouths 'thank you' from the head table.

choices.label: Tell one true story
choices.result: One true story from freshman year, carefully chosen. It's the one people repeat at breakfast the next morning, and the groom tears up.

choices.label: Remember the pact
choices.result: You raise a glass to the pact you made freshman year. He laughs so hard he can't finish his drink.
choices.lock_text: having made a pact with your college roommate

choices.label: Make peace in the toast
choices.result: You haven't really talked since college. You say so in the toast, and you say sorry. He finds you on the patio afterward.
choices.lock_text: having fallen out with your college roommate

authoring.premise: Two starters are swinging at each other by the cold tub, and the rookies are watching you.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

scenarios.title: The Quarterback's Ego
scenarios.text: The franchise quarterback blames the special teams in a press conference, by name, on camera. Twenty minutes later the reporters are standing at your locker with their phones already recording.

authoring.premise: The franchise quarterback blames the special teams in a press conference.

choices.label: Talk only about your job
choices.result: Your job is the only thing you'll talk about, and you say it calmly three times. The quarterback notices, and so does the locker room, in different ways.

choices.label: Fire back
choices.result: Special teams aren't the problem, you say, looking straight into the camera. It's the clip of the week, and the quarterback stops talking to you until December.

choices.label: Talk to him privately
choices.result: You find him at his locker after practice and ask what he actually meant. It turns out he was angry at himself. He says so at the next press conference.

scenarios.title: The Veteran Who Can't Let Go
scenarios.text: A thirty-six-year-old linebacker is getting cut on Friday, and he hasn't figured it out yet. He's still planning next year's offseason out loud at lunch.

authoring.premise: A thirty-six-year-old linebacker is getting cut, and he hasn't figured it out yet.

choices.label: Sit with him on his last day
choices.result: Lunch with him on his last day, just the two of you. He talks about his first season the whole time, and you let him.

choices.label: Get the young players to say goodbye
choices.result: The young players, quietly told to say goodbye before he's gone. Twenty of them line up at his locker, and he can't speak.

choices.label: Let it happen
choices.result: It's not your place, so you let it happen. It stays with you, the empty chair at lunch, longer than you expect.

scenarios.title: The Players-Only Meeting
scenarios.text: The team captains call a players-only meeting about {coach}'s boss, the head coach, and they want every player's vote. For the first time, they're asking the kicker.

authoring.premise: The team captains call a meeting about the coach, and they want your vote.

choices.label: Speak honestly
choices.result: Tough and fair, you say about the head coach, and you give two examples. Some agree, some don't, and the vote is closer because of you.

choices.label: Ask for the facts first
choices.result: What exactly is the problem? The meeting gets calmer as people answer, and the vote becomes a list of fixes instead.

choices.label: Abstain
choices.result: An abstention. Kickers rarely get asked anyway, and you'd rather not start now. The captains notice, and they stop asking you for a while.

scenarios.title: The Player Rep
scenarios.text: The team needs a players' union representative, the job of standing up in front of management twice a year. Nobody wants to be the one management remembers.

authoring.premise: The team needs a union representative, and nobody wants to be the one management remembers.

choices.label: Volunteer
choices.result: Volunteered. It's meetings and conference calls, and the young players start coming to you with questions about everything from contracts to pensions.

choices.label: Nominate the right person
choices.result: The veteran who should do it gets nominated by you. He accepts, grumbling, and does it brilliantly for three years.

choices.label: Leave it to someone else
choices.result: Someone else does it. You vote for them and go back to kicking, relieved, a little guiltily, every time there's a meeting.

authoring.premise: The league and the union are fighting over the next agreement, and the owners are talking about replacement players.
authoring.note: Told through teammates; no strike mechanic.

scenarios.title: The Injured Teammate
scenarios.text: A teammate who tore his knee for the team last season is cut the day he's cleared to practice. He found out in the training room, still wearing the brace.

authoring.premise: A teammate who tore his knee for the team is cut the day he's cleared to practice.

choices.label: Help him clean out his locker
choices.result: His locker, cleaned out with your help, into two cardboard boxes. He doesn't say much, and he hugs you at the car.

choices.label: Say something to the room
choices.result: A few words to the room about how this business works and what we owe each other inside it. The young players listen closely.

choices.label: Keep quiet
choices.result: Quiet. You're one bad season from the same thing, and you know it, and you kick a little angrier that week.

scenarios.title: The Owner's Gala
scenarios.text: Black tie, the owner's charity gala, and a donor who wants a photo and then a favor: a visit to his company's party next week.

authoring.premise: Black tie, the owner's charity, and a donor who wants a photo and a favor.

choices.label: Take the photo, skip the favor
choices.result: The photo is easy; the favor isn't. You smile, say your schedule is full, and he's disappointed for about a minute and forgets about it by dessert.

choices.label: Do the favor
choices.result: His company party is two hours of handshakes and lukewarm food, and at the end a check for the gala's charity with your name on it.

choices.label: Slip out before the auction
choices.result: An hour in, you slip out before the auction starts. Nobody asks you for anything, you're asleep by ten, and practice the next morning feels easy.

scenarios.title: The Podcast
scenarios.text: A popular podcast wants you for a full hour. The host is famous for getting athletes to say too much, and three of your teammates have already regretted going on.

authoring.premise: A popular podcast wants you for an hour. The host is known for getting athletes to say too much.

choices.label: Prepare and stay disciplined
choices.result: Prepared, disciplined, and still funny. It's a good episode with no headlines, and the host admits you were a hard interview.

choices.label: Be yourself on air
choices.result: Funny and honest for an hour, until one joke about a teammate gets clipped everywhere. You apologize to him before he hears it.

choices.label: Turn the podcast down
choices.result: No, politely. The host says something snide about kickers on the next episode, and your teammates send it to you, delighted.

authoring.premise: A mall signing goes three hours over, and the line still wraps around the food court.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

scenarios.title: The Awards Show
scenarios.text: The league's awards show wants you on the red carpet the night before a practice you can't miss. There's a tuxedo waiting at your hotel and a car at seven.

authoring.premise: The league's awards show wants you on the red carpet the night before a practice you can't miss.

choices.label: Walk the carpet and leave early
choices.result: The carpet, two interviews and gone before dessert. You make practice on time the next morning, tired and secretly pleased.

choices.label: Ask {coach}
choices.result: {coach} says go, and be on time. You are, at six in the morning, with makeup still behind your ear.

choices.label: Watch from home
choices.result: The awards, watched from home in sweatpants. You cheer loudly for the punter who wins, and you're asleep by ten.

scenarios.title: The National Deal
scenarios.text: A national brand wants you for a commercial that would air during every game this year: you, a ball, and a talking dog. The shoot is during your bye week.

authoring.premise: A national brand wants you for a commercial that would play during every game this year.

choices.label: Sign on for the commercial
choices.result: Signed. You're on every broadcast all season, the talking dog becomes famous, and the shoot eats your entire bye week, which you never get back.

choices.label: Shoot it in the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, or nothing, you tell them politely. They agree, the dog waits, and your bye week stays your own, with your family.

choices.label: Pass on it
choices.result: No commercial this year. You'd rather be known for kicking than for the dog, and a punter gets the part instead and loves it.

scenarios.title: The Leak
scenarios.text: Someone is leaking locker-room conversations to a beat reporter, word for word, and the coaches think it's a specialist. The punter is furious. So is {holder}.

authoring.premise: Someone is leaking locker-room conversations to a reporter, and the coaches think it's a specialist.

choices.label: Find the pattern
choices.result: Which details leak, and when? You notice the pattern and tell {coach}: it's a rookie lineman with a cousin at the paper.

choices.label: Rally the specialists
choices.result: The specialists, gathered: everyone knows what's at stake, and nobody says anything outside the room. {holder} calls it a team meeting.

choices.label: Let the coaches sort it
choices.result: The coaches will sort it out, you decide. They do, slowly, and the specialists' room stays tense and quiet for a month.

scenarios.title: The Specialists' Dinner
scenarios.text: The kicker, the punter and the snapper have had a dinner every Thursday since camp. A new punter wants in, he's nervous about asking, and the other two are looking at you.

authoring.premise: The kicker, the punter and the snapper have a weekly dinner, and a new punter wants in.

choices.label: Invite the new punter
choices.result: The new punter gets the invitation from you, and four turns out to be louder than three. The dinner gets better, and he stops eating lunch alone in his car.

choices.label: Keep it to three
choices.result: Three is the number, you decide. It stays easy and familiar, and the new punter eats alone on Thursdays for a month. You notice every time.

choices.label: Make it a unit dinner
choices.result: The whole special teams unit comes. It's chaos, two tables pushed together and a waiter who quits halfway, and it's the best night of the season.

authoring.premise: The city has noticed the team. Everyone wants a piece of the players in the last month.
authoring.note: No results; the push is the atmosphere. Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

authoring.premise: The season's slipping away, and the locker room has started counting days until the offseason.
authoring.note: Repeatable (cooldown 15-20 weeks).

scenarios.title: The Trick Play
scenarios.text: The new coordinator wants a fake field goal with you throwing the pass. You haven't thrown a football in a game since high school, and the backup quarterback is already laughing.

authoring.premise: The new coordinator wants a fake field goal with you throwing the pass, and you haven't thrown a ball since high school.

choices.label: Practice the throw
choices.result: You throw fifty passes a day for a week until the ball stops wobbling. The coordinator puts it in the playbook.

choices.label: Pitch a different fake
choices.result: A fake where the holder runs and you just block, you suggest. The coordinator likes it better, and {holder} is thrilled to finally get a carry.

choices.label: Say you're just a kicker
choices.result: Kickers kick, you say with a grin. The coordinator doesn't grin back, the fake goes to the punter, and you spend the season watching him get the credit.

authoring.premise: A teammate's night out after a home game starts at a club and ends somewhere you don't want to be.
authoring.note: Strike. Clean no.

authoring.premise: A supplement company offers you a deal for a product the league hasn't approved.
Someone at a bar is filming you while a stranger tries to start a fight.
An old friend who bets on games asks what you know about the starting quarterback's ankle.
authoring.note: Integrity strike: the worst one.

authoring.premise: A teammate rents a house for the bye week, and the guest list is long.
Your new car does zero to sixty in three seconds, and the highway is empty at midnight.
It's two in the morning and you've written four paragraphs about the general manager.
The card game in the back of the team plane has a buy-in bigger than your first car.

scenarios.title: The Team Fine
scenarios.text: The club fines you and calls you in. {coach} is in the room, and so is the general manager, who has a folder with your name on it.

authoring.premise: The club fines you and calls you in. The special teams coach is there, and so is the general manager.
authoring.note: Both choices set pro_warning (the fine is on record); owning it also sets pro_owned_it. College flags set severity through a locked choice. Every choice clears every pro strike.

choices.label: Own it
choices.result: You don't explain it away. You say what happened, what you'll change and who can hold you to it. The general manager closes the folder early.

choices.label: Explain it away
choices.result: You explain why it wasn't really your fault. The general manager listens to all of it and writes one word at the top of the page.

choices.label: Say you've been here before
choices.result: You tell them you've sat in a room like this in college and what you did after. {coach} nods slowly. The fine stands. The tone changes.
choices.lock_text: having owned a mistake before

scenarios.title: League Discipline
scenarios.text: The league office wants a meeting about the strike on your record. It isn't a conversation; it's a hearing, in a gray room, with a lawyer from the players' union at your side.

authoring.premise: The league office wants a meeting. It's not a conversation; it's a hearing.
authoring.note: Opens on the warning plus a new pro strike. suspend_weeks 2 (longer once R9 lands). Every choice clears every pro strike.

choices.label: Accept the suspension
choices.result: You accept two games and don't appeal. You practice with the scout team, and the veterans notice that you show up every day anyway.

choices.label: Fight it
choices.result: You appeal and say the league is making an example of you. The appeal fails, the suspension stands, and now the whole league knows your name for the wrong reason.

scenarios.title: The Last Warning, Pro
scenarios.text: With {coach} beside the desk, the general manager says it plainly: one more, and you're done here. Then a list of conditions slides across the table.

authoring.premise: The general manager says it plainly: one more and you're done here.
authoring.note: Every choice clears every pro strike. College last_chance adds a locked line.

choices.label: Accept every condition
choices.result: Early workouts, no nights out on the road, weekly check-ins. You sign the list. It costs you a lot of the season, and nobody has to wonder about you again.

choices.label: Push back
choices.result: You say the conditions are too much for what happened. The general manager ends the meeting. By Friday, every reporter covering the team has heard the word 'problem'.

choices.label: Say you've heard this speech before
choices.result: You tell them you got this exact speech in college, and that you kept the promise for two years. You sign the list. {coach} believes you more than the general manager does.
choices.lock_text: having had a last chance in college

authoring.premise: After a last chance, another strike: the club is done with you.
authoring.note: Sets the dismissal flag; the release happens at season end once R7 lands.

scenarios.title: Earning It Back
scenarios.text: You have a reputation in the league now. {coach} offers a way back: six a.m. workouts, a mentor from the players' union and no excuses for a full season.

authoring.premise: A new club, a short contract, and a list of conditions longer than the playbook.

choices.label: Take every hour of it
choices.result: You're there at six every day for a season, and your name stays out of every story. In the spring, {coach} tells a reporter you're not the same player, and means it.

choices.label: Do the minimum
choices.result: The workouts you can't skip, and nothing more. Nothing new goes wrong, nothing much changes, and the reputation stays exactly where it was.

choices.label: Say you've paid enough
choices.result: You say you served your suspension and don't need a program. {coach} closes the folder. It's the last offer you get here.

scenarios.title: The League's Counselor
scenarios.text: The league assigns you a counselor after the hearing. The first session is Tuesday at four, in a beige office near the airport, with a box of tissues on the table.

authoring.premise: The league assigns you a counselor after the hearing, and the first session is Tuesday.

choices.label: Go and actually talk
choices.result: You go every week and actually talk. Some of it is about the incidents. Most of it isn't, and that turns out to be the point.

choices.label: Go and say nothing
choices.result: You go every week and say as little as possible. You check the box, and the counselor writes that you checked the box.

choices.label: Bring the hard question
choices.result: In the first session you ask the question you've been avoiding: why it keeps happening. You don't get an answer that day. You get a better question.

scenarios.title: A Clean Year
scenarios.text: A full year without a fine, a headline or a hearing. The general manager stops by your locker on the last day of the season and says nothing, just nods, twice.

authoring.premise: A full year without a fine, a headline or a hearing. The general manager notices.

choices.label: Thank the people who held you to it
choices.result: You thank {coach}, the union mentor and the teammate who drove you to the early workouts. Saying it out loud makes it real.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself
choices.result: You keep it quiet and keep going. The best part of a clean year is that nobody talks about it.

choices.label: Help a rookie who's slipping
choices.result: A rookie making your old mistakes gets a breakfast invitation from you, and the whole story, start to finish. He listens to every word.

scenarios.title: Thirty
scenarios.text: You turn thirty in camp, and the trainer starts using the word 'maintenance' in every conversation. Your birthday cake has a candle shaped like an ice pack.

authoring.premise: You turn thirty in camp, and the trainer starts talking about 'maintenance'.

choices.label: Listen to the trainer
choices.result: The new maintenance routine, added without complaint: bands, heat, an extra stretching block. It's dull and it works, and your hip stops talking to you in the mornings.

choices.label: Prove you don't need it
choices.result: No maintenance, thanks; you'll prove you don't need it. Your body disagrees by October, loudly, and the trainer says nothing, which is worse.

choices.label: Celebrate with the unit
choices.result: A birthday in the cafeteria, thrown by the specialists, with the ice-pack candle and a terrible song. {holder} gives a speech about your age.

scenarios.title: The Maintenance Bill
scenarios.text: Holding on to your leg costs more every year: more treatment, more rest days, more hours in the cold tub, and more of the life outside the facility.

authoring.premise: Holding on to your leg costs more every year: more treatment, more rest, more skill points.

choices.label: Plan the year around recovery
choices.result: The whole year, planned around recovery like a second job. It's tedious, and your leg is the best it's been in three seasons.

choices.label: Work harder instead
choices.result: Harder, not smarter: more reps, more lifting, more hours. It holds, for now, and you can feel the bill coming for next year.

choices.label: Rest more, train less
choices.result: More rest, less training. Your leg feels fresh on game days and a little slower in practice, and you can't decide if that's wisdom.

scenarios.title: The Younger Kicker in Camp
scenarios.text: At thirty-five, you walk into the meeting room and a fourth-round rookie is sitting in your seat. He doesn't know it's your seat. Everyone else does.

authoring.premise: The club drafts a kicker in the fourth round, and he's sitting in your seat in the meeting room.

choices.label: Take your seat back every day
choices.result: First into the meeting room, every day after that. The seat is yours until it isn't, and you're not going to give it away for free.

choices.label: Teach him
choices.result: Your routine, your wind charts, your nerves: you teach him all of it. It's the right thing, and it makes the room trust you even more.

choices.label: Ask where you stand
choices.result: {coach}, asked plainly in the hallway. It's an open competition, the coach says, and you appreciate the honesty more than the answer.

scenarios.title: The One-Year Deal
scenarios.text: The offer is one year at the veteran minimum, delivered in a phone call that says, politely, take it or leave it. Your agent says nobody else has called.

authoring.premise: The offer is one year, the minimum, and a phone call that says take it or leave it.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.result: Signed. A year is a year, and you still love the work, and the first practice of the new season feels like a gift.

choices.label: Test the market
choices.result: The open market, tested for two weeks. Two clubs call, and one makes the same offer with more respect, and you sign with them.

choices.label: Ask home first
choices.result: {love_interest} asks you just one question: 'Do you still want it?' You do, and you sign the next morning without a second thought.

scenarios.title: The Veteran Minimum
scenarios.text: You're on the veteran minimum, a third of what you made five years ago. The rookie at the next locker drives your old car; he bought it from the dealer you sold it to.

authoring.premise: You're making a third of what you made five years ago, and the rookie next to you has your old car.

choices.label: Laugh about it with him
choices.result: Laughing about it together, at the lockers. He offers to sell it back to you at a discount, and you decline, and it becomes your running joke.

choices.label: Adjust the budget
choices.result: A smaller budget, built at the kitchen table, and nobody in the house misses the things you cut. You're surprised how little you needed.

choices.label: Kick for the next deal
choices.result: Every practice, like the next deal depends on it, because it does. It's motivating, and on bad days it's heavy.

scenarios.title: The Body Says No
scenarios.text: Your hip takes an hour to warm up now, and Monday mornings take two. The trainer has started calling your warmup 'the ceremony', and the rookies watch it like it's a show.

authoring.premise: Your hip takes an hour to warm up now, and Monday mornings take two.

choices.label: Build a new morning routine
choices.result: A new routine, built from scratch: heat, bands, a long walk, a slow stretch. It takes ninety minutes every morning, and it works.

choices.label: Push through it
choices.result: Through it, every morning, gritting your teeth. Your hip complains all season and holds, and you're tired in a new way.

choices.label: Rest more, practice less
choices.result: Less practice, more rest. You're fresher on game days and stiffer at practice, and you can't decide if it's wisdom or surrender.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Talk
scenarios.text: It's late, the house is quiet, the kids are asleep, and {love_interest} finally asks the question you've both been walking around for a year: how many more seasons?

authoring.premise: Your partner asks, gently, how many more seasons.
authoring.note: Partner version; a single player gets the same question in PRO_149 What's Next.

choices.label: Say one more
choices.result: You say one more season, and you mean it out loud for the first time. {love_interest} takes your hand, and suddenly every practice this year feels like a last one.

choices.label: Say you're not done
choices.result: It's not time yet, and you both know it. You agree to talk again after the season, and you sleep better than you have in weeks.

choices.label: Ask what they want
choices.result: You turn it around and ask what the next ten years should look like. It's the longest conversation you've had in months, and nobody mentions kicking until the very end.

choices.label: Bring out the old plan
choices.result: You find the plan you wrote in college for life after football. It's out of date and still mostly right, and the two of you rewrite it at the kitchen table until two in the morning.
choices.lock_text: having planned for life after football in college

scenarios.title: The Farewell Season
scenarios.text: Planning to retire after this season, you have to decide whether to tell the world now, or let it end quietly. Your agent has a press release drafted, just in case.

authoring.premise: Do you tell the world this is your last season, or let it end quietly?
authoring.note: The retirement itself is the player's choice on the contract screen.

choices.label: Tell the world
choices.result: The announcement, made at the first press conference of the season. Every stadium has a sign for you, and every week becomes a long goodbye.

choices.label: Let it end quietly
choices.result: Quietly, and on your own terms. Only the people closest to you know, and that's exactly how you want your last season to feel.

choices.label: Tell the team only
choices.result: The team, told in a closed meeting. The specialists make it their mission to send you out right, and {holder} doesn't make it through the meeting dry-eyed.

scenarios.title: The General Manager's Office
scenarios.text: The general manager calls you into his office and closes the door. They're going in a different direction at kicker next season, he says, and he wanted you to hear it from him.

authoring.premise: The general manager says they're going in a different direction at kicker next season.
authoring.note: Foreshadows the engine's release; retention lags a season.

choices.label: Prove them wrong
choices.result: Here or somewhere else, you'll prove them wrong. The fire is back, and you kick the rest of the season like an audition.

choices.label: Have your agent look around
choices.result: Your agent, looking around quietly. There's interest, modest and real, and two clubs ask to see you in the spring.

choices.label: Tell your family that night
choices.result: Your family, told that night at dinner. Nobody panics, and {parent} tells you he's proud no matter what, which you needed.

scenarios.title: The Comeback Workout
scenarios.text: Released last spring, signed this summer at thirty-five by a club that needed a kicker fast. Everyone in camp, including some of the coaches, thinks you're finished.

authoring.premise: Released last spring, signed this summer: everyone in camp thinks you're finished.

choices.label: Show them on day one
choices.result: On the first day of camp, and every day after, you show them. By August, nobody calls you finished, and the youngest kicker asks for your routine.

choices.label: Help the young players
choices.result: From the first day, the young players get your help: film, rides, nerves. You're the veteran they didn't know they needed, and they say so.

choices.label: Let the numbers argue
choices.result: Every kick charted, and the numbers left on {coach}'s desk every Friday. They're good numbers, and they do the arguing for you.

scenarios.title: The Broadcast Booth
scenarios.text: A network offers you a job in the broadcast booth when you're done: a three-year deal, a headset, and the chance to explain kicking to millions of people who never understood it.

authoring.premise: A network offers you a job in the booth when you're done.

choices.label: Say yes for later
choices.result: Yes, for later, with a handshake and a contract in a drawer. It's nice to know there's a door on the other side of all this.

choices.label: Ask {tyler}
choices.result: {tyler}, who's been in the booth for two years, tells you everything: the early mornings, the producers, the joy of it. You sign the next week.

choices.label: Keep the door open
choices.result: Not yet, you tell them, warmly. They say they'll ask again, and you believe them, and you put the idea away for later.

scenarios.title: The Coaching Offer
scenarios.text: A college asks if you'd coach their kickers when you retire: a small program, a good school, a field with a view of the mountains, and a head coach who used to be your holder.

authoring.premise: A college asks if you'd coach their kickers when you retire.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.result: Yes, for when the time comes. You start keeping notes on how you teach, and the head coach sends you a photo of your future office.

choices.label: Ask for time to think
choices.result: Time to think, and they give it to you gladly. You visit the campus in the spring and stand on the field for a long time.

choices.label: Stay home after football
choices.result: No, kindly. You want to be home when you're done, every night, for a long time. The college understands and keeps the door open.

choices.label: Tell them what you've learned teaching
choices.result: What you learned teaching younger kickers, explained over lunch. They offer you the job on the spot, and you shake on it.
choices.lock_text: having mentored kickers before

authoring.premise: You turn forty in camp. The rookies were in diapers when you kicked in high school.
waits_on: R1 no age cap (ages 39-41; 38 plays now)

authoring.premise: You've been the oldest player in the league for years now, and a reporter asks how long.

scenarios.title: The Last Contract
scenarios.text: This contract is probably the last one. Your agent says so out loud, gently, while you're signing it in the general manager's office, and nobody says anything for a moment.

authoring.premise: This contract is probably the last one, and your agent says so out loud.

choices.label: Make it count
choices.result: Every single day of it counts: every practice, every rep, every quiet goodbye you aren't quite ready to say out loud yet.

choices.label: Plan the end
choices.result: You plan the end with your agent and your family, calmly, at the kitchen table. It's a little sad, and you sleep well that night.

choices.label: Celebrate it
choices.result: You celebrate it with dinner at the place you went after your first contract. The same waiter is there, older, and remembers you.

scenarios.title: Your Kid Wants to Kick
scenarios.text: Your kid, twelve now, wants to kick in middle school and asks you to teach them. They've been watching you in the backyard for years, and they already have your stance.

authoring.premise: Your kid wants to kick in middle school, and asks you to teach them.

choices.label: Teach them in the backyard
choices.result: The backyard, every evening at six. They're better than you were at that age, and you don't tell them, yet.

choices.label: Keep it fun
choices.result: One tip a day and a lot of laughing. They fall in love with it the way you did, without pressure.

choices.label: Find them a good coach
choices.result: A good coach, found and hired, so you can just be the parent in the stands. It's harder than coaching, and better.

scenarios.title: The Ring of Honor
scenarios.text: The club wants to put your name in the stadium's ring of honor after you retire. The owner tells you in person, in the empty stadium, pointing at the spot.

authoring.premise: The club wants to put your name in the stadium's ring of honor after you retire.

choices.label: Call {parent} first
choices.result: {parent}, called before anyone else. He doesn't say anything for a long time, and then he asks you to describe the spot exactly.

choices.label: Ask them to wait
choices.result: Wait until you've actually retired, you ask. They agree, and it gives you something to look forward to on hard days.

choices.label: Ask to share it with the unit
choices.result: The long snapper and {holder}, you ask, should go up with you. The club agrees to think about it, and {holder} cries when you tell them.

scenarios.title: Cleaning Out the Locker
scenarios.text: The box from your old locker is still in the trunk of your car, three weeks after the release. Nobody walked by while you packed it.

authoring.premise: You're cleaning out a locker after a release for the first time, and nobody walks by.
authoring.note: At the new club, about the old one.

choices.label: Call someone from the old club
choices.result: {holder}, called from the parking lot of your new club. 'I should have come by,' they say. It helps more than you expected.

choices.label: Unpack it at the new place
choices.result: The box, unpacked at the new facility on the first day, into a new locker with the same routine. It feels like a fresh start.

choices.label: Leave it in the trunk
choices.result: The box stays in the trunk for a few more weeks. Some things take time, and you let them, and nobody asks.

scenarios.title: What's Next
scenarios.text: Your agent, {love_interest} and your accountant all ask you the same question in the same week of March, in almost exactly the same words: what's next?

authoring.premise: Your agent, your partner and your accountant all ask the same question in the same week.

choices.label: Make a real plan
choices.result: A real plan, on paper: three options, three timelines, one budget. It's the first time the future looks like something you can hold.

choices.label: Ask your family what they want
choices.result: Your family, asked directly what they want. Their answers change your whole list, and you're glad you asked before deciding anything.

choices.label: Answer after the season
choices.result: After the season, you tell everyone, and you mean it. You kick with a quiet mind, and the question waits patiently.

choices.label: Pull out the plan you already made
choices.result: You pull out the plan you started years ago. Most of it still fits, and the rest is easy to fix.
choices.lock_text: having prepared for life after football

authoring.premise: A rookie leaves a note in your locker: he grew up watching you.
waits_on: R1 no age cap (ages 39-41; 38 plays now)
authoring.note: Age 38 is reachable now (the cap retires a player after the age-38 season); ages above wait on R1.

scenarios.title: Love Again
scenarios.text: You're single in a new city. Then, at a teammate's birthday dinner, the person across the table asks a question about you instead of the league, and you're still talking when the restaurant starts stacking chairs.

authoring.premise: You're single in a new city, or the person you dated in college has followed you here, and it's starting to feel serious.
authoring.note: One scene for both paths: a player who ended things with the high school love interest meets someone new; a player who dated the college classmate makes the classmate the pro partner (locked choice). Committing re-points {love_interest} to the new partner (R8). Repeats after a breakup or divorce (cooldown 15 weeks).

choices.label: Ask to see them again
choices.result: A second dinner turns into a Sunday walk, then into a toothbrush at your place. It's new and easy, and you catch yourself smiling in film sessions.

choices.label: Enjoy being single
choices.result: Single, for now, on purpose. You cook badly for friends, sleep in on off days and answer to nobody, and it's the lightest you've felt since college.

choices.label: Keep the season first

scenarios.title: The Kid Wants to Quit
scenarios.text: Your kid wants to quit their own team, halfway through the season. They tell you in the car, staring out the window, and ask you not to be mad.

choices.label: Ask why, and listen
choices.result: Why, asked gently, and then a long time listening. It's not about the sport; it's about one coach and one bad week. You help with that instead.

choices.label: Ask them to finish the season

choices.label: Let them quit
choices.result: Quitting is fine, you say, and you mean it. The relief on their face is enormous, and they spend the spring learning guitar instead.

scenarios.title: Teenagers
scenarios.text: Your teenager comes home and says they're tired of being 'the kicker's kid' at school. Teachers ask about you, kids ask for tickets, and nobody asks about them.

authoring.premise: Your teenager says they're tired of being 'the kicker's kid' at school.

choices.label: Stay away from school
choices.result: No more school visits, no more signed balls for the auction. You disappear from their school life on purpose, and they relax within a month.

choices.label: Ask what they want people to know

choices.label: Tell them it gets easier
choices.result: It gets easier, you promise, and tell them about being {parent}'s kid in a small town. They roll their eyes, and they ask for more stories at dinner.

scenarios.title: A Second Child

authoring.premise: Another baby is coming, and the house already feels small.

choices.label: Plan the season around the baby
choices.result: The whole season, planned around the due date: flights, backups, a phone in the trainer's pocket. You're there when the baby arrives, at four in the morning.

choices.label: Make room
choices.result: A weekend of moving furniture with {sibling}, turning the office into a nursery. It's chaos and it's ready, and the older kids pick the paint.

choices.label: Ask the grandparents for help
choices.result: {parent}, asked to come and stay for the first month. The house is loud and full and happy, and everyone actually sleeps again.

scenarios.title: Someone New, Later

authoring.premise: Years after it ended, a friend's dinner party seats you next to someone who doesn't care about football at all.

choices.label: Call {best_friend} first

choices.label: Not ready yet
choices.result: A lovely evening, and a polite goodbye at the door. You're not ready yet, and you're honest enough with yourself to know it, which feels like progress.

scenarios.title: The Second Wedding
scenarios.text: Married before, both of you. Somewhere between the dishes and the dog, you start talking about doing it again with {love_interest}: smaller, quieter, and somehow harder to plan than the first time.

choices.label: The courthouse and a long dinner

choices.label: Invite the people who stayed

choices.label: Wait one more season

scenarios.title: The Anniversary

choices.label: Fly {love_interest} in
choices.result: A ticket for the last flight in, booked from the team bus. One night together in a strange city, and it's the best anniversary yet.

choices.label: Plan the real celebration

choices.label: Call for an hour
choices.result: An hour on the phone from the hotel, talking about the first year: the tiny apartment, the bad car. It's enough, almost.

scenarios.title: {parent} Moves In

authoring.premise: {parent} can't live alone anymore, and your house has a spare room.

choices.label: Bring him home
choices.result: The spare room, painted his favorite color, and his chair moved in from home. He complains for a month and then becomes the center of the house.

choices.label: Find him a good place nearby

choices.label: Share it with {sibling}
choices.result: {sibling}, called, and a plan made together: six months with each of you. It's fair, and it brings the two of you closer than you've been since childhood.

scenarios.title: {parent} in the Hospital Again
scenarios.text: Another call from home, on a Tuesday afternoon during film. This time the doctor uses the word 'months', and {parent} is the one who asks to speak to you.

authoring.premise: Another call from home. This time the doctor uses the word 'months'.

choices.label: Go home this week
choices.result: Home, this week, whatever it costs. You sit with him on the porch every evening and he tells you things he's never told anyone.

choices.label: Stay and call every night

choices.label: Bring him to a game
choices.result: A game, arranged with the club: a suite, a wheelchair ramp, his old jacket. He watches every warmup kick and cries at the anthem.

scenarios.title: The Funeral

choices.result: Back for Sunday, because he would have wanted you there. You kick with his old watch in your bag, and the whole team wears a patch with his initials.

choices.label: Send signed gear

scenarios.title: {best_friend} Is Sick

authoring.premise: {best_friend} calls with news that makes the season feel very small.

choices.label: Organize the support

choices.label: Call every night
choices.result: A call every night, ten minutes or an hour. Some nights you talk about nothing, and that's what {best_friend} needs most.

scenarios.title: {tyler} Retires

scenarios.title: The Mentor's Funeral

scenarios.title: The Coaching Clinic

authoring.premise: Someone wants to buy what you built, for more than you ever made kicking.

choices.label: Plan the next ten years

scenarios.title: The Comeback Year

choices.label: Bring the young players

choices.label: Prove it with numbers
choices.result: Every kick, charted, and the curve left on {coach}'s desk every Friday. The numbers do all the arguing for you, quietly.

scenarios.title: The Record Book

authoring.premise: You're close to a club record nobody thought a kicker would hold.

choices.label: Let yourself want it

scenarios.title: Hall of Fame Talk

choices.label: Make the case for kickers

choices.label: Laugh about it at home
choices.result: Both columns, read out loud at dinner in funny voices. Your family votes you in unanimously, and {parent} frames the good one.

scenarios.title: Your Number at the High School

authoring.premise: Your high school wants to retire your number.

choices.label: Walk out with {parent}
choices.result: Out onto the field with {parent} beside you, under the lights. The crowd stands, and {parent} squeezes your arm so hard it leaves a mark.

choices.label: Give the number to a kid

authoring.premise: A filmmaker wants to follow you for a season.

scenarios.title: The All-Decade Team

choices.label: Stay out of it

choices.label: Let yourself hope
choices.result: For a week, you let yourself hope out loud. It's fun, and you laugh at yourself for caring this much at your age.

authoring.premise: The season's over. Your body says stop, your agent says one more, and nobody at home has said anything yet.
You chose one more year. Every practice now has a little countdown in it.
The general manager calls in March. It's a short call.
They didn't say retire. They just stopped saying anything at all.

The last road trip. The flight attendants have heard, and so has the hotel.
The last home week of your career. The city knows, and so does every kid at practice.

choices.label: Keep kicking for now
choices.result: For now, you keep kicking, carefully. The doctor writes something in your file and asks you to come back in a month.

Your teammates throw a retirement party before you've even decided.

scenarios.title: Who Am I Without It

choices.result: Everything you are besides a kicker, written on a legal pad. The list is longer than you thought, and some of it surprises you.

choices.label: Walk until it's light
choices.result: A walk at three in the morning, through an empty neighborhood. The question comes with you, and so does the sunrise.

authoring.premise: You announced it. Now you want to take it back.
The last kick of your last practice. Nobody leaves the field.

scenarios.title: Young Again

choices.result: Your house, Sunday afternoon, a grill and the kids running around. Half the young players come, and it becomes a monthly thing.

choices.result: Later, at home, alone, with the sound turned low. You watch it three times in a row, and then you call {parent} to tell him about it.

choices.label: Kick through it
choices.result: Warmups, eyes down, while it plays above you. The video ends, the crowd roars, and you go back to work.

scenarios.title: The Old Teammates' Reunion
scenarios.text: Your rookie class has a reunion in a hotel ballroom. Half of them have bad knees and good stories, and the one who called home crying every night is now a surgeon.

authoring.premise: Your rookie class has a reunion. Half of them have bad knees and good stories.

choices.label: Stay until the end
choices.result: Until the last story, at two in the morning, in the lobby. You laugh harder than you have in years, and you all promise to do it again.

choices.label: Find the ones who struggled
choices.result: The ones who struggled after football, found and listened to. You leave with three phone numbers and two jobs to help with.

choices.label: Dinner and an early night
choices.result: Dinner, a few long hugs, and an early night back at the hotel. It's warm and brief, and on the flight home you're glad you went.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Wears Your Number
scenarios.text: A rookie at another club wears your number and tells a reporter you're the reason he started kicking. The clip is everywhere by morning, and your phone won't stop.

authoring.premise: A rookie at another club wears your number and says you're the reason.

choices.label: Call him
choices.result: Your call reaches him on his cell, and he's speechless for ten full seconds. You wish him luck, and he calls you every season after.

choices.label: Send him a note
choices.result: The best advice you ever got, written on a card and mailed to his locker. He tapes it inside, he says, forever.

choices.label: Smile and keep it
choices.result: A smile, kept to yourself, and the clip watched twice. You don't reach out, and it stays with you all week.

scenarios.title: A Teammate's Kid Asks for Advice
scenarios.text: A teammate's teenage kid kicks for a high school team and wants your advice. She has film on her phone and a very specific question about her plant foot.

authoring.premise: A teammate's teenage kid kicks for a high school team and wants your advice.

choices.label: Watch the film with her
choices.result: The film, watched with her twice. Her question is a good one, and the answer takes an hour and a trip to the practice field.

choices.label: Invite her to practice
choices.result: A practice pass for her and her father. She kicks on the stadium field after practice, and her face is something you'll remember.

choices.label: Answer the one question
choices.result: Her one question, answered clearly, in five minutes. She thanks you and goes off to fix it, and her father texts you a video a week later.

scenarios.title: The Coach You Outlasted
scenarios.text: The head coach who drafted you is fired after a bad season, in a short statement on a Monday. You've outlasted him. It doesn't feel like a win at all.

authoring.premise: The head coach who drafted you is fired. You're still here.

choices.label: Call him
choices.result: You call him that night. He thanks you for calling, talks about your rookie camp for twenty minutes, and you hear his family in the background.

choices.label: Steady the room
choices.result: You steady the room the next morning, before the rumors start. The new coach hears about it before you meet him.

choices.label: Keep going
choices.result: You keep going, because that's the business, and you've seen it before. You keep his old playbook on a shelf at home, though.

authoring.premise: The club's analysts present a chart: your leg is getting older faster than you are.
Your longest kick in practice is five yards shorter than last year. The coaches haven't said it, but they've noticed.
The owner who signed you dies, and the family asks you to speak.

scenarios.title: A Midnight Call From an Old Teammate

authoring.premise: A teammate from your rookie year is broke and calls you at midnight.
Retired players are organizing for better health care, and they want a current player at the meeting.
A lineman you played with for years doesn't remember your name at a reunion.

scenarios.title: The Last of Your Draft Class

authoring.premise: You're the last player from your draft class still in the league.

scenarios.title: The Kid Who Was Born on Draft Day

authoring.premise: A rookie mentions he was born the week you were drafted.
Turning forty in the league: a birthday cake in the locker room and a question in every interview.
waits_on: R1 no age cap (ages 39-41; 38 plays now)

scenarios.title: The Captaincy
scenarios.text: The team votes for captains, and for the first time in the club's history a kicker is on the ballot. Your name is written on the whiteboard in the locker room, misspelled.

authoring.premise: The team votes for captains, and for the first time a kicker is on the ballot.

choices.label: Ask for the vote
choices.result: Why a kicker can lead too: you tell the room in two minutes, plainly. You win by four votes, and they fix the spelling on the whiteboard.

choices.label: Let the room decide
choices.result: No campaign at all. The room votes you in anyway, by more, and that means more than any speech would have.

choices.label: Take your name off the ballot
choices.result: Your name, erased from the whiteboard by you. A linebacker who wanted it more gets the patch, and thanks you privately.

scenarios.title: The Big Second Contract
scenarios.text: Your agent says this is the contract that matters, the one that sets the rest of your life, and the club agrees, eventually, after a month of silence.

authoring.premise: Your agent says this is the contract that matters, and the club agrees, eventually.

choices.label: Hold firm for your number
choices.result: Three tense weeks of holding firm. You get your number, and lose some sleep getting it, and the general manager doesn't smile at you for a while.

choices.label: Take the fair deal early
choices.result: A fair deal, taken early, and you stop thinking about it entirely. Your agent calls it smart, and means it, and you sleep well all spring.

choices.label: Decide it at home
choices.result: The decision, made at home, at the kitchen table. The number matters less than you thought, and you sign happily.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Becomes a Coach
scenarios.text: {holder} retires and joins the coaching staff, with a whistle and a new office. Now {holder} is your boss, and the first meeting is tomorrow.

authoring.premise: Your holder retires and joins the coaching staff. Now they're your boss.

choices.label: Keep the friendship
choices.result: The friendship stays, and you let {holder} coach you anyway. It works, mostly, and only gets strange at parties and team dinners.

choices.label: Set new rules together
choices.result: New rules, agreed over coffee: coach at the facility, friends on the weekend. It works better than either of you expected.

choices.label: Earn their trust fresh
choices.result: {holder}, treated like any new coach, and you earn their trust again from scratch. It's strange, and it makes you both better.

scenarios.title: The Endorsement Renewal
scenarios.text: Your biggest sponsor wants to renew, with new conditions: more appearances, more posts, more of you. The contract is twice as long as the first one.

authoring.premise: Your biggest sponsor wants to renew, with new conditions.

choices.label: Accept the conditions
choices.result: Accepted. The money is good, and your weeks get much shorter, and you start to recognize the sponsor's photographer at your house.

choices.label: Halve the appearances
choices.result: The appearances, negotiated down by half, line by line. They agree, grudgingly, and you keep your Tuesdays and your sanity.

choices.label: Walk away from the renewal
choices.result: The renewal, politely declined. You get your Tuesdays back, and your agent finds a smaller, kinder deal within a month.

scenarios.title: The Hometown Charity Game
scenarios.text: You organize a charity game in your hometown with players from five clubs: a high school field, a sold-out crowd of four thousand, and a lot of favors called in.

authoring.premise: You organize a charity game in your hometown with players from five clubs.

choices.label: Run every detail yourself
choices.result: Every detail, run by you: buses, jerseys, the national anthem singer. It's exhausting, and it raises far more than anyone expected.

choices.label: Put {best_friend} in charge
choices.result: {best_friend} runs the whole day, with a clipboard and a whistle. It's the most fun either of you has had in years.

choices.label: Hire an organizer
choices.result: An event organizer who actually knows what they're doing. It runs perfectly, and it feels a little less like yours on the day.

scenarios.title: The Rival Club Calls
scenarios.text: A rival club's general manager catches you at an awards dinner and makes it very clear, without saying it outright, that they'd pay you a lot more the next time you're free.

authoring.premise: A rival club's general manager makes it clear they'd pay more, next time you're free.

choices.label: Keep it between you and your agent
choices.result: Your agent hears every word, and nobody else does. You kick the rest of the season like a player with options, calmly and well.

choices.label: Tell your own club
choices.result: Your own general manager hears about the conversation from you, the next morning. They appreciate it more than they say, and they remember it at contract time.

choices.label: Forget the conversation
choices.result: Forgotten, on purpose, by the time you're home. You kick the season out without thinking about it, and whatever comes in spring, comes.

scenarios.title: The Motivation Slump
scenarios.text: Nothing's wrong. That's the problem: practice feels like a job, the job feels like nothing, and you haven't been nervous before a game in a month.

authoring.premise: Nothing's wrong. That's the problem: practice feels like a job, and the job feels like nothing.

choices.label: Take a real break
choices.result: Days off, taken seriously for once: no film, no phone, a long hike in the hills. Some of the spark comes back, slowly, by the end of the month.

choices.label: Talk to someone
choices.result: Out loud, for the first time, to the team psychologist. It's uncomfortable and it helps, and you go back the next week.

choices.label: Set a secret goal
