choices.result: A goal nobody else knows about, written on a card in your wallet. Practice has a point again, and you catch yourself smiling during warmups.

scenarios.title: The Kid Who Copies Your Routine
scenarios.text: A high school kicker's video goes around the internet: he copies your whole routine, down to the last step and the way you tug your sleeve.

authoring.premise: A high school kicker's video goes around: he copies your routine down to the last step.

choices.label: Send him a message and cleats
choices.result: A message and a pair of cleats. His video of opening the box gets more views than yours ever did.

choices.label: Show him one fix
choices.result: A short reply video showing him one thing to fix. Kickers everywhere try it, and his school's coach writes to thank you.

choices.label: Smile and show {love_interest}
choices.result: A smile, and the video shown to {love_interest} over dinner, twice. You don't reply, and you think about it all week.

scenarios.title: A Teammate Holds Out
scenarios.text: Your closest teammate is holding out for a new contract and wants you to say something publicly. The front office is watching who stands with him.

authoring.premise: Your closest teammate is holding out for a new contract, and wants you to say something publicly.

choices.label: Back him publicly
choices.result: You back him publicly in front of the cameras. He's grateful for good, and the front office remembers your name in a different way.

choices.label: Back him privately
choices.result: Privately, at his kitchen table, you say you're with him all the way. He understands why it stays private, and wishes you'd said it louder.

choices.label: Speak for the room
choices.result: You tell reporters the whole team wants him back and leave the money to the people who handle it. Both sides nod, neither is thrilled.

scenarios.title: The Coordinator's Son
scenarios.text: The new special teams coordinator's son is a kicker on the practice squad. He's polite, talented, and his father watches every one of his kicks with great interest.

authoring.premise: The new special teams coordinator's son is a kicker on the practice squad.

choices.label: Out-kick him every day
choices.result: Better than him every single day of camp. It's awkward and undeniable, and the coordinator starts watching your kicks just as closely.

choices.label: Help the kid
choices.result: His plant foot, fixed with your help. The coordinator watches and says nothing, and something between you changes for good.

choices.label: Ask the coordinator directly
choices.result: How exactly is the job decided? You ask him straight, in his office. He respects the question and gives you a fair, specific answer.

scenarios.title: Ten Years
scenarios.text: Ten years in the league. The pension kicks in, the club gives you a watch, and the question arrives with it, uninvited: how many more?

authoring.premise: Ten years in the league. The pension kicks in, and so does the question of how many more.

choices.label: Go for more
choices.result: Not done, not close. You tell {coach} and your agent the same thing, and you start the eleventh year angrier than the first.

choices.label: Plan the next five years
choices.result: The next five years, planned with your agent and your family at the kitchen table. Everyone breathes easier, including you.

choices.label: Celebrate with the people who got you here
choices.result: A party for everyone who got you here: coaches, holders, {parent}, {best_friend}. The watch goes around the room twice, and {parent} cries.

scenarios.title: The Prime-Time Game
scenarios.text: Your first prime-time game in years, and the national broadcast crew wants an interview at the team hotel the night before. They want a 'human' story.

authoring.premise: Your first prime-time game in years, and the broadcast crew wants an interview at the hotel.

choices.label: Tell them a real story
choices.result: One good story, about kicking into a fence with {parent}. It runs before kickoff, and {parent} watches it on repeat.

choices.label: Give them ten minutes
choices.result: Ten polite minutes, then bed. The story they run is fine and forgettable, and you sleep well and wake up ready.

choices.label: Decline and watch film
choices.result: A polite no, and film in your room instead until midnight. The crew talks to the punter, who is absolutely delighted.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Advice
scenarios.text: An eleven-year veteran pulls you aside after practice, sits you on a bench by the field and says he has a few rules for surviving the league, if you're smart enough to want them.

authoring.premise: An established teammate pulls you aside with a few rules for surviving the league.

choices.label: Write them down tonight
choices.result: Every rule goes in a notebook that night. Some are about kicking; most are about money, agents and who to trust. You reread them every season after.

choices.label: Ask about his worst season
choices.result: His worst season comes out over an hour on that bench: the cut, the divorce, the comeback. You learn more from the story than from any rule.

choices.label: Nod and forget them
choices.result: Nodding politely gets you to dinner on time, and you forget the rules by dessert. Three of them come back to you later, the hard way.

scenarios.title: The First Media Interview
scenarios.text: Local reporters catch you at your locker on your second day, before anyone has taught you what not to say. There are four microphones, and one of them is very close to your face.

authoring.premise: Local reporters catch you at your locker before you've learned what not to say.

choices.label: Keep it boring
choices.result: Short, polite answers and nothing quotable. The story that runs is boring, which {coach} likes, and your agent sends you a thumbs-up you didn't expect.

choices.label: Be yourself
choices.result: You joke, tell a story about your college holder and admit you're nervous. The reporters like you, and so do the fans.

choices.label: Say something bold
choices.result: You say you'll be the best kicker in the league in three years. It's the headline, and the veterans tape it to your locker.

scenarios.title: The Missed Opportunity
scenarios.text: A bad practice in front of the whole staff: three misses in a row from your favorite spot, the general manager watching from the sideline. By lunch someone in the building is asking about your roster spot.

authoring.premise: A bad practice in front of the whole staff, and someone in the building is already asking about your roster spot.

choices.label: Find out what the staff saw
choices.result: {coach} pulls up the practice film after lunch and freezes it on your plant foot. It's a timing issue, and fixable, and you breathe properly for the first time all day.

choices.label: Kick until the lights come on
choices.result: Long after everyone leaves, you're still out there, kicking until it feels right again. The groundskeeper finally turns the lights on for you and doesn't say a word.

choices.label: Leave it at the facility
choices.result: One practice doesn't define a season, you decide, and you leave it at the facility. Tomorrow is better, mostly, though the general manager's face stays with you on the drive home.

scenarios.title: The Agent Calls
scenarios.text: Your agent calls on a Tuesday night to talk about your contract, your future and a few things you'd rather not hear, starting with the list of reasons rookies get cut before October.

authoring.premise: Your agent calls to talk about your contract, your future and a few things you'd rather not hear.

choices.label: Listen to all of it
choices.result: The whole list, start to finish, without interrupting once. It's sobering to hear out loud, and by the end you know exactly which mistakes you're never going to make.

choices.label: Ask for a two-year plan
choices.result: A real plan for the next two years arrives in your inbox by Friday, in writing, with dates. It's the first time your career has looked like something you can steer.

choices.label: Cut the call short
choices.result: Kicking is all you want to think about, so the call ends early. Your agent sends the list by email anyway, and you read it at two in the morning.

scenarios.title: The First Endorsement
scenarios.text: A local car wash offers you your first sponsorship: a billboard by the highway, four appearances in a giant foam sponge costume and a check that's small, but yours.

authoring.premise: A local business offers you your first sponsorship: a billboard, a few appearances, a small check.

choices.label: Sign with the car wash
choices.result: The billboard goes up by the highway a week later, a little blurry, and every teammate sends you a photo of it. The holder sets it as his phone background.

choices.label: Ask your agent first
choices.result: Your agent negotiates the appearances down to two and the check up by half. The owner still makes you wear the sponge costume once, and you secretly love it.

choices.label: Keep your weeks clear
choices.result: No billboard, no sponge suit, no appearances. Your weeks stay clear for kicking, your account stays the same, and the car wash signs a local weatherman instead.

scenarios.title: The Old Friend's Request
scenarios.text: {best_friend} calls from home on a Sunday night and asks you for money. It's quiet for a long time before they ask, and you can hear how much it costs them to say it.

authoring.premise: Someone from home asks you for money, and you can tell it took a lot to ask.

choices.label: Send it that night
choices.result: The money is in {best_friend}'s account before you hang up, and you never ask what it's for. They cry on the phone, and so, after the call, do you.

choices.label: Ask what it's for
choices.result: It's rent, three months behind. Paying the landlord directly makes both of you feel better, and {best_friend} sends you a photo of the receipt with a heart on it.

choices.label: Say no kindly
choices.result: No, as kindly as you can manage. It's true and it isn't, and the next phone call with {best_friend} is shorter, and the one after that doesn't come.

scenarios.title: The Long-Distance Relationship
scenarios.text: {love_interest} is three states away, and your schedule doesn't have room for flights. Your calls have started ending with long silences neither of you knows how to fill.

authoring.premise: {love_interest} is three states away, and your schedule doesn't have room for flights.

choices.label: Fly them in for the bye
choices.result: A flight for the bye week, booked that night. It's short, and it's enough until the next one, and you both cry at the airport.

choices.label: Call every night at ten
choices.result: A video call every night at ten, no matter what. Some nights it's five minutes and a yawn, and it holds.

choices.label: Put the season first
choices.result: The season comes first, you explain, and you'll make it up in the offseason. {love_interest} says okay, too quickly, and hangs up first.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Criticism
scenarios.text: {coach} tells you, in front of the specialists, that your preparation isn't professional yet. The punter suddenly studies the floor, and {holder} won't look at you.

authoring.premise: {coach} tells you, in front of the specialists, that your preparation isn't professional yet.

choices.label: Ask for specifics
choices.result: Three specific things, you ask for, and {coach} lists them on a whiteboard: film, sleep, and the way you warm up. By November you've done all three, and the coach notices.

choices.label: Show up an hour earlier
choices.result: An hour earlier every day for a month, and you never mention why. {coach} never mentions it either, but your name moves to the top of the practice sheet.

choices.label: Push back
choices.result: Your preparation got you here, you point out. The specialists go very quiet, {holder} gives you a look that says 'not now', and {coach} walks away mid-sentence.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Mistake
scenarios.text: At the team's charity gala, you trip over a cable in front of a dessert table, take the whole thing down with you, and come up wearing a cheesecake. Three cameras catch every second.

authoring.premise: You make an embarrassing mistake at a team event, and the veterans won't let you forget it.

choices.label: Laugh at yourself
choices.result: Laughing first saves you. You help clean up, then post the clip yourself with a caption about your leg strength. It's the most popular thing you've ever posted.

choices.label: Pay for the desserts
choices.result: The organizers get an apology and a check for the desserts before the night is over. They're touched, and the event coordinator invites you back to run the dessert table next year.

choices.label: Hope nobody saw
choices.result: Slipping out early doesn't help: the veterans saw, and they leave a slice of cheesecake in your locker every week for the rest of the season. You spend the night at the kicking net.

scenarios.title: The First Charity Event
scenarios.text: The club sends you to a community center's reading day, alone, with a box of picture books and no instructions. Twenty kids sit on a rug, waiting to see what a kicker is for.

authoring.premise: The club sends you to represent it at a community event, and nobody tells you what to say.

choices.label: Read to the kids
choices.result: Sitting on the floor, you read three books in terrible voices, including a very dramatic dragon. The kids demand a fourth, and one of them asks for your autograph on her shoe.

choices.label: Talk about school
choices.result: How hard school was, and why you kept going: you tell them all of it, simply. A teacher finds you afterward and says one boy in the back needed exactly that.

choices.label: Sign and leave on time
choices.result: Autographs, a smile, a group photo, and you're out on time. It's perfectly fine and nobody remembers it, including you, by the following week.

scenarios.title: The Social Media Post
scenarios.text: An old post from college resurfaces the week your name starts showing up in the papers. It's not terrible, but it's not who you are now, and a fan account has just shared it to fifty thousand people.

authoring.premise: An old post resurfaces the week your name starts showing up in the papers.

choices.label: Delete it and apologize
choices.result: Deleted, then a short apology in your own words, no statement from a publicist. It fades in a day, and two teammates text that they respected how you handled it.

choices.label: Leave it up
choices.result: Silence, and the post stays up. It keeps resurfacing every time your name trends, for a month, and the club's media staff starts sighing when you walk past.

choices.label: Get the media staff's help
choices.result: The club's media staff walks you through it in ten minutes, calmly, like they've done it a hundred times. Nobody remembers the post by Friday.

choices.label: Do what worked before
choices.result: This has happened before, so you know the steps: delete, two honest sentences, practice. It's over by lunch, and the media staff asks if you want a job.
choices.lock_text: having handled an old post the right way before

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Party
scenarios.text: A teammate is throwing a party the night before a seven o'clock workout, and the whole rookie class is going. Your phone has been buzzing about it since lunch.

authoring.premise: A teammate's party the night before an early workday, and the whole rookie class is going.

choices.label: Go for an hour
choices.result: An hour of saying hello, then home before ten. Two rookies call you boring in the group chat. In the morning meeting, you're the only one who can keep their eyes open.

choices.label: Sleep instead
choices.result: Nine hours of sleep, and the stories at breakfast are all yours to enjoy secondhand. You feel completely fine about missing them, which surprises you a little.

choices.label: Stay until the end
choices.result: Three in the morning, and you're still there. The workout is a blur, {coach} asks if you're sick, and you tell the truth, which somehow makes it worse.

scenarios.title: The New City
scenarios.text: Two months in {town}, and you've seen the facility, the grocery store and the inside of your apartment. Your blinds have been closed since September.

authoring.premise: You can explore {town} or stay in your apartment with the blinds closed.

choices.label: Explore one neighborhood a week
choices.result: A different neighborhood every week, on foot, with no plan. By midseason you know {town} better than some teammates who grew up here, and you have a favorite bakery.

choices.label: Find one place to belong
choices.result: One diner, one gym and one coffee shop, every week, until the people there know your name. It's small, and it's the first time {town} feels like yours.

choices.label: Keep the blinds closed
choices.result: The apartment stays dark between practices. It's restful and easy, and {town} stays a stranger you drive through on the way to work.

scenarios.title: The Family Visit
scenarios.text: {parent} and {sibling} want to visit for a weekend in October. Your schedule doesn't have a weekend in it, and {parent} has already looked up flights and a hotel near the stadium.

authoring.premise: Your family wants to visit for a weekend, and your schedule doesn't have a weekend in it.

choices.label: Make it work
choices.result: The guest room, practice in the morning, every evening with them. You're exhausted by Sunday and happier than you've been in weeks, and {sibling} cries a little at the airport.

choices.label: Ask them to wait for the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, you promise, with a whole week. {parent} understands right away; {sibling} is disappointed and says so, and doesn't text you for a few days.

choices.label: Bring them to practice
choices.result: Two passes to practice and lunch with the team. {sibling} meets the quarterback and talks about it for months, and {parent} keeps the visitor badge on the fridge.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Attention
scenarios.text: Someone recognizes you in the cereal aisle and follows you through three more aisles, talking the whole time about a kick you made in college that you barely remember.

authoring.premise: Someone recognizes you at the grocery store and won't stop talking.

choices.label: Be gracious
choices.result: Stopping costs you ten minutes and a photo by the frozen peas. It makes someone's week, and they post it with a caption about how nice you are.

choices.label: Keep moving, politely
choices.result: A smile, a thank-you and you keep moving. They post that you were 'a little cold', and three people you've never met argue about it for a day.

choices.label: Shop at night
choices.result: Eleven at night becomes your shopping hour. Nobody recognizes you, the cereal aisle is yours alone, and the night cashier starts saving you the good bananas.

scenarios.title: The Local Radio Appearance
scenarios.text: A sports radio show invites you on, live, during drive time. The host is famous for getting rookies to say things, and the producer has warned you there'll be callers.

authoring.premise: A sports radio show invites you on, live, during drive time.

choices.label: Prepare and go
choices.result: Three stories prepared, all light, and you stick to them. The host can't get anything controversial out of you, laughs anyway and invites you back next month.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.result: No notes. One joke lands beautifully; one answer about the coaching staff gets replayed all week, and {coach} mentions it, dryly, in the next meeting.

choices.label: Spend the hour at the net
choices.result: A polite no, and the hour goes to the kicking net instead. The host makes a joke about shy kickers on air, and you never hear it.

scenarios.title: The Practice Routine
scenarios.text: Your college routine isn't working at this level: too slow for the snapper, too long for the play clock. You need a new one by Sunday, and the veterans are watching to see what you build.

authoring.premise: Your college routine isn't working at this level, and you need a new one by Sunday.

choices.label: Borrow the snapper's rhythm
choices.result: The veteran snapper's pre-kick rhythm becomes yours, step for step. It feels strange for two days, then it feels like it was always yours, and he's quietly proud.

choices.label: Build your own
choices.result: From scratch, charting every kick for a week in a notebook. The new routine is yours entirely, and it holds up when the stadium gets loud.

choices.label: Build it with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} spends an hour with you after practice, building it piece by piece. The coach is clearly pleased you asked, and starts asking your opinion in meetings.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Upgrade
scenarios.text: A sales rep corners you after practice with expensive training equipment: a sensor suit, a kicking machine, and an app that charts every kick you've ever taken. He has a tablet and a very good smile.

authoring.premise: A sales rep wants you on expensive new training equipment, with a price to match.

choices.label: Buy the full setup
choices.result: All of it, delivered Thursday. The data is incredible, your living room is full of machines, and the bill is the kind you read twice.

choices.label: Use what the club has
choices.result: The club's staff charts you with what they already have. It's less fancy and nearly as good, and the trainer likes being asked.

choices.label: Keep it simple
choices.result: Your leg doesn't need an app, you decide. The rep leaves his card, your weeks stay simple, and you never think about sensor suits again.

scenarios.title: The First Contract Question
scenarios.text: A reporter asks at your locker whether you expect a contract extension. You haven't kicked a regular-season game yet, and the veteran kicker you replaced is standing two lockers away.

authoring.premise: A reporter asks whether you expect an extension, and you haven't kicked a regular-season game.

choices.label: Joke about keeping your locker
choices.result: Just trying to keep your locker, you say, and grin. The quote is charming, nobody reads into it, and the veteran two lockers down actually laughs.

choices.label: Say you've earned a look
choices.result: You think you've earned a look, you say. The front office reads it by dinner, and so does the veteran, who stops saying good morning.

choices.label: Leave contracts to your agent
choices.result: Contracts are your agent's job. It's dull and smart, the reporter moves on, and {coach} gives you a small nod across the room.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Struggle
scenarios.text: A fellow rookie is falling apart: late to meetings, quiet at lunch, gone the minute practice ends. Yesterday he forgot his helmet. Nobody's said anything to him yet.

authoring.premise: A fellow rookie is falling apart, and nobody else seems to notice.

choices.label: Knock on his door
choices.result: His door, after practice, and you stay for an hour. He doesn't say much about what's wrong, but he's early to the next meeting, and he sits next to you.

choices.label: Tell a veteran
choices.result: A veteran you trust hears about it quietly, from you. The veteran handles it better than you could have, and the rookie never finds out who spoke up.

choices.label: Mind your own business
choices.result: Your own roster spot is enough to worry about. He's released a month later, and you think about that empty locker longer than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Family Expectations
scenarios.text: Your family expects more now that you're earning. Cousins call about cars, an uncle about a boat, and {parent} about a roof that's been leaking since you were in high school.

authoring.premise: Your family expects more now that you're earning, and they're not shy about it.

choices.label: Set a family budget
choices.result: A yearly amount for family help, set at the kitchen table with {parent}. It's an awkward hour, and it ends the guessing, and the cousins stop calling about cars.

choices.label: Say yes to everything
choices.result: Yes to every request. It feels wonderful for a month, and your account feels it much longer, and nobody says thank you for the third one.

choices.label: Say not yet
choices.result: A rookie contract isn't forever money, you explain, as patiently as you can. Some of them understand. {sibling} doesn't, and says something you'll both remember.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Bill
scenarios.text: Your car's transmission dies the week before a road trip, in the facility parking lot, in front of the whole offensive line. The repair costs more than the car is worth.

authoring.premise: A costly bill arrives at the worst possible time.

choices.label: Fix it
choices.result: Repaired, and a week of buses to practice in the meantime. The veterans think it's hilarious and start leaving bus schedules in your locker.

choices.label: Buy something new
choices.result: A brand-new car the same afternoon. It's lovely, it smells incredible, and the payment is going to follow you around for years.

choices.label: Ride with a teammate
choices.result: Rides with a teammate until you figure it out, and the drives turn into the best part of your week. By the time your car is fixed, you're friends.

scenarios.title: The Former Coach Calls
scenarios.text: Your old college coach calls on a quiet Wednesday night to check in. After the small talk, there's a pause, and then the question: how are you really doing?

authoring.premise: Your old college coach calls to check in, and asks how you're really doing.

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.result: Harder than you expected, you admit. Your old coach tells you about every player who said the same thing in their first year, and made it anyway.

choices.label: Say it's great
choices.result: Everything's great, you insist. Your old coach doesn't believe you, says so kindly, and leaves the door open for another call.

choices.label: Ask for help with one thing
choices.result: One specific problem: your timing on short kicks. Your old coach watches your practice film that night and calls back the next morning with an answer.

scenarios.title: The Community Invitation
scenarios.text: A local high school asks you to speak to its athletes about what it takes to make it. The gym will be full, the principal has put your photo on the marquee, and you've never given a speech.

authoring.premise: A local school asks you to speak to its athletes.

choices.label: Speak honestly
choices.result: The cuts, the doubts, the practice you nearly quit: all of it comes out, simply. Three kids stay after with questions, and one of them is the school's kicker.

choices.label: Run a clinic instead
choices.result: No speech: a kicking clinic on their muddy field instead. Everyone gets filthy, the principal joins in, and the kids remember it better than any speech.

choices.label: Send your regrets
choices.result: The schedule's too full, you explain. They invite a retired linebacker instead, and you see the photos later and wish you'd gone.

scenarios.title: The Dating Question
scenarios.text: Someone you meet at a teammate's dinner party seems much more interested in the league than in you: salaries, famous teammates, whether you can get them into the owner's box.

authoring.premise: Someone you meet seems more interested in the league than in you.

choices.label: Ask them out anyway
choices.result: The date happens, and they ask a lot about the league and a little about you. You don't call again, and you learn to recognize it faster next time.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Every time football comes up, you steer away from it. By dessert, they're laughing at your terrible cooking stories, and you realize you're having a good time.

choices.label: Thank the host and go
choices.result: An early thank-you to the host, and you drive home. You'd rather be bored than be someone's résumé, and the drive home is peaceful.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Celebration
scenarios.text: The locker room has a social life: a card game in the back, a weekly dinner, a group that goes out after home games. Everyone's waiting to see how far into it the new kicker wants to go.

authoring.premise: The locker room has a social scene, and you have to decide how far into it you want to go.

choices.label: Join in, within reason
choices.result: The card game and the weekly dinner, yes; the late nights, no. By midseason you're part of the room, and nobody minds that you leave at ten.

choices.label: Pick one thing
choices.result: Just the weekly dinner. You know a few teammates well instead of all of them a little, and two of them become real friends.

choices.label: Keep to your routine
choices.result: Your routine, and nothing else: film, sleep, practice. Your kicking is sharp, and by October nobody in the room thinks to invite you anywhere.

scenarios.title: The Position Meeting
scenarios.text: Your place on the depth chart came up in a meeting you weren't invited to. The long snapper tells you about it at lunch, quietly, then goes back to his sandwich.

authoring.premise: Your place on the depth chart comes up in a meeting you weren't invited to.

choices.label: Ask where you stand
choices.result: {coach} gives you an honest answer in the hallway: safe, for now, if the next month looks like the last one. It's not comfortable, and it's clear.

choices.label: Kick and say nothing
choices.result: Silence, and the best week of practice you've had since camp. Nobody calls another meeting about you, and the snapper starts eating lunch at your table.

choices.label: Call your agent
choices.result: Your agent calls the general manager, who calls {coach}. By Wednesday everyone in the building knows you asked, and {coach} is cooler with you for a while.

scenarios.title: The New Playbook
scenarios.text: A new coaching staff arrives with a new playbook and new expectations for the specialists: three hundred pages, eleven new formations, and a written test on Friday.

authoring.premise: A new coaching staff installs a new playbook and new expectations for the specialists.

choices.label: Learn it cold
choices.result: Every page, cold, including the parts that aren't yours. The new coordinator notices you correcting a linebacker in the walkthrough and remembers your name.

choices.label: Learn your part
choices.result: Your part, perfectly, and nothing else. It's enough for the test, and you get a full night's sleep before it.

choices.label: Study with the unit
choices.result: A study session with the snapper and {holder} turns into a unit dinner, then a weekly tradition. Everyone passes, and you all argue about formations over dessert.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Comparison
scenarios.text: Every week, the local media compare you with another young kicker by name, in charts and columns and one very loud radio segment. You've never met him.

authoring.premise: The media compare you with another young kicker, every week, by name.

choices.label: Call the other kicker
choices.result: A phone call, and you're both laughing within a minute. You agree not to read anything with both your names in it, and to have dinner when your teams play.

choices.label: Put the charts on your locker
choices.result: The comparison goes up on your locker, and every practice becomes a contest. You're sharper by November, and a little more tired.

choices.label: Stop reading it
choices.result: No columns, no charts, no radio. It takes real discipline for two weeks, then it's just quiet, and you stop wondering how the other kicker is doing.

scenarios.title: The Charity Donation
scenarios.text: Your aunt calls from home: the church you grew up in needs a new roof, and she's sure you'll want to help. She has already told the whole congregation you're thinking about it.

authoring.premise: A family member asks you to donate to a cause back home.

choices.label: Give generously
choices.result: More than she asked. The church puts your name on a brass plaque by the door, which you'll be embarrassed by forever, and {parent} visits it every Sunday.

choices.label: Give what you planned
choices.result: The amount in your budget, with an explanation. She's a little disappointed and grateful anyway, and the roof gets fixed by spring.

choices.label: Run a fundraiser at home
choices.result: A fundraiser in your hometown, run with {sibling}, raises twice the money with your time instead of your account. The whole town shows up.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Advice
scenarios.text: A veteran tells you, very calmly, at lunch, how fast a career can end: his roommate from his rookie year lasted one season and now sells insurance two towns over.

authoring.premise: A veteran explains, very calmly, how fast a career can end.

choices.label: Ask what he did differently
choices.result: What did he do differently? His answer has nothing to do with kicking: he saved, he slept, he showed up early, and he never thought he was safe.

choices.label: Let it scare you
choices.result: It scares you, properly. You start saving half of every check and sleeping nine hours a night, and you check the transaction wire more than you should.

choices.label: Shrug it off
choices.result: It won't happen to you, you say with a shrug. The veteran nods slowly, like he's heard exactly that before, and finishes his lunch.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Warning
scenarios.text: Your agent warns you to be careful about where you're seen: a teammate's photo outside a nightclub at two in the morning just cost him a sponsor and a fine.

authoring.premise: Your agent warns you to be careful about where you're seen in public.

choices.label: Change your routine
choices.result: No more nights out after home games. You're bored some Saturdays and safe all of them, and the club's media staff stops looking nervous when you walk in.

choices.label: Get the real list
choices.result: A specific list of what's actually off-limits, from your agent, by text. It's shorter than you feared, and much clearer than 'be careful'.

choices.label: Brush off the warning
choices.result: You're not doing anything wrong, you insist, and keep your routine. Your agent sighs and sends a second email with the word 'please' in the subject line.

scenarios.title: The Apartment Neighbor
scenarios.text: Your neighbor works nights and practices drums at noon, which is the only hour of the day you have for a nap. It's been two weeks, and he's getting better, which is worse.

authoring.premise: Your neighbor's schedule and yours are at war, and the walls are thin.

choices.label: Knock and explain
choices.result: A knock, a short explanation, and it turns out he's a fan. He moves practice to the evening and leaves two tickets to his band's show on your mat.

choices.label: Call the building manager
choices.result: The building manager makes the drumming stop within a day. So does the neighbor's friendly wave in the hallway, permanently.

choices.label: Buy good earplugs
choices.result: Very good earplugs, and you nap anyway. It works, mostly, and the neighbor waves at you every morning, never knowing.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Criticism
scenarios.text: Somebody posts a week of your bad practice clips online, set to sad music, and fans tear into you in the replies. {parent} has found it, and has been replying to strangers.

authoring.premise: Fans tear into you online after one bad week of practice clips.

choices.label: Log off
choices.result: The apps are deleted for a week. It's quiet and it helps, and you call {parent} to ask him, gently, to stop arguing with strangers on your behalf.

choices.label: Reply with humor
choices.result: A joke about your own form, in reply, with a slow-motion clip of your worst miss. It's the most-liked reply of the week, and the tone changes.

choices.label: Save the worst one
choices.result: A screenshot of the worst reply goes on your locker. Every rep that week has a little extra in it, and the clips stop coming.

scenarios.title: The Second Contract Conversation
scenarios.text: Your agent starts talking, over a long lunch, about what your second contract could look like if you last that long. There's a napkin with numbers on it.

authoring.premise: Your agent starts talking about what your next contract could look like, if you last.

choices.label: Ask what lasting looks like
choices.result: What does the club actually look for in a second contract? The list is specific, and you can work on every item, starting tomorrow.

choices.label: Dream a little
choices.result: The house, the car, the security: you let yourself picture all of it. It's motivating, mostly, and you keep the napkin.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Not past this season, you say, and push the napkin back. Your agent grins and says that's exactly the right answer.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Rules
scenarios.text: The veterans post the locker room's unwritten rules on a whiteboard, and one of them is about you, in red marker: 'Kickers don't talk in team meetings.'

authoring.premise: The veterans post the locker room's unwritten rules, and one of them is about you.

choices.label: Laugh and follow it
choices.result: Laughing, you follow it all season. The veterans are a little disappointed you didn't fight it; they'd already planned their responses.

choices.label: Break the rule once
choices.result: Once, in a meeting, about something that matters. The room is silent, then a captain nods, and the rule is quietly erased the next morning.

choices.label: Erase it
choices.result: Erased, during lunch. It's back the next morning in bigger letters, with a drawing of you, and the whole team signs it.

scenarios.title: The Contract Extension
scenarios.text: The club wants to talk about extending your contract a year early. The general manager calls it a sign of respect; your agent calls it a discount with a bow on it.

authoring.premise: The club wants to talk about extending your contract, a year early.

choices.label: Sign early for security
choices.result: Signed, a year early. Your agent says you left money on the table; you sleep fine, and the front office starts calling you 'part of the core'.

choices.label: Bet on yourself
choices.result: Declined, politely, and you play out the deal. Every kick this season is an audition for the open market, and you can feel it in your stomach.

choices.label: Talk it over at home
choices.result: The offer goes on the kitchen table for a week. You sign a shorter version that leaves room to breathe, and everyone in the house exhales.

scenarios.title: The First Big Purchase
scenarios.text: You can finally afford the car you've wanted since you were fifteen, the one on the poster above your childhood bed. The dealer already knows your name when you walk in.

authoring.premise: You can finally afford the car you've wanted since high school.

choices.label: Buy it and drive it home
choices.result: Bought, and driven straight home to {parent}'s driveway. He walks around it three times without speaking, then asks for the keys.

choices.label: Buy something sensible
choices.result: Something sensible, with good mileage, and the rest goes in the bank. It's a good car. It isn't the car, and you notice every time you see one.

choices.label: Wait one more year
choices.result: A year's wait, on purpose. The wanting fades a little, and so does the fun of it, and you're not sure whether that's wisdom or a loss.

scenarios.title: The Regional Endorsement
scenarios.text: A regional grocery chain offers you a sponsorship worth more than your whole rookie salary: commercials, store openings, your face on cereal boxes in three states.

authoring.premise: A regional company offers you a sponsorship worth more than your rookie salary.

choices.label: Sign the deal
choices.result: Signed. The shoots take some weekends, the money is real, and {sibling} buys forty boxes of cereal with your face on them.

choices.label: Strike two clauses first
choices.result: The fine print, read twice, and two clauses struck: no appearances in season, no exclusivity. They agree, and you keep your Tuesdays.

choices.label: Keep your weekends
choices.result: A pass, and your weekends stay yours. A rival kicker takes the deal, and you see his face in every aisle for a year.

scenarios.title: The Investment Pitch
scenarios.text: A man at a charity dinner pitches you an investment: guaranteed returns, a famous partner, no risk. He's done this before, and he knows you can tell.

authoring.premise: Someone pitches you an investment that sounds too good, and they know it.

choices.label: Walk away
choices.result: You thank him and walk away. Six months later you read his name in the paper, and you pass the article to your teammates.

choices.label: Ask someone you trust
choices.result: You show it to someone you trust. They laugh, then explain exactly how it works. You learn more in an hour than in a year of statements.

choices.label: Put money in
choices.result: You put money in. The statements look great for a while, then they stop coming, and so does he. The shame lasts longer than the loss.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Mentor
scenarios.text: The club asks you to help a younger player adjust: a nervous second-year punter who eats lunch alone and calls home after every practice. Someone once did this for you.

authoring.premise: The club asks you to help a younger player adjust, the way someone helped you.

choices.label: Take the punter on
choices.result: Meals, film, the long drives home: all of it, on your shoulders for a season. He's steadier by midseason and starts eating lunch at the specialists' table.

choices.label: Be a friend, not a mentor
choices.result: Friendly instead of formal: video games, bad movies, no lectures. He calls you when it really matters, and it does, twice.

choices.label: Point him to a veteran
choices.result: A veteran with more time and more patience gets the job, at your suggestion. It works out fine, and you feel a small pang at the specialists' table.

scenarios.title: The Locker Room Reputation
scenarios.text: Younger teammates have started looking at you when something goes wrong: a bad practice, a fight in the weight room, a rumor about a trade. You're not sure when you became that person.

authoring.premise: Younger teammates have started looking at you when something goes wrong.

choices.label: Step into it
choices.result: You step into it. When the room gets loud, you're the calm voice, and by December the coaches start running things past you first.

choices.label: Pick your moments
choices.result: Rare words, carefully chosen. You speak up twice all season, in two bad weeks, and both times the room listens completely.

choices.label: Stay a kicker
choices.result: There are captains for that, you decide, and you stay a kicker. The young players find someone else, and you're relieved and a little sorry.

scenarios.title: The Coaching Change
scenarios.text: A new special teams coach arrives with a new way of doing everything: new drills, new warmups, a new word for every old thing. He's thirty-four and very confident.

authoring.premise: A new special teams coach arrives with a new way of doing everything.

choices.label: Try every new drill
choices.result: Every new drill, without complaint, for a month. Some of it actually helps, and he notices who didn't fight him.

choices.label: Keep what works
choices.result: What works, kept; what doesn't, explained calmly. He respects the reasoning, argues once, and then adopts one of your drills.

choices.label: Get to know him first
choices.result: Lunch, his story, his family, before you judge a single drill. He turns out to be nervous, and the drills make more sense after that.

scenarios.title: The Public Relationship
scenarios.text: Your relationship becomes a topic of public interest after a photo goes around, and {love_interest} didn't sign up for that. There are strangers in the comments of their private account.

authoring.premise: Your relationship becomes a topic of public interest, and {love_interest} didn't sign up for that.

choices.label: Protect {love_interest}
choices.result: Nothing about home, posted ever again, not even a photo of the dog. {love_interest} notices, and is quietly grateful, and the strangers lose interest by spring.

choices.label: Set boundaries together
choices.result: What stays private and what doesn't: decided together, at the kitchen table, with a list. It feels like a team, which it is.

choices.label: Let it blow over
choices.result: It'll blow over, you decide. It takes much longer than you thought, and {love_interest} deletes the account without telling you.

scenarios.title: The First Home Repair
scenarios.text: The roof leaks the week of a road trip, all over the living room, and the repair estimate is the size of a used car. You're in a hotel two thousand miles away.

authoring.premise: The roof leaks the week of a road trip, and the bill is enormous.

choices.label: Handle it from the hotel
choices.result: Contractors, insurance and photos, all handled by phone from the hotel. It gets done, expensively, and you miss a meeting doing it.

choices.label: Ask {parent} to oversee it
choices.result: {parent} drives over with a ladder and an opinion, and oversees the whole repair. He loves being useful, and the roof is perfect.

choices.label: Patch it for now
choices.result: A tarp and a bucket for now, the real fix in the offseason. It's cheap, and you sleep under the sound of dripping all winter.

scenarios.title: The Charity Commitment
scenarios.text: A children's literacy nonprofit asks you to become a regular supporter: not a photo at the gala, but monthly visits, a reading program, and your name on a library wing.

authoring.premise: A nonprofit asks you to become a regular supporter, not just a photo.

choices.label: Commit to monthly visits
choices.result: Monthly visits, all year. The kids know your name by spring, and one of them reads you a whole book about a dragon who kicks.

choices.label: Bring teammates along
choices.result: Teammates, signed up one by one. It becomes a team tradition, and {holder} turns out to be the best reader of all of you.

choices.label: Write a check
choices.result: A generous check and a warm letter. It helps, and the director thanks you sincerely, and you never see the library wing.

scenarios.title: The Radio Segment
scenarios.text: A sports radio station offers you a recurring weekly segment: Monday mornings, fifteen minutes, live, with a host who likes to ask about locker-room drama.

authoring.premise: You're offered a recurring weekly segment on sports radio.

choices.label: Take the segment
choices.result: Yes, every Monday at seven. You're good at it, the callers love you, and your Mondays disappear for the whole season into a radio booth.

choices.label: Try it for a month
choices.result: A one-month trial, then a decision. You keep it, shorter, with a promise from the host to leave the locker room alone.

choices.label: Keep your Mondays
choices.result: No segment. You'd rather talk about kicking with other kickers, and your Monday mornings stay quiet, slow and entirely yours.

scenarios.title: The Offseason Vacation
scenarios.text: {love_interest} wants a real vacation this offseason: two weeks, an island, no phones. You want to train. The brochure has been on the kitchen counter for a month, open to the same page.

authoring.premise: {love_interest} wants a real vacation; you want to train.

choices.label: Go, and leave the ball home
choices.result: Two weeks on the island, no ball, no film, no phone. It's the best fortnight of the year, and you come back rested and in love all over again.

choices.label: Stay and train
choices.result: Training, alone, while {love_interest} goes with friends and sends pictures of the water every day. You're stronger by July and a little lonelier.

choices.label: Find an island with a field
choices.result: A beach town with a high school field, found after two hours of searching. Mornings for kicking, afternoons for the beach. Everyone wins, sort of.

scenarios.title: The Former Teammate
scenarios.text: A former teammate can't find another job in the league and keeps calling: late at night, after he's watched your games, asking if you've heard anything from anyone.

authoring.premise: A former teammate can't find another job in the league and keeps calling.

choices.label: Keep picking up
choices.result: Every call, picked up. Mostly he needs someone to listen, and some nights you stay on the phone until he's laughing again.

choices.label: Help him find other work
choices.result: Calls to people you know about jobs outside football: coaching, sales, broadcasting. One of them works out, and he sends you a photo from his new desk.

choices.label: Let some calls go
choices.result: Some calls go to voicemail. You feel bad about it every time, and you call back on Sundays, which helps a little.

scenarios.title: The New Neighborhood
scenarios.text: You've lived on this street for two years and know nobody's name. There's a block party flyer on your door and a kid next door who kicks a ball against your garage every afternoon.

authoring.premise: You can get involved in your neighborhood or stay a stranger on your own street.

choices.label: Go to the block party
choices.result: The block party, with a casserole you bought. By the end of the night you know every name on the street, and the neighbors start bringing food after losses.

choices.label: Help with the youth league
choices.result: The neighborhood youth league gets a volunteer coach once a week. The kid next door is on your team, and he's terrible, and you love it.

choices.label: Keep to yourself
choices.result: You keep to yourself. It's quiet and private, and a little lonely when the street fills with music on Saturday nights.

scenarios.title: The Financial Mistake
scenarios.text: An investment you were sure about turns out not to be smart: a restaurant that closed, a fund that froze, a statement you read three times in the car outside the facility.

authoring.premise: An investment or a purchase wasn't as smart as it looked.

choices.label: Cut the loss
choices.result: The loss, cut cleanly, and a lesson learned. It stings for a month, and then it becomes a story you tell rookies.

choices.label: Tell {love_interest} everything
choices.result: Everything, at the kitchen table, including the part you were embarrassed about. It's a hard talk and a good one, and you make the next decision together.

choices.label: Bury it in work
choices.result: Work, to forget it: early mornings, long sessions, no thinking. It doesn't quite work, and the statement is still in the glove box.

choices.label: Call the advisor you trust
choices.result: The one advisor who has always told you the truth gets a call that afternoon. You make a plan together, you stick to it, and the hole closes by spring.
choices.lock_text: having learned about money the hard way

scenarios.title: The Family Conversation
scenarios.text: You and {love_interest} start talking about starting a family, late at night, and neither of you knows the right time. The schedule, the contract, the next city: everything feels uncertain.

authoring.premise: You and {love_interest} talk about starting a family, and neither of you knows the right time.

choices.label: Decide on now
choices.result: Now, you both say, at almost the same moment. It's terrifying and right, and you laugh for ten minutes afterward.

choices.label: Plan around the seasons
choices.result: A plan, built around the contract and the seasons: when, where, who helps. It's sensible, and it makes the dream feel real.

choices.label: Agree to wait
choices.result: Waiting, for now, you both agree. The conversation comes back every few months, a little more urgent each time, and a little warmer.

scenarios.title: The Family Business
scenarios.text: A cousin wants your money and your name to expand the family store into three towns. The whole family is waiting for your answer, and Thanksgiving is in two weeks.

authoring.premise: A relative wants your money and your name to expand the family business.

choices.label: Invest
choices.result: You invest and put your name on the sign. The opening is a family party, and for the first time in years, everyone is in one room.

choices.label: Invest, quietly
choices.result: You put in money but keep your name off the sign. It's safer, and your cousin is a little hurt by the distance.

choices.label: Turn the cousin down
choices.result: No, as kindly and clearly as you can manage. Thanksgiving is quieter this year, and you're sure it was the right answer, mostly.

scenarios.title: The Memorabilia Deal
scenarios.text: A memorabilia collector wants to pay you to sign five hundred footballs in one afternoon, in a hotel ballroom, with a man counting and a camera to prove each one is real.

authoring.premise: A collector wants to pay you to sign five hundred footballs.

choices.label: Sign all five hundred
choices.result: Five hundred signatures in one long afternoon. Your hand hurts for days, the check is large, and the man counting never smiles once.

choices.label: Add a hundred for charity
choices.result: All five hundred, plus a hundred extra for the children's hospital auction. The auction raises more than your check, and the collector pays for the extra hundred.

choices.label: Sign for kids at the fence
choices.result: No ballroom, no counting man. You'd rather sign for kids at the practice fence, for free, and you do, every Thursday.

scenarios.title: The Young Kicker's Question
scenarios.text: A college kicker emails you for career advice. It's a long email, carefully written, and the question at the end is a good one: how do you know when to change and when to wait?

authoring.premise: A college kicker emails you for career advice, and it's a good question.

choices.label: Write a real answer
choices.result: A long, honest answer, written over two evenings. He prints it out, and two years later he sends you a photo of it taped inside his locker.

choices.label: Call him instead
choices.result: A phone call instead of an email. You talk for an hour, and he sounds exactly like you did at twenty, which is strange and a little moving.

choices.label: Send a short reply
choices.result: A short, kind reply and a 'good luck'. He's grateful, and you wonder later what the longer answer would have been.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Savings
scenarios.text: A financial advisor reviews your long-term plan and asks a question you can't answer: what does your life cost after football, per year, in today's money?

authoring.premise: A financial advisor reviews your long-term plan and asks a question you can't answer.

choices.label: Learn the answer
choices.result: The answer, learned over two weeks of spreadsheets, and the next ten questions too. You understand your own money for the first time, and it's calming.

choices.label: Bring {parent} to the next meeting
choices.result: {parent} comes to the next meeting with a legal pad and better questions than yours. You make the plan together, and he insists on paying for lunch.

choices.label: Trust the advisor
choices.result: The advisor knows best, you decide, and stop asking questions. It's easy and restful, and you never learn the number.

scenarios.title: The Public Appearance
scenarios.text: You're invited to a high-profile charity gala in black tie: actors, owners, a senator, a string quartet. You don't own a tuxedo, and the event is Saturday.

authoring.premise: You're asked to attend a high-profile event in a suit you don't own yet.

choices.label: Go and enjoy it
choices.result: A rented tuxedo, a long night and people you didn't know existed. You enjoy it more than you expected, and someone from a children's charity asks for your number.

choices.label: Go with a purpose
choices.result: A plan, three introductions, and home by eleven. You leave with three useful numbers and a sponsor for your youth camp.

choices.label: Stay home
choices.result: Home, in sweatpants, with takeout and a movie. Nobody at the gala notices except your agent, who sends a single sad emoji at midnight.

scenarios.title: The Family Holiday
scenarios.text: The schedule lands on a family holiday again, the third year in a row. {parent} has already set a place for you at the table, just in case.

authoring.premise: The schedule lands on a family holiday again.

choices.label: Bring the holiday to you
choices.result: The whole family, flown in for the weekend. Dinner is in a hotel ballroom, and it's still home, and {sibling} carves the turkey badly.

choices.label: Keep your routine and call
choices.result: Your routine, and a long call between meetings. They put you on speaker at the table, and you hear everyone laughing.

choices.label: Plan a second celebration
choices.result: A second holiday, planned for the bye week, with everything: the dishes, the games, the arguments. Everyone says it's fine. It mostly is.

scenarios.title: The Teammates' Dispute
scenarios.text: Two teammates ask you to settle an argument about who gets the corner locker by the heater. It's been going on for a week, and they both say you're the only fair one.

authoring.premise: Two teammates ask you to settle an argument, which means picking a side.

choices.label: Make them talk it out
choices.result: Both of them, in a room, talking it out in front of you. It takes forty minutes, ends with a handshake, and they decide to share.

choices.label: Pick the right side
choices.result: The right side, after listening to both. One of them sulks for a week, and then admits you were right, grudgingly.

choices.label: Let them settle it
choices.result: Settle it yourselves, you tell them, and walk away. They do, eventually, with a coin flip, some shouting and a handshake.

scenarios.title: The Sponsored Posts
scenarios.text: A supplement-free sports drink company offers to pay you for sponsored posts. The product is fine, mostly, and the contract has a clause about 'authentic enthusiasm'.

authoring.premise: A company offers to pay for sponsored posts, and the product is fine, mostly.

choices.label: Take the deal
choices.result: The deal, signed. The posts do well, the money is real, and the 'authentic enthusiasm' feels a little hollow every time.

choices.label: Test it for a month
choices.result: A month of actually drinking it before you post a word. It's genuinely good, and your posts say so honestly.

choices.label: Keep your page yours
choices.result: No sponsored posts, ever. Your page stays yours, full of your dog, your family and very bad photos of sunsets.

scenarios.title: The Long-Term Commitment
scenarios.text: {love_interest} wants to talk about where you'll live after football. It's a quiet Sunday, and they've made a list of places on the back of an envelope.

authoring.premise: {love_interest} wants to talk about where you'll live after football.

choices.label: Let {love_interest} choose
choices.result: Their choice, from the envelope: a town near the coast, near their family. It's the right call, and you both know it.

choices.label: Make the list together
choices.result: A list together, with pros and cons in two colors. Your hometown wins by a point, and {parent} cries on the phone when you tell him.

choices.label: Say there's still time
choices.result: There's still time, you say. {love_interest} says there isn't always, and puts the envelope away in a drawer you both pretend not to see.

scenarios.title: The Injury Prevention Program
scenarios.text: The club wants you on a new training and recovery program: sleep tracking, cold tubs, a mobility routine at six in the morning. The sports science staff is very excited about it.

authoring.premise: The club wants you on a new training and recovery routine.

choices.label: Follow it to the letter
choices.result: Every piece of it, exactly. Your legs feel younger by October, and the sports science staff starts using your numbers in presentations.

choices.label: Add your own work
choices.result: The program, plus your own work on top. You're stronger and more tired, and the staff worries quietly about the extra load.

choices.label: Do the minimum
choices.result: The minimum: the cold tubs, never the six o'clock mobility. The trainers notice right away, and so, by December, does your hip.

scenarios.title: The Younger Teammate's Mistake
scenarios.text: A rookie makes a mistake: he missed a meeting, then lied about why. He comes to you, not the coaches, white-faced, asking what to do before anyone finds out.

authoring.premise: A rookie makes a mistake and comes to you, not the coaches.

choices.label: Walk him to the coaches
choices.result: Down the hall, together, and you stand beside him while he tells them. It goes better than he feared, and he never lies to a coach again.

choices.label: Listen first
choices.result: Listening first, all of it, and then helping him find the words. He goes in alone, which matters to him.

choices.label: Tell him what you'd do
choices.result: Exactly what you'd do, step by step. He does it, it works, and he thanks you without quite looking at you.

scenarios.title: The Personal Trainer
scenarios.text: A private trainer who works with three Olympic athletes could change your whole offseason, for a price that makes your advisor wince. They have one opening.

authoring.premise: A private trainer could change your offseason, for a price.

choices.label: Hire the trainer
choices.result: Hired, for the summer. It's brutal and scientific, and you come back to camp faster, leaner and slightly afraid of the trainer.

choices.label: Ask for a trial week
choices.result: A trial week first. It's good, so you hire them for half the summer, and keep the other half for your own work.

choices.label: Train the way you always have
choices.result: Your own routine, the one that got you here. It's familiar and cheaper, and you wonder all summer what you're missing.

scenarios.title: Dinner With Influential People
scenarios.text: Your agent invites you to a private dinner with influential people in the league: two owners, a network executive and a former commissioner. Dress code: 'nice'.

authoring.premise: Your agent invites you to dinner with influential people in the league.

choices.label: Be yourself
choices.result: Good stories, honestly told, and you laugh at your own mistakes. Two of the owners remember your name the next season.

choices.label: Mostly listen
choices.result: Mostly listening. You learn how the league actually works, who decides what and why, and you write it all down in the car.

choices.label: Skip the dinner
choices.result: No dinner. Your agent sighs and goes alone, and comes back with a story about you that isn't quite true.

scenarios.title: The Homecoming Event
scenarios.text: Your high school invites you back for its homecoming game. They want you at the pep rally, on the field at halftime, and in the trophy case photo with your old coach.

authoring.premise: Your high school invites you back for its homecoming.

choices.label: Walk the halls with {parent}
choices.result: The halls, with {parent}, in the afternoon. A teacher still has your old essay about wanting to be a kicker, and reads it aloud.

choices.label: Talk to the team
choices.result: The football team before the game, in the old locker room. The kicker can't stop grinning, and you leave him your cleats.

choices.label: Send a halftime video
choices.result: A video, played at halftime on the old scoreboard. They cheer anyway, and someone films the crowd cheering for you and sends it.

scenarios.title: The Team's Future
scenarios.text: The franchise is talking about a full rebuild: younger, cheaper, faster. A reporter says there's a list of veterans who might be traded, and your name is on it.

authoring.premise: The franchise is talking about a full rebuild, and your name is on a list.

choices.label: Make yourself essential
choices.result: The one veteran they can't rebuild without: that's the plan, and you work like it. The list changes by spring.

choices.label: Have your agent find out
choices.result: Your agent finds out which list it is. It's the good one, for now, and you breathe for the first time in a week.

choices.label: Invest in the young players
choices.result: The young players get your time, because they're the future and so, maybe, are you. The coaches notice who's helping.

scenarios.title: The New Family Responsibility
scenarios.text: A family member needs more of your time than the season has: {sibling} is going through a divorce, and calls every night after the kids are asleep.

authoring.premise: A family member needs more of your time than the season has.

choices.label: Make the time
choices.result: Flights on off days, calls every night. You're exhausted and present, and {sibling} says later that you were the reason they got through it.

choices.label: Build a plan with the family
choices.result: A family plan, so nobody carries it alone: {parent} takes Mondays, you take Thursdays, everyone takes Sunday. It works better than anyone hoped.

choices.label: Promise the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, promised, and kept. It's a long wait for both of you, and the calls in between are short.

scenarios.title: The Offseason Media Tour
scenarios.text: Your growing reputation comes with an offseason full of interview requests: podcasts, morning shows, and a magazine that wants to photograph you on a beach.

authoring.premise: Your growing reputation comes with an offseason full of interviews.

choices.label: Say yes to most
choices.result: Most of them, yes. Your name is everywhere by June, your phone never stops, and you're more tired than in season.

choices.label: Do three, and do them well
choices.result: Three interviews, carefully chosen and well prepared. One of them becomes the clip people share whenever your name comes up.

choices.label: Keep the summer quiet
choices.result: A quiet summer and your training, no interviews. Nobody photographs you on a beach, which suits you fine, and your agent sighs.

scenarios.title: The Career Milestone
scenarios.text: You reach a career milestone the club makes a big deal about: a graphic on the scoreboard, a ball in a case, and a question about how you want to celebrate.

authoring.premise: You reach a milestone and have to decide how to celebrate it.

choices.label: Celebrate with the specialists
choices.result: Dinner with the specialists, on you, at the steakhouse. {holder} gives a speech that is mostly about {holder}, and it's perfect.

choices.label: Celebrate at home
choices.result: The people who knew you before, at home: {parent}, {sibling}, old friends. The ball in the case goes on {parent}'s mantel.

choices.label: Thank the room one by one
choices.result: Every person in the building, thanked one by one: trainers, equipment staff, the snapper, the cafeteria. It takes all day and it's worth it.

scenarios.title: The Room Starts Looking at You
scenarios.text: Teammates have started bringing their problems to your locker: contracts, girlfriends, coaches, homesick kids, a lineman's divorce. You're not sure when you became that person.

authoring.premise: Teammates have started bringing their problems to your locker.

choices.label: Make time
choices.result: You make time for every one of them, even when it costs you film work. You're more tired, and the room is steadier for it.

choices.label: Listen
choices.result: Mostly, you listen. It turns out that's what they need, and the young ones start bringing you coffee as a kind of payment.

choices.label: Set limits
choices.result: You set limits: after practice, never before. A few people take it personally, and you keep enough of yourself to do the job.

scenarios.title: The Coaching Staff Meeting
scenarios.text: A new coach wants to change the preparation routine that got you here: a new warmup, a new film schedule, and a new word for 'hold' that nobody can pronounce.

authoring.premise: A new coach wants to change the preparation routine that got you here.

choices.label: Explain the routine
choices.result: Every piece of your routine, explained with reasons. He keeps most of it, changes the film schedule, and drops the new word entirely.

choices.label: Try it his way
choices.result: His way, for a month, honestly. Some of it sticks, and the coaches notice that the veteran didn't fight them.

choices.label: Find the middle over lunch
choices.result: The middle ground, found over lunch at a diner. It's mostly your routine, with his film schedule, and you both claim victory.

scenarios.title: The Family Schedule
scenarios.text: Your kids' games and your schedule are in a war you keep losing: soccer on Saturdays, recitals on Thursdays, and a road trip every other weekend of the fall.

authoring.premise: Your kids' games and your schedule are in a war you keep losing.

choices.label: Make every game you can
choices.result: Every game you can make, even if it means a red-eye and a nap in the car. The kids look for you in the stands, and find you more often than not.

choices.label: Plan the season on one calendar
choices.result: One big calendar on the kitchen wall, with every game, recital and road trip in different colors. It's chaos made visible, and it helps.

choices.label: Watch the videos after practice
choices.result: The videos, watched in the locker room after practice, every one. It's not the same, and the kids know it, and they send them anyway.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Plan
scenarios.text: You sit down at the kitchen table with a calculator and a yellow pad and try to work out how much you'll need after football. The number is bigger than you expected.

authoring.premise: You sit down and work out how much you'll need after football.

choices.label: Do the math
choices.result: The math, done properly with an honest advisor over three meetings. It's sobering and useful, and you finally know what 'enough' looks like.

choices.label: Do it with {love_interest}
choices.result: {parent} sits beside you with a second calculator and decades of experience. You make the plan together, and it's better for it.

choices.label: Leave it for next year
choices.result: Next year, you decide, and the yellow pad goes in a drawer. The number keeps growing in your head anyway.

scenarios.title: The Former Teammate's Retirement
scenarios.text: A teammate you've lined up beside for years retires on a Wednesday. By Thursday morning his locker is empty, his nameplate is gone, and the room sounds different.

authoring.premise: A longtime teammate retires, and the locker room feels different.

choices.label: Keep in touch
choices.result: You keep in touch. He calls on game days with notes from his couch, and the calls get funnier the longer he's away.

choices.label: Fill the space
choices.result: You start doing the things he used to do: the jokes before meetings, the check-ins on rookies. It's harder than he made it look.

choices.label: Let it be different
choices.result: You let it be different. Rooms change; this one will too. You notice his empty chair less each week, and feel guilty about that.

scenarios.title: The Younger Generation
scenarios.text: A rookie asks how you handle the pressure, standing by the kicking net after practice, and you realize you've never once said it out loud.

authoring.premise: A rookie asks how you handle the pressure, and you realize you've never said it out loud.

choices.label: Say it out loud
choices.result: For the first time, you find the words: the breath, the one thought, the forgetting. He writes them down, and so, later, do you.

choices.label: Show him instead
choices.result: Not words: you take him to the field and show him your routine, breath by breath, kick by kick. He gets it faster that way.

choices.label: Tell him it comes with time
choices.result: It comes with time, you tell him. It's true, and it isn't much help, and you think about it on the drive home.

scenarios.title: The New Contract Negotiation
scenarios.text: Your agent wants a longer deal, four years with guarantees, and the club wants a shorter one, two years and incentives. They've been stuck for three weeks.

authoring.premise: Your agent wants a longer deal, and the club wants a shorter one.

choices.label: Take the shorter deal
choices.result: Two years, and you bet on yourself. Your agent grumbles, the club is relieved, and you feel lighter than you have in weeks.

choices.label: Fight for the longer deal
choices.result: Four years, and you fight for them: a month of calls, a lot of silence. You get three, and some sleepless nights.

choices.label: Talk to the club yourself
choices.result: The general manager, called directly, to meet in the middle. Three years, fair guarantees, and an agent who sulks for a week.

scenarios.title: The Media Debate
scenarios.text: On a sports show, two analysts spend ten minutes arguing about whether you're still among the best kickers in the league. Your phone fills with clips.

authoring.premise: Analysts debate whether you're still among the best in the league.

choices.label: Use it
choices.result: You watch it once and put the losing argument on a card in your locker. Every practice that week, you kick like you're answering it.

choices.label: Ignore it
choices.result: You turn off the television and leave your phone in the car during practice. By Thursday the debate has moved on, and so have you.

choices.label: Do impressions with the unit
choices.result: You laugh about it with the specialists, who do impressions of both analysts all week. It's the loosest the unit has been all year.

scenarios.title: The Community Commitment
scenarios.text: A local charity wants you as its face, year-round: the posters, the hospital visits, the winter coat drive, a fun run in your name. It's a real commitment, and a real honor.

authoring.premise: A local charity wants you as its face, year-round.

choices.label: Commit
choices.result: The full year, committed. It's a lot of evenings, and the coat drive breaks the city's record, and you shake hands with every volunteer.

choices.label: Bring teammates
choices.result: You bring teammates so the work is shared. It becomes a team tradition, and the young players start signing up on their own.

choices.label: Do the big events
choices.result: The big events only: the gala and the coat drive. It helps, and you can tell from the director's face that she hoped for more.

scenarios.title: The Expensive Lifestyle
scenarios.text: Your household's expenses have quietly doubled in two years: a second car, a bigger house, three subscriptions to things nobody watches, and a gardener for a garden you never visit.

authoring.premise: Your household's expenses have quietly doubled.

choices.label: Cut back together
choices.result: An evening with the statements and a highlighter. Some things go, and nobody misses them, and the household feels lighter.

choices.label: Make a plan at home
choices.result: The plan, made at home, out loud, with everyone in the house. It's an awkward talk and a relief, and the budget goes on the fridge.

choices.label: Let it ride for now
choices.result: Later, you'll deal with it later. The statements keep coming, a little bigger each month, and you stop opening them on Mondays.

scenarios.title: The Advisor's Concern
scenarios.text: Your financial advisor slides one line of your statement across the table and asks, carefully, whether you still want to be in it. It's the investment a teammate talked you into.

authoring.premise: Your financial advisor questions one of your investments, carefully.

choices.label: Listen and adjust
choices.result: You listen, ask the questions you skipped the first time, and move most of the money out. It costs you a little, and you sleep better.

choices.label: Get a second opinion
choices.result: You show it to someone you trust before deciding. They read it twice, sigh, and explain the part you didn't understand. You get out together.

choices.label: Keep it
choices.result: It stays in your portfolio. You like the idea and the teammate, and you tell yourself the advisor is being careful. The statements keep arriving.

scenarios.title: The Team Rebuild
scenarios.text: The club has started replacing veterans with younger, cheaper players. Every week another familiar locker is cleared out, and you've started counting the ones that are left.

authoring.premise: The club starts replacing established players with younger ones.

choices.label: Stay ahead
choices.result: You get ahead of the clock: earlier mornings, cleaner numbers. If they want to replace you, they'll have to find someone better.

choices.label: Help the young players
choices.result: You help the young players learn the job. It's the right thing, and it makes you the veteran the club can't afford to lose.

choices.label: Talk to your agent
choices.result: An honest talk with your agent about the next two years, at a diner. It's a hard conversation, and a relief to finally have it.

scenarios.title: The New Special Teams Coach
scenarios.text: The new special teams coach stops a drill in front of the whole unit to ask why you still warm up the way you did as a rookie. Everyone is watching to see what you do.

authoring.premise: The new coach challenges your preparation, publicly.

choices.label: Answer with data
choices.result: You bring him three seasons of charts after practice, in his office, with the door closed. He reads every page and changes one drill, not yours.

choices.label: Answer with work
choices.result: You say nothing and out-work everyone for a week. He stops asking in public, though you can tell the question is still there.

choices.label: Talk to him alone
choices.result: You ask for ten minutes alone and tell him what the routine is for. He listens, and the next morning he warms up the young kicker your way.

scenarios.title: The Mentor's Retirement
scenarios.text: The special teams coach who rebuilt your swing in your second season is stepping away at the end of the year. He hasn't told the room yet; he told you first.

authoring.premise: A coach who shaped your career is stepping away.

choices.label: Thank him
choices.result: You drive to his house on a Tuesday and thank him in his kitchen. He waves it off, then walks you to the car and doesn't let go of the handshake.

choices.label: Organize a send-off
choices.result: You call every kicker and punter he ever coached. Eleven of them show up for his last practice, and he has to turn around to the fence for a minute.

choices.label: Leave a note
choices.result: You write him a note and leave it in his playbook. He never mentions it, but on his last day it's the only thing he takes from the desk.

scenarios.title: The Old Rival
scenarios.text: A kicker you competed against for years, the one who beat you for a job early on, reaches out of nowhere. He's out of football now, and he wants to have coffee.

authoring.premise: A competitor from years ago reaches out out of nowhere.

choices.label: Meet for coffee
choices.result: Coffee, then lunch, then three hours. It's warmer than you expected, and you both admit you used to watch each other's every kick.

choices.label: Ask what he needs
choices.result: What does he need? It's advice, about life after football, and you give it honestly, and he writes everything down.

choices.label: Reply politely
