choices.result: A polite reply, warm and short. You leave it there, and you think about the old job battle all week.

scenarios.title: The Family Business Dispute
scenarios.text: A business with relatives in it is turning into a family fight: a cousin wants to expand, an uncle wants out, and everyone wants you to decide at Thanksgiving.

authoring.premise: A business with relatives in it is turning into a family fight.

choices.label: Bring in a mediator
choices.result: A professional mediator, hired before the holiday. It's expensive and it works, and Thanksgiving is merely awkward instead of explosive.

choices.label: Step back from the business
choices.result: Out of the business, and into the family. You sell your share to the cousin, and dinner that year is the warmest in years.

choices.label: Take charge of it
choices.result: In charge, for a season, making the hard calls yourself. It's a lot of work, the business steadies, and a few people stay mad.

scenarios.title: The College Invitation
scenarios.text: A university you never played for invites you to speak to its football program. The head coach says the kickers have been asking for you by name all spring.

authoring.premise: A university invites you to speak to its football program.

choices.label: Speak to the team
choices.result: You give the team a short talk about failing in front of people. The kickers stay after and ask questions until the groundskeeper turns off the lights.

choices.label: Spend the day
choices.result: You spend the whole day: meetings, lunch, practice. By the end, a freshman kicker who barely spoke at breakfast is showing you his notebook.

choices.label: Send a video
choices.result: A video message, recorded in your kitchen and sent with a signed ball. It's thoughtful and it plays well, and the kickers watch it twice.

scenarios.title: The Team's Direction
scenarios.text: You're not sure the franchise is going in the right direction, and a respected columnist asks you about it on the record, with a recorder on the table.

authoring.premise: You're not sure the franchise is going in the right direction, and someone asks you on the record.

choices.label: Say something careful
choices.result: Something careful and true, with no names. Fans respect it; the front office notices, and the general manager calls you in for a long talk.

choices.label: Back the club
choices.result: The club, backed publicly and fully. The front office is grateful, and you're not entirely sure you believe what you said.

choices.label: Say it to the club
choices.result: To the club, not to the columnist: your concerns, in the general manager's office the next morning. They listen, and one thing changes.

scenarios.title: The New Home
scenarios.text: Your family has outgrown the house: three kids, two dogs, one bathroom that everybody fights over every morning, and a garage completely full of kicking nets.

authoring.premise: Your family has outgrown the house.

choices.label: Let the kids choose their rooms
choices.result: A bigger house, and the kids pick their rooms first, loudly. The move is chaotic and happy, and the dogs love the yard.

choices.label: Add a room instead
choices.result: An addition instead of a move, built over the offseason. The kids keep their school and their friends, and you keep your street.

choices.label: Make it work another year
choices.result: One more year in the small house, creatively. It's crowded and warm, you build bunk beds yourself, badly, and {sibling} helps.

scenarios.title: The Injury Prevention Debate
scenarios.text: You and a trainer disagree about your recovery routine: they want more rest days; you want more work. It's turned into an argument in front of the whole training room.

authoring.premise: You and a trainer disagree about your recovery routine.

choices.label: Compare the numbers
choices.result: Both of you bring numbers to a meeting. The routine you end up with is better than either plan, and you shake hands.

choices.label: Do it your way
choices.result: Your way, with more work. Your leg holds, and the trainer stays unconvinced and writes it down in your file.

choices.label: Trust the trainer this time
choices.result: The trainer's way, this time, without arguing at all. They notice the trust, and your body thanks you for it by November.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Committee
scenarios.text: Teammates ask you to represent them in a hard conversation with the coaches: practices are too long, the young players are exhausted, and two have been hurt.

authoring.premise: Teammates ask you to represent them in a hard conversation with the coaches.

choices.label: Speak for them
choices.result: Their case, made calmly and clearly by you in the coaches' office. The coaches change one thing, the practice length, and the room notices who asked.

choices.label: Bring a proposal
choices.result: A proposal, not a complaint: a new practice schedule with the same work in less time. The coaches adopt half of it.

choices.label: Suggest a captain
choices.result: A captain should do it, you suggest. One does, less well, and the young players stop asking you for things.

scenarios.title: The Charity Board
scenarios.text: A children's nonprofit you've supported for years invites you to join its board. The meetings are monthly, the budget is tight, and the work is real.

authoring.premise: A nonprofit invites you to join its board.

choices.label: Join and work
choices.result: You join and actually work: budgets, hiring, a summer program. The meetings run long, and you've never been prouder of a spreadsheet.

choices.label: Join as an adviser
choices.result: You join as an adviser, with a seat at four meetings a year. You help where a famous name helps and stay out of the rest.

choices.label: Stay a donor
choices.result: A polite no to the board, and a generous donation with a long letter. They read the letter aloud at their next meeting.

scenarios.title: The Business Partner's Exit
scenarios.text: A partner wants out of a business you built together: the restaurant, the dealership, the start-up, whichever it is. He's tired, and he wants his money back by spring.

authoring.premise: A partner wants out of a business you built together.

choices.label: Buy him out fairly
choices.result: A fair buyout, with lawyers and a handshake at the end. He leaves happy, and the business is all yours now, for better and worse.

choices.label: Sell it together
choices.result: You both sell, and split it evenly down the middle. The business goes to new owners, and the friendship stays completely intact.

choices.label: Run it alone
choices.result: Alone, with his share bought on a payment plan. It's more work than you thought, and you learn a great deal about payroll.

scenarios.title: Everyone Wants You There
scenarios.text: Your family wants you at more events than you can make: a cousin's wedding, a niece's recital, {parent}'s retirement party, a reunion. All of them are in October.

authoring.premise: Your family wants you at more events than you can make.

choices.label: Pick the ones that matter most
choices.result: The ones that matter most, chosen carefully: {parent}'s party and the recital. You make every one, and nobody asks about the rest.

choices.label: Share your calendar
choices.result: Your whole calendar, shared with the family. The arguments get shorter, and the cousin moves the wedding by a week.

choices.label: Promise the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, promised to everyone, and kept. It's a long wait, and the family photos from October are missing you.

scenarios.title: The New Contract Structure
scenarios.text: The club offers a shorter deal with incentives you're not sure you'll hit: percentages, long kicks, playoff games. Your agent calls it 'a bet on you'.

authoring.premise: The club offers a shorter deal with incentives you're not sure you'll hit.

choices.label: Sign and chase them
choices.result: Signed, and every incentive goes on the inside of your locker. You chase them all season, and you hit two of three.

choices.label: Negotiate the incentives down
choices.result: The incentives, renegotiated to numbers you can actually hit. It takes a week, and the club agrees because you asked nicely.

choices.label: Ask {holder} what they think
choices.result: {holder}, who has watched every one of your kicks, says 'Sign it' without hesitation. You do, and you feel calm about it all season.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Rumors
scenarios.text: The media have started asking how much longer you'll play: at your locker, on the radio, in a column titled 'The Last Good Years'. You're thirty-one, and you feel fine.

authoring.premise: The media have started asking how much longer you'll play.

choices.label: Give the same answer every time
choices.result: 'As long as I'm good,' every time, to every reporter, word for word. They stop asking by October, bored, which was the point.

choices.label: Joke about the question
choices.result: A joke about needing a walker for the post-game interview. The clip goes around the league, and the columnist writes a nicer column.

choices.label: Stop answering questions
choices.result: Practice instead of interviews, every single day. Your silence says more than any answer could, and your kicks say all the rest.

scenarios.title: The Rookie's Confidence
scenarios.text: A young teammate is crumbling under online criticism after a bad game: he's stopped eating lunch with the team, and he reads the comments in the training room between treatments.

authoring.premise: A young teammate is crumbling under criticism.

choices.label: Tell him about your worst week
choices.result: Your worst week as a pro, told to him in full, in an empty meeting room. He laughs at the worst part, which is how you know it worked.

choices.label: Take him to dinner
choices.result: Dinner, with no football talk at all: his hometown, his family, his terrible taste in music. He comes back to lunch the next day.

choices.label: Get him off the apps
choices.result: Delete them, you tell him, for one month. He does it, grudgingly, and by the end of the month he's himself again.

scenarios.title: The Former Coach's Advice
scenarios.text: An old coach, retired now, calls on a Sunday and tells you to start thinking about your next chapter. 'Not because you're done,' he says. 'Because you'll be surprised how fast it comes.'

authoring.premise: An old coach tells you to start thinking about your next chapter.

choices.label: Make a list
choices.result: A list of things you'd want to do after football, started that night on the back of a playbook. It's longer than you expected, and some of it excites you.

choices.label: Ask him what he did
choices.result: What did he do when it ended? He tells you, over an hour, the hard parts included, and you take notes without meaning to.

choices.label: Not yet
choices.result: Not yet, you tell him, there's more kicking in you. He laughs and says that's what he said, and hangs up kindly.

scenarios.title: A Town's Thank-You
scenarios.text: Your hometown wants to honor your career with a dinner, a plaque and a key to the city, and you're still playing it. The mayor's office has already printed the invitations.

authoring.premise: Your town wants to honor your career, and you're still playing it.

choices.label: Accept with your family beside you
choices.result: Accepted, with {parent} and {sibling} at the head table. It's a great night, and {parent} keeps the key to the city in his truck.

choices.label: Ask them to wait until you're done
choices.result: Wait until you're done, you ask kindly. They agree, a little relieved, and it gives you something to look forward to.

choices.label: Turn it into a youth clinic
choices.result: A youth clinic instead of a dinner: two hundred kids, a muddy field, and the mayor holding for you once, badly.

scenarios.title: The Guest Analyst
scenarios.text: A network offers you a guest analyst spot during your off week: a studio, a tie, a monitor full of other kickers, and a producer in your ear.

authoring.premise: A network offers you a guest analyst spot during your off week.

choices.label: Do it and enjoy it
choices.result: You do it, and you're good at it, explaining a kick in ways nobody has heard before. Your phone fills with texts from teammates and agents.

choices.label: Prepare like a game week
choices.result: Film of every kicker in the league, studied for three days. You say one smart thing on air, and it's the clip of the week.

choices.label: Rest during the off week
choices.result: No studio this time. It's your off week, and your body and your family come first, so the network books a punter instead.

scenarios.title: The Family Financial Decision
scenarios.text: You and {love_interest} disagree about a major purchase: a lake house, two hours away, that one of you loves and the other thinks you'll never use.

authoring.premise: You and {love_interest} disagree about a major purchase.

choices.label: Let {love_interest} decide
choices.result: Their decision, fully. It's the right call, and you know it the first weekend you sit on the dock together.

choices.label: Sleep on it for a month
choices.result: A month, before anyone decides anything at all. The decision makes itself in the end, and neither of you has to win the argument.

choices.label: Make your case
choices.result: Your case, made carefully at the kitchen table with a spreadsheet and a chart. You win, and the house is very quiet for a whole day.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Contract
scenarios.text: A young teammate is in his first big negotiation and comes to your locker with the offer folded in his pocket. He wants to know what you'd do.

authoring.premise: A teammate asks you how to handle his negotiation.

choices.label: Tell him what you learned
choices.result: You tell him everything you learned, including the mistakes that cost you. He takes notes on a napkin and gets a better deal than yours.

choices.label: Introduce your agent
choices.result: You introduce him to your agent over lunch. It goes well, and he thanks you in the locker room loudly enough to embarrass you both.

choices.label: Tell him to trust his agent
choices.result: You tell him to trust his agent and not to read the comments. It's good advice, and he looks like he wanted more.

scenarios.title: The Offseason Commitment
scenarios.text: Your family wants you home for the offseason; your training plan says otherwise. {parent} has already cleared out your old room, and your strength coach has already booked the gym.

authoring.premise: Your family wants you home; your training plan doesn't agree.

choices.label: Go home and train there
choices.result: Home, with a plan: the old high school field in the mornings, family in the afternoons. Everyone's happy, including your leg.

choices.label: Stick to the plan
choices.result: The plan, followed exactly, in your training city. Home waits, and the calls are long, and your leg has never felt stronger.

choices.label: Bring them to you
choices.result: The family, flown in for a month to your training city. It's crowded and loud, and {sibling} learns to hold.

scenarios.title: The Hall of Fame Conversation
scenarios.text: A broadcaster asks, on air, whether you ever think about your legacy. It's a soft question, and it lands harder than he meant it to.

authoring.premise: A broadcaster asks whether you ever think about your legacy.

choices.label: Give an honest answer
choices.result: You say you think about the next kick, which is true. Later, in the car, you think about the question for a long time.

choices.label: Talk about the people
choices.result: You talk about the people who got you here: {parent}, your first coach, the holders. The clip is the one your family keeps.

choices.label: Laugh it off
choices.result: You laugh and say you'll worry about it when you're old. Your teammates tease you about it, and the question stays with you.

scenarios.title: The Young Kicker's Arrival
scenarios.text: A rookie kicker asks to learn your routine, step by step: the breath, the count, the spot on the ball. He's brought a notebook and a very serious face.

authoring.premise: A rookie asks to learn your routine, step by step.

choices.label: Teach him everything
choices.result: Every step, and then why each step is there. He fills the notebook, and you realize, explaining it, that you understand it better too.

choices.label: Let him shadow you
choices.result: Seven days of shadowing: he does everything you do, one step behind. By Friday he's found his own version, which suits him better.

choices.label: Keep a few things yours
choices.result: Most of it, taught generously; a few things, kept. Every kicker needs a secret or two, and he'll find his own.

scenarios.title: The Business Reputation
scenarios.text: A customer's angry post about your business has been shared all over town, with your face in the picture. Your name is on the sign, so it's your problem now.

authoring.premise: A public complaint threatens your business's reputation.

choices.label: Fix the problem
choices.result: You find out what actually went wrong, fix it, and say so publicly in plain words. A few people unfollow, more come back, and the manager stops dreading Mondays.

choices.label: Call the customer
choices.result: You call the customer yourself. They don't believe it's you at first, then talk for twenty minutes. Their next post is about the phone call.

choices.label: Let the managers handle it
choices.result: You leave it to the managers. They handle it fine, slowly, and for a month people bring it up whenever they recognize you.

scenarios.title: The Team's Community Day
scenarios.text: The club asks you to organize its community day: two thousand fans, a stadium tour, a kicking contest for kids, and a budget that is mostly enthusiasm.

authoring.premise: You're asked to organize the club's charity day.

choices.label: Run the whole day
choices.result: Every detail, run by you, with a clipboard and a whistle. It's the best community day the club has ever had, and you lose your voice.

choices.label: Bring the players' families
choices.result: The players' families, invited to help run it. It becomes a tradition, and the kids of players teach the kids of fans to kick.

choices.label: Help where you're needed
choices.result: Help wherever you're needed, and the staff leads. It runs fine, and you spend the whole afternoon signing autographs, happily.

scenarios.title: The Family Milestone
scenarios.text: A major family occasion falls on a game weekend: {parent}'s seventieth birthday, with the whole family flying in from three states. The party is Saturday night.

authoring.premise: A major family occasion falls on a game weekend.

choices.label: Fly in for the night
choices.result: A Friday night flight, the party, and a dawn flight back. You're exhausted at the game, and {parent} talks about your toast for years.

choices.label: Stay with the team and call
choices.result: With the team, and a long video call into the party. They put you on a laptop at the head table, and you watch {parent} blow out the candles.

choices.label: Plan a second party
choices.result: A second celebration, for the bye week, at your house. {parent} gets two birthdays this year and says it's the best one yet.

scenarios.title: The Old Teammate's Request
scenarios.text: A former teammate is starting a business and asks you to back him. He's earnest, he's prepared, and he's never run anything in his life.

authoring.premise: A former teammate asks you to back his new venture.

choices.label: Back it with conditions
choices.result: You back it with conditions, a lawyer and a quarterly meeting. He grumbles about the paperwork and thanks you for it later.

choices.label: Back him fully
choices.result: You back him fully, because he's your friend. It's a risk, and he calls after every small win like a kid with a report card.

choices.label: Say no
choices.result: You say no, kindly. He understands, mostly, and you both pretend at the next reunion that it didn't change anything.

scenarios.title: The Next Chapter Conversation
scenarios.text: {love_interest} wants to know, over a late dinner, what you picture for life after football. It's a simple question, and you realize you've never answered it out loud.

authoring.premise: {love_interest} wants to know what you picture for life after football.

choices.label: Picture it together
choices.result: The picture, painted together, piece by piece: a town, a porch, a coaching job. It sounds good, and you both go quiet for a while.

choices.label: Each make a list
choices.result: Two lists, written separately and compared over coffee. They overlap more than you thought, and the differences are interesting, not scary.

choices.label: Not yet
choices.result: Not there yet, you say honestly. {love_interest} waits, patiently, and the question comes back every spring, a little warmer each time.

scenarios.title: The Playbook Test
scenarios.text: The special teams coordinator quizzes the rookies on the playbook, out loud, at seven in the morning, in front of the veterans. He starts with you.

authoring.premise: The special teams coordinator quizzes the rookies on the playbook, out loud, at 7 a.m.

choices.label: Know it cold
choices.result: Every question, answered cleanly. The coordinator moves on quickly to the next rookie, which is the highest compliment he gives.

choices.label: Bluff through it
choices.result: Two answers bluffed with confidence. The coordinator knows, and assigns you a page of the playbook to copy by hand, in pen, by Monday.

choices.label: Admit you don't know
choices.result: One answer you don't know, and you admit it and ask for the right one. The coordinator respects it, and the veterans notice.

scenarios.title: Learning the Snap Count
scenarios.text: The long snapper's rhythm is completely different from anything you had in college: faster, flatter, with a pause you can't predict. Practice is tomorrow, and the snapper doesn't do small talk.

authoring.premise: The long snapper's rhythm is different from anything in college, and practice is tomorrow.

choices.label: Ask for extra snaps
choices.result: Fifty extra snaps after practice, and he agrees with a grunt. By the end, you can hear the rhythm in your sleep, and he nods once on the way out.

choices.label: Adjust your timing alone
choices.result: Counting in your head all evening, you rebuild your approach alone in the living room. It works by the second day, mostly.

choices.label: Ask the snapper to adjust
choices.result: Can he speed up for you? He laughs and says no. Then, the next morning, without a word, he does it anyway.

scenarios.title: The Wind Tunnel
scenarios.text: The stadium's wind swirls in a way no film can show: in from the left at the bottom, out to the right at the top. The veterans just laugh when you ask about it.

authoring.premise: The stadium's wind swirls in a way no film can show, and the veterans just laugh about it.

choices.label: Kick in it every day
choices.result: Every day after practice, you kick into the swirl until you can feel it before it moves the ball. Your leg is sore, and the swirl stops surprising you.

choices.label: Ask the grounds crew
choices.result: The grounds crew have watched that wind for twenty years. They show you exactly which flags to watch, and one of them draws you a map on a napkin.

choices.label: Listen at lunch instead
choices.result: Instead of asking, you listen at lunch. Three veterans tell you everything about the wind, one story at a time, over a week.

scenarios.title: The Scout Team
scenarios.text: You spend practice kicking for the scout team, against the starters, and nobody important watches. The coaches are at the other end of the field.

authoring.premise: You spend practice kicking for the scout team, and nobody watches.

choices.label: Treat it like the real thing
choices.result: Every scout-team rep, like it's the real thing. Nobody watches, and you get better anyway, and the scout-team players start cheering your makes.

choices.label: Get to know the scout team
choices.result: Every name on the scout team, learned by Friday. They become your favorite people in the building, and they save you a seat on the bus.

choices.label: Save your leg
choices.result: Easy reps, and your leg stays fresh. It's sensible, and you notice by Thursday that you don't feel like part of anything.

scenarios.title: The Weight Room Pecking Order
scenarios.text: The weight room has a pecking order, and rookies lift last, after the linemen are done with every rack. By the time you get a bench, it's lunch.

authoring.premise: The weight room has a pecking order, and rookies lift last.

choices.label: Lift at dawn
choices.result: Six in the morning, before the linemen arrive. It's lonely and very effective, and the strength coach starts unlocking the door for you.

choices.label: Spot a lineman
choices.result: An offer to spot a veteran lineman, and he accepts with suspicion. By the end of the week, he's saving you a rack and calling you 'kicker' fondly.

choices.label: Take what's left
choices.result: Whatever's free, without making a thing of it. Nobody notices you, which is fine for now, and you finish your lifts on the stretching mats.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Manager
scenarios.text: The equipment manager can make your life easy or miserable: cleats, balls, the locker by the heater or the one by the door. You've been here a week and haven't said hello.

authoring.premise: The equipment manager can make your life easy or miserable, and you haven't said hello yet.

choices.label: Bring coffee
choices.result: Coffee for the equipment staff on Monday, and you learn every name. Your cleats are perfect all season, and you end up in the locker by the heater.

choices.label: Ask how the balls are prepared
choices.result: How are game balls prepared? He tells you all of it, for an hour, with visible joy. You learn more about kicking than you expected.

choices.label: Keep it professional
choices.result: Hello, thank you and nothing more. It's fine, nothing special happens, and your locker stays the one by the door.

scenarios.title: The First Fine
scenarios.text: A fine slip in your locker after the first team flight: a dress-code violation you didn't know existed. Your socks, apparently, were the wrong color, and the veterans have already framed a photo of them.

authoring.premise: You're fined for a dress-code violation you didn't know existed.

choices.label: Laugh and pay it
choices.result: Paid in cash, with a grin, and you wear the loudest socks you own to the next team meal. The room loves it, and the fine committee adds a new rule in your honor.

choices.label: Read the whole rulebook
choices.result: The full team rulebook, forty pages, read in bed that night. You find two more rules you've been breaking and fix both before anyone notices.

choices.label: Pay it and go kick
choices.result: Paid, with some grumbling, and the irritation goes straight into an extra session at the net. Your leg feels better than your pride by dinner.

scenarios.title: The Meal Money
scenarios.text: The per diem envelope on the first road trip is thicker than any scholarship check you ever got in college. The veterans are already planning where theirs is going tonight.

authoring.premise: The per diem envelope on the first road trip is thicker than your college scholarship check.

choices.label: Put it in the bank
choices.result: The whole envelope goes in the bank, and you eat the team meals. By December the road trips have quietly paid for your offseason trainer.

choices.label: Take the rookies out
choices.result: The rookie class eats like kings for one night on your envelope. It's gone by dessert, and four rookies will remember it for years.

choices.label: Treat yourself, a little
choices.result: A good dinner alone, a good book from the airport and a long nap. It feels like being a grown-up, and you send {parent} a photo of the dessert.

scenarios.title: Rookie Year Taxes
scenarios.text: Your first tax bill as a pro arrives in a thick envelope: a number nobody prepared you for, due in a month, with forms from every state you played a road game in.

authoring.premise: Your first tax bill as a pro is a number nobody prepared you for.

choices.label: Hire an athletes' accountant
choices.result: An accountant who only works with athletes takes the whole envelope off your hands. It's done in two weeks, correctly, and you learn what a 'jock tax' is.

choices.label: Ask a veteran at lunch
choices.result: One veteran at lunch gives you his accountant's number and a story about his first year that makes you laugh until your stomach hurts.

choices.label: Do it yourself
choices.result: A long weekend with spreadsheets and coffee. It's stressful, probably right, and you feel strangely proud when you click the last button.

scenarios.title: Free Cleats
scenarios.text: A shoe company offers you free cleats and a small contract, if you wear them on camera. The cleats are bright orange, and your old pair has been with you since college.

authoring.premise: A shoe company offers free cleats and a small contract, if you wear them on camera.

choices.label: Sign and lace up
choices.result: Signed, and the orange cleats arrive the next day. They're fine, the check pays for your offseason training, and the veterans call you 'traffic cone'.

choices.label: Test them for a week
choices.result: A week of testing before you sign anything. They're good, so you sign, with a clause that lets you wear your old pair if they ever hurt.

choices.label: Keep your old cleats
choices.result: Your old cleats stay. Your feet are happy and your account is the same, and the equipment manager pats them like an old dog.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Ball Room
scenarios.text: The equipment staff prepares the game balls in a back room that smells like leather and brushes, and you have opinions about how the balls feel. Nobody has asked for them yet.

authoring.premise: The equipment staff prepares the game balls, and you have opinions about them.

choices.label: Learn how it's done
choices.result: An afternoon in the ball room with the staff, watching every step. Your opinions get much better informed, and much quieter.

choices.label: Thank the staff every day
choices.result: A thank-you after every practice, every day. By October they start showing you the game balls on Friday, which nobody else gets.

choices.label: Kick every practice ball
choices.result: Every practice ball, kicked, until you can feel the difference between them in your sleep. Your leg aches, and the balls stop surprising you.

scenarios.title: The Trainer's Table
scenarios.text: The athletic trainer presses a thumb into your hip and says your hip flexor is tight. You think it's nothing. The trainer is still pressing, and looking at you over their glasses.

authoring.premise: The athletic trainer says your hip flexor is tight, and you think it's nothing.

choices.label: Do the stretches
choices.result: Every stretch, every day, exactly as written. The tightness is gone in a week, and the trainer says 'told you' with great satisfaction.

choices.label: Kick on it anyway
choices.result: Kicking through it works: the hip holds. It nags all month, like a stone in your shoe, and you start every practice a little worried.

choices.label: Take a day off kicking
choices.result: A full day off kicking, which feels like a crime. It helps more than you'd like to admit, and you come back loose.

scenarios.title: Your First Locker
scenarios.text: Your name is on a strip of tape above a locker between two veterans who haven't introduced themselves. One is eating a sandwich. The other is staring at you like you're a rumor.

authoring.premise: Your name on tape above a locker between two veterans who haven't introduced themselves.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to both
choices.result: A handshake from one, a grunt from the other. By October, the grunt is your favorite person in the building and steals your snacks.

choices.label: Let your work introduce you
choices.result: Head down, work loud. It takes a month, and when the welcome comes it's real: the grunting veteran saves you a seat on the plane.

choices.label: Make the locker yours
choices.result: A photo of your family and a paper calendar go up first. It makes the place feel like yours, and {parent} asks for a picture of it.

scenarios.title: The Group Text
scenarios.text: The specialists have a group text, you've learned. It's very active, it's apparently hilarious, it has a name nobody will tell you, and you're not in it yet.

authoring.premise: The specialists have a group text, and you're not in it yet.

choices.label: Ask the punter to add you
choices.result: In by lunch, at your own request. The first message after you join is a meme about your haircut, which is how you know you're in.

choices.label: Wait to be added
choices.result: No asking. After a good week of practice, you're added without a word, and {holder} sends a single thumbs-up that feels like a medal.

choices.label: Live without it
choices.result: No group text, no notifications. It's quieter, and you miss every inside joke in the specialists' room for a month.

scenarios.title: The Ride to Practice
scenarios.text: You don't have a car yet, and the veteran who offered you rides keeps forgetting. You've been standing in the parking lot of your building at six in the morning twice this week.

authoring.premise: You don't have a car yet, and the veteran who offered rides keeps forgetting.

choices.label: Ride with another rookie
choices.result: Rides with {backup}, every day. The drives turn into the best part of the week: bad music, worse coffee, and the start of a real friendship.

choices.label: Take a car service
choices.result: A car service, a book and twenty quiet minutes. It's expensive and relaxing, and you arrive calmer than anyone in the building.

choices.label: Bike to practice
choices.result: Five miles each way on a secondhand bike. Your legs are tired by Wednesday and strong by October, and the strength coach loves it.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Show
scenarios.text: The rookies have to put on a talent show for the veterans on the last night of camp. Your only talent is kicking, and the stage is a cafeteria table.

authoring.premise: The rookies have to put on a talent show for the veterans.

choices.label: Read a poem about the snapper
choices.result: A dramatic poetry reading about the long snapper's hands, with a candle. The room cries laughing, and the snapper asks for a copy.

choices.label: Run the whole show
choices.result: The rookies' acts, organized and timed like a practice script. It's the best show in years, and {coach} asks who ran it.

choices.label: Do a card trick
choices.result: One card trick, and you sit down. It's fine, nobody remembers it by breakfast, and you sleep well while the veterans argue about the poem.

scenarios.title: The Fan Event
scenarios.text: At a season-ticket holders' event in a hotel ballroom, everyone wants a picture with the new kicker. An old man in a thirty-year-old jersey is first in line.

authoring.premise: A season-ticket holders' event, and everyone wants a picture with the new kicker.

choices.label: Take every picture
choices.result: Every picture, and a dozen names learned. The old man and his wife sit behind the bench for years after, waving at you before every game.

choices.label: Bring the specialists along
choices.result: The punter, the snapper and {holder} join you, and the fans love the 'kicking unit' photo. It ends up on the team's website.

choices.label: Stay your hour
choices.result: Your hour, then home to the couch. It's perfectly fine, you don't learn a single name, and the old man in the jersey waves at somebody else.

scenarios.title: The Hometown Paper
scenarios.text: Your hometown paper runs a full-page story about you, with a photo from your senior prom: the rented suit, the haircut, the corsage. The veterans have already found it.

authoring.premise: Your hometown paper runs a story about you with a photo from your senior prom.

choices.label: Send them a better photo
choices.result: A call to the paper, a laugh, and a better photo sent over. They run both side by side the next week, and {parent} buys ten copies.

choices.label: Own the prom photo
choices.result: The prom photo stays. By Friday it's taped to your locker, courtesy of the veterans, and you sign it for them.

choices.label: Thank the reporter
choices.result: A thank-you call to the reporter who wrote it. They become the first person to tell your story right, and they'll be at your retirement.

scenarios.title: The Card Signing
scenarios.text: A trading card company wants your signature on a thousand cards in one afternoon, in a hotel conference room with bad coffee and a man counting.

authoring.premise: A trading card company wants your signature on a thousand cards in one afternoon.

choices.label: Sign all thousand
choices.result: A thousand signatures in four hours. Your hand hurts for two days, the check is nice, and your signature gets worse with every hundred.

choices.label: Sign some for charity
choices.result: Two hundred cards, and a full set donated to a children's hospital raffle. The raffle raises more than the check would have.

choices.label: Pass on the cards
choices.result: No cards this time. Your hand is grateful, and the company signs a punter instead, who sends you a smug photo of his check.

scenarios.title: The Holder Who Won't Talk
scenarios.text: Your new holder is all business and doesn't talk to rookies: no small talk, no jokes, just the laces and the spot. Three practices in, you've heard eleven words.

authoring.premise: Your new holder is all business and doesn't talk to rookies.

choices.label: Learn the routine by watching
choices.result: No words needed: you learn {holder}'s routine by watching every rep. By week three, you're in sync without a word, and that's its own kind of friendship.

choices.label: Win the holder over
choices.result: Lunch, questions about their family, patience. It takes a month, and then {holder} won't stop talking, mostly about their dog.

choices.label: Out-prepare the holder
choices.result: Early every day, until {holder} starts showing up even earlier. Neither of you says a word about it, and the holds get very clean.

scenarios.title: The First Night Game
scenarios.text: Your first night game under the stadium lights is tomorrow, and you can't sleep. It's two in the morning, and the hotel air conditioner sounds like a crowd.

authoring.premise: The first night game under the lights, and you can't sleep the night before.

choices.label: Do nothing all day
choices.result: Reading, a long nap and absolutely nothing else all day. You're calm by warmups, which surprises everyone, including you, and the snapper asks your secret.

choices.label: Call the team psychologist
choices.result: The team psychologist answers at seven and gives you two breathing exercises. You use both, and the lights feel smaller.

choices.label: Call {parent}
choices.result: {parent} tells you about every night game he ever watched you play, back to peewee. You laugh yourself to sleep by three.

scenarios.title: Sleeping on the Plane
scenarios.text: The team plane leaves at midnight, and you have never once slept on a plane. The veterans have pillows shaped like footballs and a card game going in the back.

authoring.premise: The team plane at midnight, and you can't sleep on planes.

choices.label: Bring a sleep kit
choices.result: An eye mask, earplugs and a pillow. The veterans mock you mercilessly, and you sleep four hours while they don't.

choices.label: Join the card game
choices.result: The card game in the back, for matchsticks, not money. You lose badly and make three friends who teach you every rule wrong.

choices.label: Watch film all flight
choices.result: Film on your tablet the whole flight. You land exhausted and very prepared, and {coach} sees the screen on the way off the plane.

scenarios.title: The Hotel Roommate
scenarios.text: Your road roommate snores, sleepwalks and talks about his ex all night. Last trip he tried to leave the room in his sleep, and you caught him at the elevator.

authoring.premise: Your road roommate snores, sleepwalks and talks about his ex all night.

choices.label: Listen to him
choices.result: Listening, mostly. He's going through a lot, and you become his person on road trips, the one he calls after the bad weeks.

choices.label: Ask for a new roommate
choices.result: The travel staff finds you a new roommate. You sleep, and he's a little hurt, and lunch is awkward for a week.

choices.label: Earplugs and house rules
choices.result: Earplugs, a lights-out time and a chair against the door. It mostly works, and he starts calling you 'the warden'.

scenarios.title: The Waiver Wire
scenarios.text: A rookie from your class is cut on Tuesday morning and claimed by another club within an hour. His locker is empty before you've finished your coffee.

authoring.premise: A rookie from your class is cut and claimed by another club within an hour.

choices.label: Text him congratulations
choices.result: A congratulations text, sent before lunch. He calls every Sunday that season to compare notes on being new, and you end up rooting for his team twice.

choices.label: Treat it as a lesson
choices.result: A lesson about how fast this league moves, written on the inside of your locker door. You kick extra that afternoon.

choices.label: Feel it, then sleep
choices.result: One evening to feel it: the speed, the empty locker, the coffee going cold. Then you go to sleep, and the next day is just a day.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Contract
scenarios.text: You finally read your rookie contract all the way through, at the kitchen table, with a highlighter. It's forty pages, and some of the words you've only seen in movies.

authoring.premise: You finally read your rookie contract all the way through.

choices.label: Call your agent with questions
choices.result: Six questions to your agent, by phone, for an hour. You learn what a guarantee really means and which clause could cut you for nothing.

choices.label: Tape up the incentives
choices.result: The incentive clauses go inside your locker door, highlighted in yellow. Every practice has a number attached to it now, and you can't stop seeing them.

choices.label: Trust your agent
choices.result: Skimmed, and trusted to your agent. It's fine, probably, the highlighter dries out in the drawer, and you never quite learn what's in there.

scenarios.title: The Kicker Down the Hall
scenarios.text: The punter is your age and acts like he's been in the league twenty years: tells you where to stand, how to stretch, which coffee to drink. You share a meeting room every day.

authoring.premise: The punter is your age and acts like he's been here twenty years.

choices.label: Become friends anyway
choices.result: Friends, anyway, over a month of bad coffee. It turns out he's as nervous as you are and has been faking it since camp.

choices.label: Make every drill a contest
choices.result: Every specialist drill becomes a quiet competition between you. You both get better, and the coaches start scheduling you together.

choices.label: Keep your distance
choices.result: Polite distance. The specialists' room is awkward all season, and you notice how quiet it is when he's not there.

scenarios.title: The Film You Hate
scenarios.text: The coaches pull up your college film in a dark meeting room, and it looks completely different from how you remembered it: slower, stiffer, younger. Someone pauses on your worst kick.

authoring.premise: You watch your own college film with the coaches, and it looks different now.

choices.label: Write down every flaw
choices.result: Every flaw the coaches point out goes on a list. It's a long list, two pages, and you laminate it and keep it in your kicking bag all season.

choices.label: Fix one thing a week
choices.result: One flaw a week, fixed and charted. By midseason, the old film looks like someone else's, and {coach} uses it to teach the rookies.

choices.label: Call your college coach
choices.result: Your college coach watches the same film that night and calls back laughing: he always knew about the plant foot. You talk for an hour.

scenarios.title: Your Parents in the Stands
scenarios.text: {parent} drives eleven hours to see you kick in person for the first time as a pro. He arrives a day early, in his old team jacket, with a cooler of sandwiches.

authoring.premise: {parent} drives eleven hours to see you kick in person for the first time.

choices.label: Spend every minute together
choices.result: Every free minute, together: the hotel breakfast, the walk around the stadium, the sandwiches. He doesn't stop smiling all weekend.

choices.label: Give him the full tour
choices.result: The full tour: the locker room, the field, the coaches. He shakes {coach}'s hand twice and tells the equipment manager about your peewee days.

choices.label: Stick to game-week habits
choices.result: Your routine stays exactly the same, and you see him after. He understands completely, and you wish, driving home, that you'd done more.

scenarios.title: The Sibling Who Wants to Visit
scenarios.text: {sibling} wants to spend spring break at your apartment: a week of sleeping on your couch, eating your food and seeing what the league is like up close.

authoring.premise: {sibling} wants to spend his spring break at your apartment.

choices.label: Take him everywhere
choices.result: Everywhere, all week: practice, the team cafeteria, the stadium at night. {sibling} thinks you're the coolest person alive, and says so to everyone.

choices.label: Put him to work
choices.result: Your youth clinic gets a volunteer for a week, and {sibling} turns out to be great with the kids. You see him differently after it.

choices.label: Say not this year
choices.result: Not this spring, you explain; it's too busy. {sibling} is disappointed, goes to a friend's beach house instead, and sends you a photo of the ocean.

scenarios.title: The College Teammates' Chat
scenarios.text: Your old college teammates' group chat is on fire: everyone wants inside stories from the league. Who's mean, who's rich, who's actually funny. They're asking you by name.

authoring.premise: Your old college teammates' group chat wants inside stories.

choices.label: Tell the funny ones
choices.result: The funny stories, yes; the private ones, never. The chat loves you, and {best_friend} starts calling you 'the insider' in every single message.

choices.label: Keep the team private
choices.result: The team stays private, you explain. It's a little awkward, and it's right, and two old teammates respect it more than they say.

choices.label: Mute the chat
choices.result: Muted for the season. You miss some good jokes, and come back in January to four thousand messages and a nickname you'll never shake.

scenarios.title: The Old Flame
scenarios.text: Someone you dated in college messages you the week your first big headline runs. It's friendly, a little nostalgic, and it's the first time you've heard from them in two years.

authoring.premise: Someone from college messages you the week your first big headline runs.

choices.label: Meet for coffee
choices.result: Coffee, an hour that turns into three. It's warm and a little strange, you're glad you went, and you both leave it there.

choices.label: Ask yourself why now
choices.result: Why now? You don't answer it, even to yourself, and keep things friendly from a distance. The messages fade by the end of the month.

choices.label: Leave it on read
choices.result: Left on read. It's simpler, and on bad nights you wonder about it for a minute before you fall asleep.

scenarios.title: Your First Bad Practice Week
scenarios.text: Five bad practices in a row, and the coaches have stopped saying 'next one'. On the sixth day, nobody says anything at all, which is worse.

authoring.premise: Five bad practices in a row, and the coaches have stopped saying 'next one'.

choices.label: Strip it back with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} strips your routine back to the basics: three steps, one thought, no extras. It's humbling to start over, and by Thursday it works.

choices.label: Kick until it's back
choices.result: Every night, until the field lights come on, until it's back. Your leg is heavy, and the sixth bad practice never comes.

choices.label: Talk it through with {holder}
choices.result: {holder} has seen this before and says so over coffee: everybody hits the wall once. It helps more than the kicking.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Car
scenarios.text: A veteran tosses you his keys after practice and asks you to move his car. It costs more than your parents' house, it's parked on a slope, and it's raining.

authoring.premise: A veteran tosses you his keys and asks you to move his car, which costs more than your house back home.

choices.label: Move it very carefully
choices.result: Very, very carefully. He notices how carefully, and from then on he calls you by your name instead of 'kicker'.

choices.label: Ask what it cost him
choices.result: What did it cost, and would he do it again? His answer is long and honest, and it's about much more than the car.

choices.label: Hand the keys back
choices.result: Not comfortable driving it, you admit. He laughs, moves it himself in the rain and tells the story at lunch, kindly, with you as the sensible one.

scenarios.title: Learning to Cook
scenarios.text: Your first apartment, and your diet is cereal, takeout and whatever the team cafeteria sends home with you. The nutritionist has started looking at you sadly.

authoring.premise: Your first apartment, and your diet is cereal and takeout.

choices.label: Learn five meals
choices.result: Five meals, learned and cooked on rotation. Your energy in practice is better within a week, and you can make a very good omelet.

choices.label: Start a cooking night
choices.result: A Sunday cooking night with two rookies and {backup}. Everyone burns something, the fire alarm goes off twice, and nobody cares in the slightest.

choices.label: Sign up for a meal service
choices.result: A meal service, expensive and perfect. You never think about food again, never learn to cook, and the delivery driver knows your schedule better than you.

scenarios.title: The Team Nutritionist
scenarios.text: The team nutritionist reviews three days of what you've eaten, one page at a time, and doesn't hide her reaction to the gas station burritos.

authoring.premise: The team nutritionist reviews what you eat and doesn't hide her reaction.

choices.label: Follow her plan
choices.result: Her plan, to the letter. You feel better by week two, and she puts a gold star on your locker, which you pretend to hate.

choices.label: Ask for a kicking plan
choices.result: A plan built for kicking power, strict and specific. It's hard to follow and it works, and your leg feels heavier in a good way.

choices.label: Change breakfast
choices.result: Breakfast, and only breakfast, for now. It's a start, she says, and she means it kindly, and you notice the difference by Friday practice.

scenarios.title: The Sleep Study
scenarios.text: The club puts every rookie through a sleep study, and your results are embarrassing: five hours a night, phone in your hand until two, a bedtime that moves around like the wind.

authoring.premise: The club puts every rookie through a sleep study, and the results are embarrassing.

choices.label: Fix your sleep
choices.result: Every recommendation: a dark room, no phone, the same bedtime. Your practices improve within two weeks, and you dream again.

choices.label: Just go to bed earlier
choices.result: An hour earlier, nothing fancier. It helps a lot, and your phone still comes to bed with you, which the sleep coach pretends not to know.

choices.label: Compare results at lunch
choices.result: Everyone's results are terrible, it turns out. You laugh about it for a week, and the rookies start a 'lights out by ten' bet for push-ups.

scenarios.title: The Team Psychologist
scenarios.text: The club's team psychologist stops you in the hallway and offers you a standing Tuesday appointment. No pressure, they say; most of the veterans have one.

authoring.premise: The club's sports psychologist offers you a standing Tuesday appointment.

choices.label: Take the Tuesday slot
choices.result: Tuesdays at two, every week. Some weeks you talk about kicking; most weeks you talk about everything else, and that's the point.

choices.label: Say you're fine
choices.result: Fine, you say, and you are, mostly. The psychologist leaves the door open with a small nod, and the Tuesday slot stays empty for weeks.

choices.label: Build a routine with them
choices.result: The sessions become a workshop for your pre-kick routine: breath, count, one thought. It's the best thing you do all year.

choices.label: Pick up where you left off
choices.result: What worked in college goes straight to the psychologist in the first session, so the two of you skip a month of getting to know each other.
choices.lock_text: having worked with a sports psychologist in college

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Doesn't Make It
scenarios.text: The rookie you came in with is released after his first season. By noon his locker is empty, his nameplate is in the trash, and his parking spot already has someone else's car in it.

authoring.premise: The rookie you came in with is released after his first season.

choices.label: Help him pack
choices.result: His things, carried to the car with you. He thanks you for being the only one who came, and you both pretend not to be upset.

choices.label: Kick harder
choices.result: Harder than you've kicked all year, that afternoon, alone on the far field. The empty locker is still there in the morning when you come in.

choices.label: Ask your agent what would have saved him
choices.result: What could have saved him? Your agent's answer is a list: the weight room, the meetings, the attitude. You take every item seriously.

scenarios.title: The Practice-Field Fan
scenarios.text: A kid watches every practice from behind the fence with a cardboard sign that has your name on it, spelled almost right. He's been there every day for two weeks.

authoring.premise: A kid watches every practice from behind the fence and holds up a sign with your name.

choices.label: Go sign the sign
choices.result: Over to the fence after practice, and you sign the sign, fixing the spelling. He's there every day after that, beaming.

choices.label: Get him onto the field
choices.result: One kick on the real field, arranged with the club. He talks about it for years, and so do his parents.

choices.label: Wave every day
choices.result: A wave, every day, and you keep walking. He waves back every day with the whole sign, and by October the sign is spelled right.

scenarios.title: Kicks for the Hospital
scenarios.text: The club runs a kick-a-thon for the children's hospital, and you're the main event: a donation for every kick you make in an hour, with the patients watching from the sideline.

authoring.premise: The club runs a kick-a-thon for a children's hospital, and you're the main event.

choices.label: Kick for the full hour
choices.result: A full hour without stopping. Your leg is jelly, and the total is the biggest the hospital has ever seen.

choices.label: Let the kids kick too
choices.result: Every kid gets a turn at the tee. The donations drop a little; the photos are the best of the year, and a nurse cries.

choices.label: Recruit the specialists
choices.result: The punter, the snapper and {holder} join in, and it turns into a contest. The crowd doubles, and so does the total.

scenarios.title: The Night Before Your Debut
scenarios.text: The night before your first regular-season game, and your phone won't stop: old coaches, cousins, a girl from your third-grade class. It's ten o'clock and you're wide awake.

authoring.premise: The night before your first regular-season game, and your phone won't stop buzzing.

choices.label: Phone off, early night
choices.result: The phone goes in a drawer at eight, and you read until you fall asleep. Nobody's message is more important than the morning.

choices.label: Answer two people
choices.result: {parent} and {best_friend}, nobody else. Their messages are the right ones, and you fall asleep with the phone on your chest.

choices.label: One more look at the plan
choices.result: The special teams plan, once more, then sleep. You walk in calm, and {coach} notices you're the only rookie not pacing.

scenarios.title: The Debut Week Interview
scenarios.text: The national broadcast crew wants five minutes with the rookie kicker before your first game. The producer has a clipboard and very specific ideas about your 'story'.

authoring.premise: The national broadcast crew wants five minutes with the rookie kicker.

choices.label: Tell your real story
choices.result: Kicking in the backyard with {parent}, into a fence with a hole in it. It makes the broadcast, and {parent} watches it forty times.

choices.label: Keep it to football
choices.result: Football only, short and polite. The crew thanks you, nothing makes air, you're secretly glad, and {parent} is quietly disappointed for a day.

choices.label: Talk about the unit
choices.result: The snapper and {holder}, mostly, and how a kick is really three people. The specialists' chat is very happy, and {holder} pretends to be annoyed.

scenarios.title: The Team Photo
scenarios.text: The team photo, and you're in the back row next to a lineman who has never learned your name. He calls you 'kick' and asks which number you are.

authoring.premise: The team photo, and you're in the back row next to a lineman who's never learned your name.

choices.label: Introduce yourself again
choices.result: Your name, again, with a handshake. He laughs, and from then on he calls you by name, loudly, across the cafeteria.

choices.label: Smile for the flash
choices.result: A smile, the flash, and back to the locker room. You're the blurry one in the corner of the framed print.

choices.label: Organize a specialists' photo
choices.result: A specialists-only photo afterward, organized by you. It ends up framed in the facility hallway, and {holder} puts a copy on their fridge.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Payday Dinner
scenarios.text: Your rookie class decides to celebrate your first full paychecks together at a restaurant you can't pronounce, with a menu that doesn't have prices on it.

authoring.premise: Your rookie class decides to celebrate your first full paycheck together.

choices.label: Go and enjoy it
choices.result: The whole night, every course. The bill is absurd, the night is worth it, and you all take a photo with the chef.

choices.label: Suggest a cheaper place
choices.result: A cheaper place with the same view, you suggest. Half the class comes, the rest think you're cheap, and your half has more fun.

choices.label: Order in
choices.result: Takeout, alone, on the couch. Your account is happier than you are, and you see the photos the next morning.

scenarios.title: The Trainer's Warning
scenarios.text: A trainer stops you in the hallway and quietly warns you about the supplements a veteran keeps recommending to the rookies. Some of them, the trainer says, aren't on the approved list.

authoring.premise: A trainer warns you about the supplements a veteran keeps recommending.

choices.label: Make a rule for yourself
choices.result: A rule, made that night: nothing the club hasn't approved, ever. You sleep better knowing it, and the trainer notices.

choices.label: Warn the other rookies
choices.result: The other rookies hear exactly what the trainer said, from you. Two of them throw theirs out that night, and one of them thanks you a year later.

choices.label: Let the veterans sort it out
choices.result: Not your business, you decide, and you never ask what the others are taking. You're fine. You're not sure all of them are.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Talks Too Much
scenarios.text: A rookie in your class keeps posting locker-room jokes online: who fell asleep in meetings, who cried at a movie on the plane. The veterans are getting angry, and they've noticed you sit with him.

authoring.premise: A rookie in your class keeps leaking locker room jokes online.

choices.label: Talk to him privately
choices.result: A quiet word in the parking lot. He genuinely didn't know it was a big deal, deletes four posts on the spot and buys the veterans breakfast on Friday.

choices.label: Let a veteran handle it
choices.result: A veteran you trust hears it from you, and handles it better than you could have: one sentence in the weight room, and the posts stop.

choices.label: Let him learn the hard way
choices.result: Not your fight, you decide. The veterans handle it loudly, with a whole-team meeting, and the rookie doesn't speak to anyone for a week.

scenarios.title: The Specialist Meeting Room
scenarios.text: The specialists' meeting room is the size of a closet, with a broken projector, one working outlet and a mop bucket nobody has moved since September. Three of you share it every morning.

authoring.premise: The specialists' meeting room is the size of a closet, and three of you share it.

choices.label: Ask for a real room
choices.result: The operations staff gets a polite, specific request from you, with a floor plan. You get a real room by Monday, and the punter calls you a hero for a month.

choices.label: Make the closet great
choices.result: Snacks, a better extension cord and a lamp from home. The closet becomes the best room in the building, and the linebackers start asking to visit.

choices.label: Use the film room at night
choices.result: The main film room after hours, empty and quiet. You learn more alone there in a week than in a month of closet mornings.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Bus
scenarios.text: After a road practice you get on the wrong team bus, fall asleep, and wake up alone at the airport cargo terminal. Your phone is at four percent, and the team plane leaves in three hours.

authoring.premise: You get on the wrong team bus after a road practice and end up at the airport alone.

choices.label: Post it in the group chat
choices.result: A photo of you alone at the cargo terminal goes to the group chat. The nickname 'Freight' sticks for a whole season, and you secretly love it.

choices.label: Call the travel staff
choices.result: Four percent is enough for one call to the travel staff, who send a car. You're back before anyone notices, except the travel director, who never forgets.

choices.label: Wait with a book
choices.result: Three hours with a paperback and a vending-machine dinner until the team arrives. Nobody believes your story, and the snapper still brings it up.

scenarios.title: Your First Billboard
scenarios.text: Your face goes up on a billboard by the highway for a local bank, forty feet wide, smiling a smile you don't remember making. You drive past it twice on the way to practice.

authoring.premise: Your face goes up on a billboard by the highway, and you drive past it twice.

choices.label: Send a photo home
choices.result: A photo from the shoulder goes to {parent}, who drives three hours just to stand under it and take his own. He frames it for the hallway.

choices.label: Take a different road
choices.result: A different route to practice, every day. It's too strange to look at your own face that big, and you feel silly about it.

choices.label: Earn the billboard
choices.result: Billboards are for people who've earned them, you decide, and you kick an extra hundred balls that week to start.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Retirement Party
scenarios.text: A veteran you barely know is retiring after eleven seasons, and the whole team is expected at the party in a hotel ballroom. He has never said more than three words to you.

authoring.premise: A veteran you barely know retires, and you're expected at the party.

choices.label: Listen to the stories
choices.result: An evening of stories at the back table: the old coaches, the cut days, the plays nobody filmed. You learn more about the league in one night than in a month.

choices.label: Stop by briefly
choices.result: Half an hour, a handshake and a congratulations. He remembers your name, which surprises you both, and you're home by nine.

choices.label: Toast for the rookies
choices.result: A short toast on behalf of the rookies, written on a napkin at the table. The veteran shakes your hand for a long time afterward.

scenarios.title: The Mentor Who Leaves
scenarios.text: The veteran who took you under his wing in camp is traded on a Tuesday night. By Wednesday morning his locker is empty and his name is off the parking spot.

authoring.premise: The veteran who took you under his wing is traded to another club.

choices.label: Help him pack the car
choices.result: His car, packed at midnight, with you carrying the heavy boxes. You keep in touch every week, and he texts you after every one of your games.

choices.label: Take his place in the room
choices.result: For the next rookie, you start doing exactly what he did for you: lunch, film, the long talks. It's the best way to thank him.

choices.label: Kick the sting out
choices.result: The sting goes into extra work that afternoon. It helps, a little, and you still look at his empty locker every morning.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Other Rookies
scenarios.text: Your agent has four rookie clients, and from how long your calls take to be returned, you can tell you're fourth. The last text you got was a thumbs-up to a question.

authoring.premise: Your agent has four rookie clients, and you can tell you're fourth.

choices.label: Ask for a written plan
choices.result: A written plan and a monthly call, requested politely and firmly. You get both, and your agent starts calling first.

choices.label: Be impossible to ignore
choices.result: The client who's impossible to ignore, that's the plan, and you kick like it all month. Your agent calls in October to say the club asked about you.

choices.label: Let it ride
choices.result: Rookie contracts are fixed anyway, you reason, and let it ride. It's fine for now, and you wonder about next year.

scenarios.title: The Practice Squad Promotion
scenarios.text: {backup}, your friend from the practice squad, is promoted to the active roster on Thursday. They find out in the hallway and call you before they call home.

authoring.premise: A friend from the practice squad is promoted to the active roster.

choices.label: Take them to dinner
choices.result: Dinner, your treat, at the place with the good steaks. {backup} cries at the table, and so do you, a little, into your water.

choices.label: Introduce them around
choices.result: Every veteran you know, introduced by name. {backup} fits in by the end of the week, and the room starts calling you two a package deal.

choices.label: Text congratulations
choices.result: A congratulations text, and an early night. {backup} replies with eleven exclamation points and a photo of the new locker, and doesn't sleep at all.

scenarios.title: The Bad Haircut
scenarios.text: The rookies get haircuts from the veterans, whether they want them or not. There's a folding chair in the middle of the locker room, a pair of clippers and a line.

authoring.premise: The rookies get haircuts from the veterans, whether they want them or not.

choices.label: Volunteer to go first
choices.result: First in the chair, by choice. It's terrible, a stripe down the middle, and you wear it proudly for a month while the veterans take photos.

choices.label: Negotiate a better cut
choices.result: A less terrible haircut, negotiated in exchange for carrying the pads for a week. The veterans respect the deal more than the hair.

choices.label: Hide in the training room
choices.result: The training room, behind the cold tub. They find you anyway in ten minutes, and your haircut is worse for the delay.

scenarios.title: The Family Group Chat
scenarios.text: Your family group chat has become a running commentary on your career, including every miss in every practice clip anyone posts, with {parent} giving technical notes.

authoring.premise: Your family group chat has become a running commentary on your career.

choices.label: Roast yourself first
choices.result: You join in and roast yourself before anyone else can. The chat becomes the best part of your week, and {sibling} makes you a highlight reel of your worst kicks.

choices.label: Set one rule
choices.result: One rule for the chat: no football after nine. Everyone sleeps better, and {parent} breaks it exactly once, for a good reason.

choices.label: Mute it for the season
choices.result: Muted until the season ends. {parent} is offended for a week and then sends you a long letter, on paper.

scenarios.title: The Fantasy Football Message
scenarios.text: A stranger messages you at midnight about his fantasy team. He is very angry that you only kicked one field goal, and he has a lot of opinions about your hips.

authoring.premise: A stranger messages you about his fantasy team, and he's angry.

choices.label: Reply with a joke
choices.result: A reply: you'll try harder for his team specifically. He becomes your biggest fan, buys your jersey and sends you a photo in it.

choices.label: Leave it unanswered
choices.result: Unanswered, and there will be more. You go to sleep, and he messages twice more before morning, then never again.

choices.label: Block strangers' messages
choices.result: Blocked, and messages from strangers turned off entirely. Your phone goes quiet at night for the first time since the draft.

scenarios.title: Your First Credit Card Bill
scenarios.text: Your first credit card statement as a pro arrives, four pages long, and you don't remember half the charges. One of them is a subscription to a magazine about boats.

authoring.premise: Your first credit card statement as a pro, and you don't remember half the charges.

choices.label: Go through every line
choices.result: Every line, with a highlighter, at the kitchen table. Four subscriptions canceled, including the boat magazine, which you still don't remember ordering.

choices.label: Pay it and forget it
choices.result: Paid in full, and forgotten. The same thing happens next month, and the month after, with slightly different boats, and you stop opening the envelopes.

choices.label: Ask a veteran at lunch
choices.result: A veteran at lunch shows you the app he uses and his worst statement ever, which makes yours look like a grocery list. You laugh until it hurts.

scenarios.title: The Gym Membership
scenarios.text: A fancy downtown gym offers you a free membership if you post about it twice a month. It has cold plunges, a juice bar and a kicking net on the roof.

authoring.premise: A fancy gym offers you a free membership if you post about it.

choices.label: Take it and train there
choices.result: Accepted, posted twice, and you train there all offseason. The equipment is incredible, and the rooftop net has a view of the whole city.

choices.label: Stay with the club's staff
choices.result: The club's facility, where the staff knows your body. It's less glamorous, and nobody there asks you to post anything.

choices.label: Get the rookies in too
choices.result: The rookie class gets memberships too, at your request. You all train there together, and the juice bar never recovers.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Coach From College
scenarios.text: Your college kicking coach calls: he'll be in town next week and wants to come watch a practice. He's the one who taught you everything, and he hasn't seen you kick in a year.

authoring.premise: Your college kicking coach wants to come watch a practice.

choices.label: Get him a pass
choices.result: A pass, a seat by the field, and he watches every single kick. His notes run three pages, and one of them fixes your short game.

choices.label: Send him film instead
choices.result: Film sent by email, and his notes come back by morning, just as sharp. He signs off 'proud of you', which you read twice.

choices.label: Not this season
choices.result: This season isn't a good time, you explain. He understands completely, and you feel bad about it every time you see a whistle.

scenarios.title: The Cold-Weather City
scenarios.text: Your first winter in a cold-weather city. It's nine degrees at practice, the ball feels like a rock, and the veterans are wearing shorts to prove a point.

authoring.premise: Your first winter in a cold-weather city, and the ball feels like a rock.

choices.label: Kick outside every day
choices.result: Outside every day, whatever the temperature. By December you've stopped noticing the cold, and the ball stops feeling like a rock.

choices.label: Learn the equipment tricks
choices.result: How do they keep balls warm on the sideline? The equipment staff shows you every trick, legal and almost-legal, over hot chocolate.

choices.label: Build a warm-up routine
choices.result: A warm-up routine that keeps your leg loose between kicks: bands, a heated bench, two layers you can strip off. It's half the battle.

scenarios.title: The Hot-Weather Road Game
scenarios.text: A road game in a city where it's ninety degrees in December. The practice field is shimmering, the trainers are handing out salt tablets, and your cleats are sticking to the turf.

authoring.premise: A road game in a city where it's ninety degrees in December.

choices.label: Follow the hydration plan
choices.result: The trainer's hydration plan, to the letter, down to the ounce. You feel great all week while two linemen end up on IVs.

choices.label: Save your energy
choices.result: Every ounce of energy, saved: shade between drills, no extra kicks, a cold towel on your neck. You're fresh on game day.

choices.label: Kick in the heat
choices.result: Midday kicks, on purpose, to get used to it. You're exhausted, and your leg knows exactly how the ball flies in thick air.

scenarios.title: The Long Flight
scenarios.text: A five-hour flight to a road game, and the veterans play cards the whole way in the back, loudly, with a scoreboard taped to a seat.

authoring.premise: A five-hour flight to a road game, and the veterans play cards the whole way.

choices.label: Watch and learn the game
choices.result: Watching, then learning the rules, then playing for matchsticks. By landing you know every veteran's story and lose very gracefully.

choices.label: Sleep all five hours
choices.result: Eye mask, earplugs and five hours of real sleep. You land fresh and rested, and the card players land looking like they've been through a war.

choices.label: Learn the stadium
choices.result: The scouting report, twice, and the stadium's wind charts. You know every flag on that field before the wheels touch down, and {coach} quizzes you on the bus.

scenarios.title: The Jersey Number
scenarios.text: You don't get the number you wore in college: a veteran linebacker has it, and he's had it for eight years. The equipment manager hands you a list of what's left.

authoring.premise: You don't get the number you wore in college, and someone else wants it anyway.

choices.label: Pick a new one and let it go
choices.result: A new number, no fuss. The linebacker hears about it and thanks you, and gives you his old practice jersey as a joke.

choices.label: Pick a number with meaning
choices.result: Your birthday, from the list. It feels strange for a month and like yours by October, and {parent} buys the jersey first.

choices.label: Make the new number famous
choices.result: The new number is going to mean something, you decide, and you write it on your kicking tee. Every practice feels like a down payment.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Quiz
scenarios.text: The coaches give the rookies a written quiz on the club's history: championships, legends, the year the stadium roof blew off. It's Friday, and nobody told you there'd be a quiz.

authoring.premise: The coaches give the rookies a quiz on the club's history.

choices.label: Study all week
choices.result: The club's history, studied every night. You ace the quiz, and the coaches start telling you stories nobody else gets.

choices.label: Study in a group
choices.result: A study group in the hotel lounge, with flashcards and pizza. Everyone passes, and the rookie class has its first inside joke.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.result: Winged, and half right. The veterans laugh at your answer about the stadium roof for the rest of the season, and you laugh with them.

scenarios.title: The Holiday Away From Home
scenarios.text: Your first holiday away from your family: a hotel near the stadium, a room-service menu and a phone full of photos from the dinner table at home.

authoring.premise: Your first holiday away from family, in a hotel near the stadium.

choices.label: Join dinner by video
choices.result: A video call into the family dinner, propped up on the table between the potatoes. It's silly and wonderful, and {sibling} feeds the phone a bite.

choices.label: Gather the stranded rookies
choices.result: The rookies who can't go home, gathered in the hotel restaurant for a long dinner. It becomes a tradition, and you run it every year after.

choices.label: Rest and watch movies
choices.result: Room service and three movies in a row. It's quiet and restful and a little sad, and you call home twice.

scenarios.title: The Team Thanksgiving
scenarios.text: A veteran and his family host a holiday dinner for the young players who can't go home: long tables in his backyard, his grandmother's recipes, and kids running everywhere.

authoring.premise: The veterans host a holiday dinner for the young players who can't go home.

choices.label: Go early and help cook
choices.result: Early, with an apron. The veteran's grandmother adopts you for the night, teaches you her stuffing and sends you home with leftovers.

choices.label: Eat and go home happy
choices.result: Dinner, far too much of it, and home happy by nine. It's the best meal you've had since camp, and you sleep like a stone.

choices.label: Bring a dish from home
choices.result: {parent}'s recipe, cooked badly, and the story behind it. The table goes quiet while you tell it, and somebody asks for seconds.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Baby
scenarios.text: A teammate's baby is born on a game week, in the middle of the night, and the whole locker room is celebrating with a cake shaped like a football and a banner made of tape.

authoring.premise: A teammate's baby is born on a game week, and the whole locker room celebrates.

choices.label: Organize a team gift
choices.result: A team gift, organized by you: a tiny jersey with every player's signature. The teammate tears up at his locker and can't speak.

choices.label: Congratulate him and work
choices.result: A congratulations and a hug, then back to your routine. He's grateful, and he's not thinking about anyone's routine this week.

choices.label: Cover his meeting notes
choices.result: His special teams meeting notes, covered by you all week, so he can stay home. He comes back to a binder with his name on it.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Year Review
scenarios.text: {coach} closes the office door and sits you down for an honest review of your first season: a folder of charts, a laptop of clips, and a list that starts with the word 'concerns'.

authoring.premise: {coach} sits you down for an honest review of your first season.
